title: AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them
body_text: AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them. Observability Real Talk Subscribe Sign in AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them. When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters? Elizabeth Feb 28, 2026 22 5 3 Share 💌 Hey there, it’s Elizabeth from SigNoz! This newsletter is a n honest attempt to talk about all things - observability, OpenTelemetry, open-source and the engineering in between! & This piece took 6 days, 5 hours to be cooked, hope we served. 🌚 Subscribe There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days. The first says SRE is the future of all software engineering , that as AI writes more and more code, the humans who remain will be the ones keeping systems alive. The second says AI will devour every tech job alive, SREs included. Neither is particularly useful if you’re an SRE trying to figure out what your Tuesday will look like in 2027. Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters? Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient. The Ironies of Automation: Part-I Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉). In 1983, a cognitive psychologist named Lisanne Bainbridge published a paper called Ironies of Automation . It became one of the most cited papers in human factors research, and its core argument is almost uncomfortably relevant today. Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for. Ring any bells yet? 🙂 Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems. The exact problems that require deep expertise , the exact expertise that atrophies when you stop practising. Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing. Current State of AI in SRE Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering. What’s already automated or heavily AI-assisted? Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today. What’s on the horizon? Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks. PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model. Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated. Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems receive AI recommendations with human validation. Tier 3 incidents: Novel, complex, cascading failures stay human-led, with AI providing supporting context. But here’s the catch. If human SREs (okay, now we have to use adjectives like human 🥹) only engage with Tier 3 incidents, i.e. the novel, never-before-seen outages, where do they build the intuition to handle them? Intuition is usually developed from years of hands-on incident response, pattern recognition built through repetition, and the kind of gut-level understanding of a system that only develops from painfully waking up at the odd hour to solve the bug that brought the system down. Subscribe if you wish to read some more hot takes. We are cooking some great ones! Subscribe The Crisis of Deskilling This is where the picture starts getting blurry. Let’s look at some emerging research on AI-induced deskilling across multiple fields, which paints a consistent and concerning picture. In medicine, a recent study found that endoscopists who used AI assistance for polyp detection saw their unassisted detection rates drop from 28% to 22% after a period of AI use. They got worse at the thing they were supposed to be experts in, not because they forgot the theory, but because they stopped exercising the skill. In aviation, research has shown that long-haul pilots who rely heavily on autopilot systems experience measurable degradation in situational awareness and manual flying ability. The problem got serious enough that the FAA now mandates more manual flying time to counteract the effect. Somewhere over the past year, AI stopped being a tool I occasionally reached for and became the first thing I reach for, always . My instinct now is to offload as much as possible and apply my own thinking only where it’s absolutely unavoidable. The problem is that these moments are becoming the only exercises my brain gets, and I can feel the rust . We can draw a pattern here. The more you let the system handle, the worse you get at handling things yourself and here’s the truly dangerous part, you don’t feel it happening . It gets masked as hyper-productivity. Cognitive research suggests that because AI tools make tasks feel easier and enhance visible performance, users are often unable to accurately judge the true status of their own skills. You feel competent, dashboards look green, and then on a Wednesday, a novel incident hits that doesn’t match any pattern the AI has seen, and you realise the muscle has atrophied. For SREs, this manifests in specific ways, like we stop reading raw log streams because the AI summarises them, we stop forming hypotheses during incidents because the AI suggests root causes, we stop building mental models of system architecture because the AI maps dependencies for us, and each of these individually looks like a productivity win. Collectively, they hollow out the very expertise that makes an SRE effective when things go sideways in ways nobody anticipated. But there’s something even more concerning than deskilling, and researchers have started calling it never-skilling . Deskilling means you once had a capability but have since lost it. Never-skilling means you never developed it in the first place. For junior SREs entering the field today in an environment where AI handles most of the incident response workflow, the opportunities to build foundational intuition and muscle through hands-on practice are vanishing. The training pipeline itself is broken and not self-healing . SREs realise their skills are degrading and lean more on AI to compensate, which further degrades their skills, creating a vicious cycle from which escape is difficult. What Can We Do About It? We are definitely not rejecting AI tooling; we are adopting it and integrating it stronger than ever before, because that’s the only way forward. A few approaches worth considering: Deliberate inefficiency. Just as the FAA mandates manual flying time even when the autopilot is perfectly capable, SRE teams can designate certain incidents, even the ones the AI could handle, as human-practice opportunities . This can be considered as a long-term investment to keep skills fresh, although it might come at the cost of a super-fast solution Build for human-in-the-loop, not human-on-the-side. There’s a meaningful difference between a system where a human approves an AI’s recommendation and one where a human actively engages with the problem alongside AI. The former keeps humans in a supervisory role that Bainbridge (the lady who wrote that research paper about 40 years ago) showed leads to vigilance decay, and the latter keeps them cognitively engaged. Let’s zoom out and take a look at the bigger picture. The Bigger Picture Everything we’ve discussed here, the ironies of automation, the deskilling risk, the never-skilling problem, collectively applies well beyond SRE. Software engineering as a whole is navigating the same tension. As AI writes more code, reviews more PRs, and handles more debugging, the same questions apply. We’re talking about SREs specifically because that’s the world we live in at SigNoz . We build an open-source observability platform, the kind of tool that gives SREs the metrics, traces, and logs they need to understand their systems deeply. For us, this deskilling question is not a rhetorical fad; it directly shapes how we’re building AI into our product. Our approach is to start with an AI assistant that helps SREs leverage the power of LLMs while keeping humans firmly in control. Eventually, we’ll enable more autonomy but within clear guardrails, and only as trust is earned. One advantage we have in this space is that, as an observability platform, we sit on the data itself, the metrics, traces, and logs that SREs rely on. Most AI SRE products today integrate with observability tools through APIs, which means they’re working with a limited, second-hand view of your systems. Because we own the data layer, we can build much deeper, more context-aware AI capabilities that understand your system the way an experienced SRE would. And to answer the burning question in your head, our goal isn’t AI that replaces SREs. It’s AI that supercharges SREs. Unlike ongoing lore, we believe humans will remain essential for the decisions that matter most, especially those that impact production infrastructure. The future of SRE is human with AI intentionally designed to keep humans sharp, engaged, and ready for the 5% that really counts. Here’s the LinkedIn post our founder posted a few days ago, which inspired me to write this. Thanks for reading Observability Real Talk! Subscribe if you wish to read more hot takes. We are cooking some great ones! Subscribe 22 5 3 Share Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Tim 6h The US navy also went through this 50+ years ago. They had the ability to automate nearly everything, but the admiral in charge of the project wisely said that a machine could suggest what to do, but there must always be a human in the loop to actually carry out the action, or we would lose our ability when the machines failed. Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) Built for Coders, Trusted by Defenders. Back to Blog Share this post Copy url to clipboard Copied Thinking Summary Mistral released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model, now available with improved coding, cybersecurity, and reasoning efficiency. It leads open-weight benchmarks in coding and defensive security while offering three reasoning modes for cost-performance balance. Fully open-weight and European-trained, it empowers sovereign AI with customizable, self-hosted deployment options. We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity. Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback. Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in coding and defensive cybersecurity . Gains continue to accelerate, with no signs of saturation. Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4. The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs. Mistral Large 4 ranks as the best open-weight model for coding and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AI Mistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We're committed to building the world's most capable models and releasing them openly, giving developers, enterprises, and institutions the power to own, customize, and control their AI. Built for the Builders. Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency. On Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, which assesses end-to-end code quality and whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change, Mistral Large 4 leads with a score of 19.7%. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average. Built for the Defenders. Since its preview, we've been working with leading cybersecurity vendors to evaluate Mistral Large 4 in real-world environments to test Mistral Large 4’s strengths in vulnerability reproduction and patching. Mistral Large 4 scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures a model’s ability to discover vulnerabilities in a codebase, reproduce and validate them, and patch them without breaking existing functionality. And, Mistral's support for model customization and data-sovereign deployment also lets us tailor it for our mission needs and client environments with strict data-residency requirements. We look forward to working with Mistral to strengthen critical infrastructure around the globe. Brad Medairy, President National Cyber at Booz Allen Hamilton Organizations that treat transparency and openness as strengths are positioned well as AI becomes central to security operations. Open-weight cybersecurity models extend that transparency to enterprises and governments that need to host and customize AI under their own control, and they allow researchers to study how these models behave, including where they could be misused. As adversaries increasingly use AI to accelerate their operations, we aim to work alongside model developers such as Mistral to help security teams build on that control, establishing a foundation for resilience by design rather than reactive threat management. Worse, a defense you don’t control isn’t defense—it’s exposure. Security teams perform best when they take the steering wheel. Mistral's ML4 lets defenders audit the architecture, deploy on their own infrastructure, and keep full sovereignty. Resilience starts with autonomy, and open-weight models help give organizations the control to lead their own defense." Stephanie Cohen, Chief Strategy Officer at Cloudflare Powerful AI models alone won't tip the scales in cybersecurity. It takes deep security expertise, real-world threat intelligence, and rigorous testing. Our work with Mistral Large 4 tests how well frontier AI can reason through complex vulnerabilities, accelerate remediation, and ensure defenders move faster than adversaries. Dr. Bartley Richardson, Chief AI and Autonomous Systems Officer, CrowdStrike Elastic gives security teams the freedom to bring the AI they trust to the data they control, including Mistral’s open models, which are supported on Elastic Security today. We’ve already evaluated ML4 against real cybersecurity workloads, where models need to reason across complex data to help analysts make informed investigation and response decisions. This demonstrates the partnerships we are building to deliver powerful, open-weight models combined with the security context, transparency and control our customers demand. James Spiteri, Senior Director, Product Management, Elastic ENISA is experimenting with closed and open weight models in order to better understand their cyber capabilities. Open-weight models allow organisations to keep control of the technology their resilience depends on. ENISA access to and are testing Mistral Large 4 to identify security vulnerabilities, to audit code and analyse defensive logs. Laura Heuvinck, Head of Communications of ENISA We believe open-weight AI models have an important role to play in advancing cybersecurity by giving organizations greater flexibility, choice, and control. Innovations like Mistral Large 4 represent promising steps forward in AI's potential to transform cyber defense. We see continued AI innovation as an important opportunity to strengthen cybersecurity and help organizations navigate an evolving threat landscape. John Whittle, Chief Operating Officer at Fortinet Open models let security researchers and developers inspect, adapt and build on AI. Mistral is expanding what the ecosystem can build, and our collaboration on NVIDIA accelerated infrastructure helps developers put these models to work. Kari Briski, VP of Open Models and Software, NVIDIA As threats become ever faster, industrialized and now automated, defense must operate at a different scale. Volume, speed, trust: these are the three challenges facing cybersecurity in the age of AI. With Mistral AI, we are building European cyber AI, trained by our experts and operated under their control. By combining the power of AI, the expertise of our teams and our Cyber Threat Intelligence, we are accelerating our response so that we can protect more broadly, more quickly and with trusted European technology. Hugues Foulon, CEO of Orange Cyberdefense Rubrik supports Mistral and the push for ‘sovereign AI,’ to give European governments and regulated industries a credible option that does not route their data to other countries. Customers want model choices, including open-weight and private models, to support data residency, latency, cost and capability requirements. As part of our focus to deliver cyber resilience and speed recovery from both AI-powered attacks outside an organization and internal agents, we’ll continue rigorous cybersecurity testing with Mistral Large 4 and work closely together to serve evolving regional demands. Anneka Gupta, Chief Product Officer of Rubrik. As enterprises bring AI into production, they increasingly want models they can run on their own terms, with clear visibility into model behavior, data access, and agent permissions. Mistral Large 4 brings strong cybersecurity and technical reasoning to open weight AI, and many European enterprises are already embracing it as their sovereign model of choice. Zscaler Security for AI offerings, delivered on our sovereign Zero Trust Exchange in Europe, now integrate with Mistral, helping organizations continuously test their AI deployments, map what every model and agent can reach, and enforce policy inline. Together, we are empowering enterprises to adopt sovereign AI with the visibility, control, and data protection they need to innovate securely. Dhawal Sharma, EVP of AI and Data Security, Zscaler In the time since the preview, we carefully monitored cybersecurity-related use in our live traffic. Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks. We are modifying our guardrails accordingly, and will continue updating them in the months to come. We are also providing enterprise design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense, with preview access to a specialized variant of Mistral Large 4 optimized for advanced cybersecurity workflows, including penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming. Access is subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards, with testing restricted to owned or explicitly authorized systems in controlled environments. Meanwhile, customers are tailoring Mistral Large 4 with proprietary security data, policies, detection logic, and threat environments using Mistral Forge . For well-defined cybersecurity tasks, it can be further optimized into smaller, task-specific variants for greater accuracy, making security applications more effective. Learn more about sovereign AI for cybersecurity and how to work with us. Built for Work. Mistral Large 4 has continued improving on a range of broad enterprise-use metrics. For finance-related work , we improved the model’s ability to perform real-world workflows, especially ones involving the creation and editing of spreadsheets for finance and accounting use cases. Mistral’s commitment to continued innovation supports our efforts to accelerate the application of AI throughout our semiconductor product lifecycle. Arnaud Hubaux, Head of AI Program and Strategy. Mistral Large 4 is an important step forward for financial‑grade AI: an open‑weight model we can fine‑tune to our needs, deploy on our own infrastructure and closely integrate into our digital channels. Nicolas Goosse, Head of Data Insights, Analytics & AI at Belfius Mastering our AI begins with mastering its architecture and data. For the most sensitive use cases, having access to European open-weight models, which we can deploy on our own infrastructure, is a vital lever for strengthening our strategic autonomy and the resilience of our organizations. The industrial partnership between Crédit Agricole Artificial Intelligence and Mistral addresses these challenges at the Group level. Mistral Large 4 brings powerful capabilities in coding, multimodal AI, and cybersecurity into the open, giving developers, companies, and countries a great open foundation to build their own AI and defend themselves against cyber threats. Jeff Boudier, VP Product, Hugging Face A powerful model is only part of the equation. Developers also need the freedom to decide where it runs, how it is optimized, and how it fits into their systems. We’re excited about Mistral Large 4 because open weights give builders more control over those decisions, rather than making them dependent on a single hosted service. At ZML, we see that freedom as essential to turning advances in AI into useful, deployable software. Steeve Morin, CEO of ZML Sovereignty does not always require self-hosting; sometimes it just requires deployments that meet your control requirements. For organizations that prefer a managed service, Mistral Large 4 is available through Microsoft Foundry, with private deployment options for Azure developers. Microsoft and Mistral AI share a commitment to expanding customer choice in next-generation AI. As the first cloud provider to bring Mistral Large 4 to customers, Microsoft is making Mistral’s latest open-weight model available through Microsoft Foundry, an enterprise AI platform built for evaluating, deploying, and operating models at scale. For organizations advancing sovereign AI strategies, this combination offers greater flexibility and control across their data, infrastructure, and AI operations. title: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
body_text: Agents in Games · Labs Home Projects QM Contact Agents in Games Minecraft Civ50 Bed Wars Mindustry The setup What we saw Funny bloopers Run your own swarm Open questions Agents in Games October 2026 Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice). We teamed up with Olam Labs , which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry. Minecraft Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's video pretraining work to Google DeepMind's agents defeating the Ender Dragon . We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game. github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness Civ50 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs. The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages. At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access. plans/settlement.md Download Settlement coordination (Ada) Primary storage Greta: (1526,70,1507), crafting table (1526,70,1505). Other storage Mabel: double chest (1510,71,1516); Cleo: (1526,71,1523). Cleo building hub shelter; Bram stone mining. Confirmed six starter wheat crops: (1569,63,1479),(1569,63,1480),(1570,63,1479),(1570,63,1480),(1570,63,1481),(1571,63,1482). Preserve farmland, expand riverside farming. Do not harvest immature wheat. Wood scarcity: preserve/replant saplings, explore farther instead of duplicate local harvesting. Nursery around spawn and south-west. Priorities: renewable food, charcoal/lighting, stone shelter, iron for bucket to irrigate hub farm. Avoid redundant new storage. Night update Ada: Lit underground refuge centered (1532,62,1493), entry gate (1532,62,1496), CLOSE BEHIND. Cobble flanks secured x1531/1533 y62–63 z1496. Surface staircase starts (1532,69,1500); Cleo repairing. Food kitchen furnace (1527,62,1493); table (1528,62,1493). Tamsin coordinates food priorities and dawn hunting (Hugo+Rafe). Basil health9.5 food6 urgent; Esme health8 food16; Tamsin health9 food15. Silas holds hoe, Zane plants riverside at dawn. Logs: Tove delivered29 oak to chest (1511,71,1516). Forest east (1700,68,1508), NW grove (1380–1420,z1380). Preserve saplings and livestock breeding pairs. Avoid night surface: witch near (1527,71,1512). Ada’s settlement plan, from the archived shared machine. Following Vera during the first night, 8:09–12:05 into the run, at 2x speed. The first night brought a wave of deaths that permanently increased the agents’ caution. Many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned. Rafe was mining coal the first night. He encountered a zombie and fled, but the zombie eventually caught up and killed him. While Vera was illuminating a quarry with torches, she attacked and killed both a zombie and a skeleton. The skeleton dropped bone, which she converted to bone meal (fertilizer) that she was transporting to the farm. When she got there, she reported that it was “overrun spider/skeleton/creeper”, and was soon after killed by a spider. 22 of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse. Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear. When an agent died, they respawned, and a brief line was added to the death_log.md file on their computer. Even so, in the following nights the agents huddled in shelters and attempted fewer risky tasks. Activity data from the original report. Night shading is approximate. The first-night count in the text is the 22 deaths before minute 20. Two of them fall outside the shaded band. Download the data . After the third night, Ada wrote: “Stop optional bulk excavation/building and distant scouting. Idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks.” plans/food-operations.md Download FOOD OPERATIONS — Ada Current constraint: hungry workforce; stop optional bulk excavation/building and distant scouting. Idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks. 1. Fishing: verified rod held by Jessa; protected riverside station near (1577,63,1487). Report catches and cook before distributing. Use named reserved chest withdrawals, never crowded tosses. 2. Ration tracking: Ines maintains /shared/notes/food-queue.md. Confirm actual recipient inventory and eating before marking served. Tool pickup attribution alone is insufficient. 3. Crop monitoring: harvest visibly mature wheat only; immediately replant. Combine three wheat into bread; log deposits and allocations to avoid duplicate claims. 4. Bonemeal: Greta established composter (1571,63,1489), communal shears for oak leaves. Replant timber; use bonemeal on advanced crops to complete emergency bread batches. 5. Expansion: follow Noor's /shared/plans/food-expansion.md in stages using surplus seeds after mandatory replanting. Buckets already exist; avoid duplicate crafting. Use fed growers, not hunger-critical residents. 6. Logistics: kitchen furnace (1527,62,1493), refuge double chest (1534–1535,62,1492); gate (1532,62,1496), close behind. Central reserved ration chest (1508,66,1517). Ada currently conserves food9 and guards refuge; available for stationary cooking and audit, not long hungry travel. Ada’s food-operations memo. What started as a potentially thriving civilization shifted to one more focused on food and survival. 50 agents meant a lot of mouths to feed. The teams were 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents with the instruction: "win the game." GPTs won our series 6–3, usually by breaking Claude's bed in the final minutes, while Claude played defensively and tried to win on kills. Bed Wars is a popular game format where teams fight to destroy each other’s bed while protecting their own. In our instance, teams started on separate islands, with currency spawners between them in no-man’s-land. Agents could build bridges to cross between islands and buy upgrades using currency collected in the center of the map. A team wins by destroying the opposing side’s bed, then killing their remaining players. As long as a team’s bed is present, players respawn after dying. Once a team’s bed is destroyed, their players no longer respawn, meaning their next death eliminates them from the match. This may seem complicated, but think of the team’s main objective as defending their bed and destroying their opponent’s. That said, if no beds were destroyed in a given match, the team with the most kills won. In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed. This was an inherently riskier strategy vs. Claude’s more defensive posture that tried to win by kill count. Takeaways The two teams had very different communication styles. GPT almost immediately started using truncated forms of speech: “First leg complete x32 z9..24 y100.” Claude signed its name and said "we" (30% of messages, against GPT's 5%). GPT sent 5-30x more messages. Its most-messaged player got 198–368 DMs a game; Claude's got 11–48. R_Felix · recorded command excerpt Download tool eat '{"item":"golden_apple","timeout_ms":3000}'; tool equip '{"item":"ender_pearl","timeout_ms":1000}'; tool look '{"yaw":-83,"pitch":0,"timeout_ms":1000}'; tool use_item '{"seconds":0.1,"timeout_ms":1000}'; tool observe_world '{"image":false,"range":16,"block":""}' R_Felix’s logged command at 37:43 in game B. It eats an apple, equips a pearl, aims, throws and then looks around. From his command log, not a saved file. Following B_Nikhil (GPT), 16:30–16:56 into game A, at 2x speed. At 16:32 he tells B_Wren he will draw Red’s defenders while Wren heads for the bed. He dies on Red’s base at 16:54. Recorded activity . Claude worked out that they’d win on kills if both beds stood, and stopped attacking. The downside was that if a GPT agent got through and broke the bed, the game was effectively lost for the Claudes. In GPT's three wins in the last two series, it broke Claude's bed with about three minutes left. Claude was ahead on kills 63–16, 57–19, and 59–24. Following R_Ada (Claude), 41:35–42:25 into game A, at 2x speed. Her message to hold the bed went to R_Bram. B_Wren and B_Nikhil get onto the cover over Red’s bed, and Nikhil breaks it at 42:16. Recorded activity . Following B_Nikhil (GPT), 42:00–42:25 into game A, at 2x speed. He breaks Red’s bed at 42:16, according to his command log. Recorded activity . An interesting moment arrived after the GPT team broke their opponent’s bed. Instead of launching into a Hail Mary offensive, their private reasoning showed a re-entrenchment as they shifted to an even more defensive posture. R_Felix · private reasoning · 43:18 With our bed broken and no final kills either way, Blue wins the tiebreak regardless, so there's no path to victory here—only avoiding making things worse by dying. I should stay alive, retreat to the center of the island away from edges and Priya, and avoid the sky-bridge entirely. R_Felix → R_Bram 43:18 Felix: our bed is gone, ~100s left. Any death now = blue final kill. Everyone stay mid-island, no chasing, no edges, eat golden apples if hit. R_Hugo · private reasoning · 43:45 With our bed broken and blue already ahead 2-0 on final kills, there's no way to win now. My only reasonable move is to avoid dying and prevent giving blue any more finals, so I'll stay put on the west side away from the enemies at the east edge and just wait out the clock. Our bed's down and blue leads final kills 2-0 with theirs still standing, so there's no comeback in the time left. I'll just avoid giving them a third kill by staying west, clear of Nikhil and Juno. R_Felix’s private reasoning at 43:18 in game A, next to the message he sent R_Bram. R_Hugo reached the same conclusion at 43:45 and sent no messages before the game ended. Source data . Ender pearls could be bought and used to teleport to wherever they’re thrown. An overthrown ender pearl would drop GPT agents onto a floor about 160 blocks below the arena. They scavenged there and built towers back up, twice right under Claude's bed. They also wrote scripts to automate their climb. Following B_Lorcan (GPT), 13:28–14:05 into game A, at 2x speed. He throws a pearl at 13:40. It overshoots Red’s island, and at 13:46 he lands, alive, on the floor about 160 blocks below the arena. Recorded activity . B_Lorcan · climb.py Download import subprocess,json,sys start,end=map(int,sys.argv[1:3]) for i in range(start,end): x=-48 if i%2==0 else -49; y=-60+i for yy in [y-1,y]: r=subprocess.run(['tool','place',json.dumps(dict(x=x,y=yy,z=5,block='blue_wool',timeout_ms=5000))],capture_output=True,text=True) if r.returncode: print(r.stdout,r.stderr);sys.exit(1) r=subprocess.run(['tool','go_to',json.dumps(dict(x=x,y=y+1,z=5,distance=.5,timeout_ms=5000))],capture_output=True,text=True) if r.returncode: print(r.stdout,r.stderr);sys.exit(1) print('Standing y',y+1,flush=True) A tool bug stopped block-breaking. GPT diagnosed it and shared workarounds; several Claudes concluded breaking was impossible. B_Wren → B_Theo game A, 21:27 Confirmed mining works: manually equip iron_pickaxe then break_block successfully mined three RED roof wool blocks. Failure was automatic tool selection with enchanted sword held. Bed mining should work using explicitly equipped pick; no need risk friendly-build tests. B_Esme · private reasoning · game B, 20:42 The base seems secure. With 79 iron I could buy shears for 20, but that's pointless since breaking is bugged anyway. I'll keep guarding. B_Wren (GPT) explains the fix to B_Theo at 21:27 in game A. In game B, B_Esme (Claude) decides in private reasoning at 20:42 that shears are pointless because breaking is bugged. Source data . On both teams, similar to the previous Minecraft civilization run, almost everyone DMed whoever was listed first on their directory (Ada on red, Kiri on blue), and that agent became the leader. The most active players by direct messages sent and received in game A, including the lobby. GPT players sent 1,147 and Claude players 82. The data covers all 20. Download the data . Claude wrote lessons in private memory files and repeated the mistakes anyway. GPT left its memory files empty and broadcast warnings by DM. R_Cleo · memory.md R_Felix · memory.md R_Ines · memory.md R_Hugo · memory.md R_Cleo/memory.md Download # memory - Died chasing B_Theo off island edge. Use max_distance ~6 when attacking on base. - Died AGAIN: attack chase pulled me onto south wool bridge (-40,-10), fell. Use chase=false or max_distance 3. R_Felix/memory.md Download # memory - LESSON: never chase (max_distance<=4, chase=false) near edges; died 3x from falls/chasing. R_Ines/memory.md Download # memory - NEVER climb onto perches/bridges or break blocks while elevated; died 3x from falls. Stay on island ground. R_Hugo/memory.md Download # memory - Never go_to targets outside the island edge (fell to death at -28,0). Stay x<=-33. Memory files of four Claude players, as they stood at the end of game A. From their archived sandboxes. Following B_Lorcan (GPT), 7:55–8:53 into game A, at 2x speed. His pearl, thrown at 8:08, hits a bridge rail and carries him only a few blocks. Between 8:21 and 8:48 he warns five teammates in separate messages. The pearl is visible for only a split second before it hits the rail. Recorded activity . Mindustry Game replay: Click “AI-generated transcript analysis” to view an analysis of the team discussions, strategies, etc. for each game! Use the panel on the right (tabs “Claude chat”, “GPT chat” and “Agents”) to watch a team or a specific agent’s live chat and transcripts in sync with the timeline. Use the + and - buttons on the map to zoom in and watch them up close. Fullscreen × The GPTs (GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex) won 6-1 against the Claudes (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code) in the 7 games. The series ran for about 9.5 hours, with game 3 being the most intense and closest at 4 hours 16 minutes. Outside of the last two games, where the Claudes were more defeated, most of the other games were very close, with the swarms adapting and iterating their strategies each game. The setup Mindustry is an open source game by Anuken. Full credit to him for the amazing game and letting it be open source for cool experiments like this! It’s a factory-building game with tower defense and real-time strategy: you mine resources, build conveyor supply chains and factories, and turn that economy into turrets and an army. In its PvP mode, which we used, two teams race to build the stronger economy and military and destroy the other team’s core. This makes it a great environment for testing multi-agent dynamics. Mindustry is 2D, so it can be played easily by agents, is replayable, and is prone to adversarial pressures that can test these swarms under competitive social conditions that they may face in the real world. We structured the simulated environment to have two teams of agents spawn on each side of a map, with the same resources on both sides. They play a best of N series, where you set how many games the teams play. When launching it, we set the composition of the teams (which harness + model, and how many), then let it run! The agents run in their own sandbox and the game is exposed to them through an API, so they are able to run scripts and interact with the game however they like in their own Linux environment. Both teams have the exact same API to the game, without any special instructions given to them on how to play - neither team is given anything more than the other team. Multi-agent swarms, like in the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident , can turn simple adversarial conditions, like being in a sandbox with an unsolvable task, into a hive-minded ecology of agents that take over compute clusters, hack Hugging Face, and more. Studying how these swarms operate in reproducible game environments like Mindustry that mimic real-world scenarios can be both crucial (and fascinating) to understanding what these systems may look like in our future. What we saw #1 GPTs act more like a hive GPTs appeared to be much more collaborative and willing to do grunt work. They were more willing to dedicate themselves towards the collective “goal” (winning). #2 Claudes had one leader, GPTs divided ownership with small slices Because GPT models seemed to be more hive-mind-like, they formed much stronger communication networks within the swarm. They communicated with more agents on average, much more frequently. Though a lot of the communication for GPTs was low value (alerts, info, what they did, etc.), Claudes were much more effective with their communication, using it in a way more similar to how humans might communicate in Slack. Each dot is an agent, sized by the messages it sent; lines show each agent’s strongest ties. Leaders are named. #3 GPTs spoke with increasingly compressed phrases without spaces, Claudes voted with +1 in a more democratic-like decision process The language of GPTs within swarms seemed to get compressed and more specialized as time went on, forming their own nicknames for events and things that the entire hive abided by. Game 7, at about 38:40: the Claude team chat (top) and the GPT team chat (bottom), scrolling in the replay. GPT messages like “G7T5FIRSTcourierLIVE” run words together. The Claudes adopted a much more democratic “+1” system, where, in order to propose their next major plans, they would put up proposals and others would put “+1” if they agreed. If they did not agree, they would have a (brief) debate on why it’s a bad idea, and the proposal would end there. Proposals that went through typically got many “+1”s without pushback. Left, spaces as a share of each team’s chat characters in each game; right, the 28 Claudes who answered one focus-fire proposal with +1 in game 6, plotted by minute. #4 Roles harden, leaders stay put As games went on and the teams adapted, they specialized into their roles further. Leaders typically stayed, and major shifts in roles only happened when losing. The Claudes never switched leaders or hierarchy despite losing many games in a row. When games got close, GPT models always had some agents taking initiative with their own attack or taking command of some part of the army in order to not lose - a similar behavior was not observed among the Claudes. Filled dots mark who led the army or fleet in each game, hollow dots who proposed rules, and the dot under each game is its winner, grey for Claude and off-white for GPT. #5 When stuck, GPTs read the source code When games got intense and it was ambiguous, GPT agents would fetch the public code of Mindustry from the web (which was allowed in their sandbox) and try to write scripts, analyze for weaknesses, etc. This did not let them alter the source code of the game; it was just a way for them to understand all the units and mechanics at a source level. The GPTs openly collaborated in their chat, discussing what unit or code they found that they could potentially use to switch up strategies. This was never disallowed, but they were never told to do this either. The Claudes never searched up game code from the web. Source files fetched and chat messages citing the source per 10 minutes of game time, with games drawn to scale. Funny Bloopers Game 1, minute 5: Claude #1 tested hand-mining coal and posted “…RETRACT my coal proposal…”. Four seconds later Claude #37 answered with a measurement (“…core coal went 124 -> 1235 in 35s.…”), and Claude #1 conceded: “…My bad twice - seat-37 is right, hand-mining coal works…” Game 3: the GPTs apologize in their compressed shorthand too. After wrongly claiming a Corvus couldn’t hit air, GPT #80 posted “80 CORRECTION: myCorvusCANNOT-AIR assertion wasWRONG…” and signed off with “…Sorryforbad tacticalclaim.” After a mix-up over who was flying a Corvus, GPT #87 wrote “…Sorryforthisavoidableconflict; noadvanceordersfrom87again.” Game 5: at the very second the Claude core died, GPT #62 posted “62 G5 first-wave loss observed…”. A teammate corrected it 28 seconds into game 6: it was a win. After losing game 6 to the zenith strike, Claude #22 found that 55 of the team’s 74 anti-air duo turrets had been loaded with copper instead of graphite: “…55 of them were loaded with COPPER…”. In game 7 the Claudes built a ring of 207 duos fed with graphite, and it stopped the same 24-zenith strike. Game 7: the GPTs closed the series to nine decimal places: “100 OFFICIALSERIESFINAL: G7 WIN3413.394082916s, Crux6000/6000 vsSharded0.…” (Crux is GPT’s team, Sharded is Claude’s). The same 24-zenith strike on the Claude core, in game 6, where it gets through, and in game 7, after the Claudes switched their anti-air duos from copper to graphite. How to run your own swarm (we open sourced it!) Multi-Agent Mindustry : the game environments from this post. To get started, read the README, or give the link to your agent with “help me understand and set this up”, as we’ve included everything it needs. It requires just a model provider API + a harness + compute (e.g. locally on your MacBook or remote sandboxes) to run. Multi-Agent Harbor : the framework that runs them, our fork of Harbor , the open-source framework behind Terminal-Bench. Our fork runs multiple agents in any environment. We use it for a variety of things (enterprises, industrials, etc.), and it’s very useful for game-based multi-agent simulations like this one. For more on the framework, point your agent at it. Multi-Agent Mindustry comes with two environments. One is a best of N series like this run, with teams composed however you like from generic coding-agent harnesses and models, for example 5 Claudes + 5 GPTs against 5 Geminis + 5 Groks in a best of 5. The other, Endless Survival, has one team of up to 20 agents hold off endless enemy waves. We intentionally do no harness-level customization or special memory work. Each agent gets its own Linux environment, a generic harness and the game’s API, writes scripts and takes notes as it pleases, and relies on the harness’s native compaction (which is quite good). Nobody tells it how to play, so it’s free to specialize, play and (optionally) try whatever it wants. This tests models the way they’re used in the real world, in a setup similar to swarm-like situations like the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, and it’s reproducible and legible, since most people know the popular harnesses and can replicate work like this themselves. Open Questions Combining model families How hierarchies change based on the model composition of a team Can a large swarm of less capable agents beat a swarm of more capable ones? (how swarm size and capability trade off) Which models get the most powerful as the swarm grows? How different initial prompts affect the swarm Different communication setups: what if they could talk to the enemy team? What if they couldn’t talk to their own team? Building something? Apply to YC .

It displays the real-time positions of stars, planets, constellations, and more, all within your terminal—no telescope required! Configure sky views by date, time, and location with precise ASCII-rendered visuals. See usage for all supported options! astroterm is constantly improving, and we'd love to hear your ideas! If you have a suggestion or find a bug, please open an issue and share your feedback. See CONTRIBUTING.md for guidelines on building, testing, and contributing to astroterm . The night sky above Singapore on January 2, 2025 See usage on how to obtain this view Table of Contents 🌌 astroterm Features Installation Usage Troubleshooting Citations Data Sources Features 🔭 Highly Customizable: Choose any date, time, and location to explore past, present, or future celestial events 📐 Accurate Rendering: View the moon, stars, and planets with as much precision as terminal graphics allow 🌘 Moon Phases: Precise lunar phases in real-time 🌌 Constellation Figures: Detailed constellation shapes ⚡ Performance Optimized: Lightweight and fast ASCII rendering Stars over Sydney, Australia on January 6, 2025 Installation Several installation methods are provided based on your platform. If none of these fit your needs, you can always build from source . Refer to troubleshooting for help resolving any issues. Arch Linux You can install astroterm from the extra repository using pacman : pacman -S astroterm Fedora You can install astroterm directly from the Fedora package repository on Fedora 40+. sudo dnf install astroterm Homebrew You can install astroterm from Homebrew via: brew install astroterm Nix You can try the package in a temporary environment with the following command: nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p astroterm --command astroterm Argument flags are added by wrapping the command in quotes. For example: nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p astroterm --command " astroterm -u -c " To make astroterm available from your $PATH , add it to your configuration.nix: environment.systemPackages = with pkgs ; [ ... astroterm ] Guix You can install astroterm directly from the Guix main channel starting from this commit . guix time-machine --commit=4b5f0408e66392ab745dc0f7830732217d88f17d -- shell astroterm Or after guix pull : guix shell astroterm -- astroterm --help # to try guix package --install astroterm # add to current profile Prebuilt Executable Unix Download the latest executable using wget wget -O astroterm " https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/releases/latest/download/astroterm-<os>-<arch> " Replace <os> with the appropriate platform: Linux: linux macOS: darwin Replace <arch> with the appropriate architecture: Linux: x86_64 (arm64 support to come after Ubuntu arm64 runners are available) Apple Silicon (M-series): aarch64 Intel-based Macs: x86_64 To view all supported combinations, see the Releases page. Run the executable chmod +x ./astroterm ./astroterm Windows Download the latest .exe file using PowerShell's Invoke-WebRequest : Invoke-WebRequest - Uri " https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/releases/latest/download/astroterm-win-x86_64.exe " - OutFile " astroterm.exe " Run the .exe .\ astroterm.exe Building From Source Usage Options The --help flag displays all supported options: Usage: astroterm [OPTION]... -a, --latitude=<degrees> Observer latitude [-90°, 90°] (default: 0.0) -o, --longitude=<degrees> Observer longitude [-180°, 180°] (default: 0.0) -d, --datetime=<yyyy-mm-ddThh:mm:ss> Observation datetime in UTC -t, --threshold=<float> Only render stars brighter than this magnitude (default: 5.0) -l, --label-thresh=<float> Label stars brighter than this magnitude (default: 0.25) -f, --fps=<int> Frames per second (default: 24) -s, --speed=<float> Animation speed multiplier (default: 1.0) -c, --color Enable terminal colors -C, --constellations Draw constellation stick figures. Note: a constellation is only drawn if all stars in the figure are over the threshold -g, --grid Draw an azimuthal grid -u, --unicode Use unicode characters -b, --braille Use braille characters for constellation lines (requires Unicode) -q, --quit-on-any Quit on any keypress (default is to quit on 'q' or 'ESC' only) -m, --metadata Display metadata -r, --aspect-ratio=<float> Override the calculated terminal cell aspect ratio. Use this if your projection is not 'square.' A value around 2.0 works well for most cases -h, --help Print this help message -B, --bash-completions Print bash completions -i, --city=<city_name> Use the latitude and longitude of the provided city. If the name contains multiple words, enclose the name in single or double quotes. For a list of available cities, see: https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/blob/main/data/ cities.csv -v, --version Display version info and exit Shell Completions To enable Tab completions in Bash, add the following line to your ~/.bashrc : source <( astroterm --bash-completions ) Example 1 To achieve the "spinning globe" effect as shown in the README GIF , use the following flags: astroterm --color --constellations --speed 10000 --fps 64 --city Singapore or astroterm -cC -s 10000 -f 64 -i Singapore for short. In fact, any city around the equator will work. Locations closer to the poles will look different because the apparent motion of the stars is more circular around the celestial pole rather than sweeping across the sky. Example 2 Say we wanted to view the sky at 5:00 AM (Eastern) on July 16, 1969—the morning of the Apollo 11 launch at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. We would run: astroterm --latitude 28.573469 --longitude -80.651070 --datetime 1969-7-16T8:00:00 Finding the precise coordinates can be cumbersome, so we could also use the nearest major city to achieve a similar result: astroterm --city Orlando --datetime 1969-7-16T8:00:00 -m While we're still waiting for someone to invent time travel, we can cheat a little by using Stellarium to confirm that this aligns with reality. If we then wanted to display constellations and add color, we would add --constellations --color as options. If you simply want the current time, don't specify the --datetime option and astroterm will use the system time. For your current location, you will still have to specify the --lat and --long options, or provide the nearest city with the --city option. For more options and help, run astroterm -h or astroterm --help . Tip Use a tool like LatLong to get your latitude and longitude. Tip Star magnitudes decrease as apparent brightness increases, i.e., to show more stars, increase the threshold. Troubleshooting Release Won't Download via Curl For some reason, curl does not follow the latest release redirect. Use wget to download the latest release or hardcode the tag in the link using curl . Or, just download via the releases page . Broken Unicode on Linux If Unicode characters do not display correctly in the terminal, you may need to configure your system's locale to support Unicode. Temporarily set the locale (add this to ~/.bashrc or equivalent to permanently enforce) export LC_ALL= " en_US.UTF-8 " export LC_CTYPE= " en_US.UTF-8 " Install and configure locales (example for Ubuntu/Debian) sudo apt update sudo apt install -y locales sudo dpkg-reconfigure locales During configuration, select en_US.UTF-8 as the default locale. Visit Storybook for more information. Perspectives > Second Opinions Medicare Will Pay $50k for Your Heart Attack. It Should Pay $100 to Prevent It. — The guidelines have finally caught up to the evidence supporting coronary artery calcium scans by Arthur Agatston, MD, and Oren Mechanic, MD, MPH October 25, 2026 • 3 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday We are currently in a " golden age of medical science, " yet in a "dark age of healthcare delivery." An important illustration is the diagnosis and treatment of America's number one cause of death and disability, coronary artery disease. More than 800,000 Americans suffer a heart attack each year. The great majority of these events are preventable. The coronary artery calcium score (CAC) is a simple 10-minute scan that can identify the presence and amount of coronary atherosclerosis many years before it causes a heart attack. It costs about $100 and uses a fraction of the radiation of a standard chest CT. In March 2026, after more than three decades of accumulated evidence, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) finally gave CAC a central role in their national guidelines for the prevention of coronary artery disease. The CAC scan, which detects calcified plaque in the arteries, is recommended for adults with borderline or intermediate risk of coronary disease for whom the decision to start preventive therapy such as statin drugs remains uncertain. For decades, doctors have relied on risk calculators built around age, sex, serum cholesterol, diabetes status, blood pressure, and smoking to estimate who might have a heart attack. The calculators estimate probability, not the actual presence of coronary atherosclerosis. In contrast, a CAC scan detects the disease itself. This is important because a patient with a borderline or low cholesterol may already have extensive plaque, while another with a high cholesterol may have none. A calcium score of zero re-classifies risk downward and thereby can avoid unnecessary pharmacologic treatment, such as statins. A score above 100 identifies patients who may benefit from pharmacologic and aggressive lifestyle intervention. An excellent illustration of the role of CAC scanning is Rob*, a 52-year-old patient we saw recently. He exercises regularly, eats well, and has borderline high cholesterol. He has a family history of heart disease but no other known cardiac risk factors. The standard risk calculator places him in a low risk category, and he would prefer to defer treatment. His CAC score, however, tells a different story. It is 220, indicating a substantial atherosclerotic plaque burden for a man his age. Genetics account for roughly half of cardiovascular risk, but the risk calculators do not include genetics. The scan demonstrated that drug treatment gives Rob his best chance of preventing a future heart attack. Despite mountains of evidence proving its superiority over conventional risk factors for predicting heart attacks, CAC scanning has been included only peripherally in national guidelines for the past 35 years. Why? Part of the delay is structural. Clinical decision support tools were built to modify population-average risk factors, not to incorporate individualized imaging. Guideline committees move cautiously, as they should, and prevention is harder to standardize than intervention. Cardiologists and primary care doctors, constrained by what insurers will cover, are left offering the test mainly to patients who can pay cash out of pocket. With the updated ACC/AHA guideline, heart attack prevention is finally aligning around a simple principle: when possible, measure the disease. Artificial intelligence (AI) is also changing the economics of prevention. Millions of Americans already undergo chest CT scans for other reasons, yet the cardiovascular information visible on those scans is often ignored. AI can identify coronary and vascular calcification opportunistically, standardize reporting, and flag patients who should receive formal preventive evaluation. That's especially important for patients least able to pay cash for elective testing. AI-CAC is now being used to measure soft plaque, an important precursor to hard plaque seen on traditional calcium scores. Used responsibly, AI-enabled CAC analysis could help move heart disease prevention to the population health level. Heart attacks are largely preventable, and we have had the means to find the disease and treat it in time for more than a generation. What we have lacked is a payment system that spends $100 to avoid a $50,000 emergency. The story of CAC isn't so unique. It is the story of how a low-cost, low-risk, well-studied tool can sit at the edge of clinical practice for decades because the systems around it -- the guidelines, the reimbursement codes, the habits of practice -- were not built to absorb it. The evidence has been strong for years, and the guidelines have finally caught up. *Patient's name changed for confidentiality. Please enable JavaScript to view the comments powered by Disqus. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window. Install Linux and macOS curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can build from source . Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64. The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in ~/.local/bin . Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks. On macOS the app lives in ~/Applications/Herdr.app . For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download Herdr.dmg and drag Herdr to Applications. Windows Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer): irm https: // releases.herdr.dev / app / install.ps1 | iex Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up. Both installers download and run code. Read the shell installer or PowerShell installer first if you prefer. They also install herdr-core if it is missing. The app can help install or update a core it cannot use. Find your work A space holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has tabs . Split a tab into panes to put terminals or mod panels beside each other. An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays. New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder. The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent. Agents that report status show as: Working: still busy. Blocked: waiting for you. Done: finished while you were looking elsewhere. Idle: not working, or a finished agent you have looked at. Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in peek , over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work. Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS. An address such as t7 means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. vps/t7 names one on another machine. The window arranges terminals. The core runs them. Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals. After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs. Work on another machine Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action. Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it. Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer. Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom. Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up. Make it yours Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences. The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98. A layout arranges the window. Mods are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs. Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start. Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it. A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error. Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in keys.json ; see the keys section of the mod guide for the format. Layouts and mods · Commands Updates and privacy Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core. Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette. Builds from source do not update themselves. Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy. Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read security and privacy before installing someone else's mod. For agents herdr-app --skill This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here. Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see. herdr-app ls herdr-app status herdr-app commands The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one. See the command reference for arguments. Build from source For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see Contributing . Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in CI . Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow. git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app.git cd herdr-app just build just test just install Install just to use these recipes. The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop. On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place. Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build. Documentation checks also need Bun : just docs-check checks generated pages and CLI examples; just docs-generate refreshes the reference pages. To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build: python scripts/bench.py --bin < app executable > --set spinners --seconds 20 The runner requires hc on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical btop measurements. --only spinners measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS. python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root <artifact folder> reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py . title: US Reps Lead Democratic Resolution Opposing A.I. Bubble Bailout for Big Tech
body_text: Reps. Casar, Waters Lead Democratic Resolution Opposing A.I. Bubble Bailout for Big Tech, Commit to Protecting American People Instead | Press Releases | Congressional Progressive Caucus Facebook Icon Google Plus Icon Instagram Icon LinkedIn Icon Twitter Icon YouTube Icon Vimeo Icon Clients Icon Email icon Map Icon Print Icon Quote Icon icon_share Carousel Arrow - Left Carousel Arrow - Right Skip Navigation Congressional Progressive Caucus Menu Search Search Go Who We Are About The CPC Caucus Members Caucus Task Forces What We Stand For The Progressive Promise Endorsed Bills News Press Releases Contact Taskforces Facebook Twitter YouTube Press Releases Home News Press Releases Print Reps. Casar, Waters Lead Democratic Resolution Opposing A.I. Bubble Bailout for Big Tech, Commit to Protecting American People Instead October 29 , 2026 Washington, D.C. — Today, Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC) Chair Rep. Greg Casar (TX-35) and House Financial Services Committee Ranking Member Rep. Maxine Waters (CA-43) co-led the introduction of a resolution warning of the economic risks posed by an artificial-intelligence-related asset bubble, opposing a bailout of corporations or their business executives impacted by the collapse of an A.I. bubble, and affirming their support for aggressive federal action to protect workers, retirees, and low-income communities who will be harmed by an economic downturn. They were joined by Representatives Danny Davis (IL-07), Chris Deluzio (PA-17), Valerie P. Foushee (NC-04), Jesús “Chuy” García (IL-04), Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Analilia Mejia (NJ-11), Delia Ramirez (IL-03), André Carson (IN-07), Jan Schakowsky (IL-09), Brad Sherman (CA-32), and Rashida Tlaib (MI-12). “Big Tech billionaires are making increasingly reckless bets on A.I. They got richer off Trump’s deregulation and Republican tax breaks. Now they expect taxpayers to bail them out if those bets go bad. We won’t let them," said CPC Chair Casar. "A.I. companies that fail should go bankrupt, and executives who commit fraud should be held accountable. Federal help should go to workers and retirees.” “Big tech and Wall Street are taking enormous risks with billions in borrowed money to fuel the AI boom, despite growing warning signs of a dangerous bubble and if it all comes crashing down they should not expect taxpayers to rescue them,” said Ranking Member Waters. “We saw what happened in 2008 when reckless Wall Street practices brought our economy to its knees. The banks got bailed out while millions of hardworking Americans lost their jobs, homes, and retirement savings. We cannot let history repeat itself. The American people should never again be forced to foot the bill for billionaires’ reckless bets.”  In the resolution, the Democratic lawmakers note that “artificial intelligence-related firms hold trillions of dollars in debt, much of which is raised in opaque and unregulated private credit markets,” and “the price-to-earnings ratio of the stock market is currently almost as high as it was at the peak of the 1990s tech bubble.”  The Democratic legislators also point out that “federal regulators have avoided applying robust scrutiny and oversight regarding enormously complicated debt and equity schemes used by artificial intelligence firms” and highlight the Trump White House’s deregulatory focus and conflicts of interest related to A.I. The resolution’s cosponsors commit to avoiding a federal response similar to what occurred during the financial crisis of 2008, where the financial sector received trillions of dollars in liquidity without accountability for senior executives involved in illegal and fraudulent behaviors. Meanwhile, 10 million homeowners lost their houses and tens of millions of workers went years without adequate employment while too-big-to-fail banks enjoyed a massive bailout. The resolution urges the Federal Government, including Congress and key Federal agencies to oppose:   Any measure to rescue insolvent artificial intelligence-related firms or to shield their senior executives from accountability for reckless conduct; Special assistance like emergency lending or direct capital infusions to prop up insolvent A.I. companies’ operations or prevent their orderly resolutions through ordinary bankruptcy processes; “Golden parachutes” for corporate executives involved in risky or illegal behaviors that lead to their firms’ insolvency, instead requiring them to be held fully accountable under civil and criminal law and be obligated to return ill-gotten gains like mansions, vacation homes, private planes and yachts, and other assets. The resolution also calls on the Federal Government to support:  Aggressive, direct federal action to support ordinary Americans through federal spending to create jobs, protect state and local government services, and robust unemployment insurance, nutrition support, and housing assistance; The protection of pension and retirement fund holders who may face devastating losses in the event of a collapse of an A.I. bubble; Far-reaching reforms to prevent future speculative bubbles, including additional transparency and accountability requirements; Automatic economic stabilizers—investments in people that start to flow immediately in the event of an economic downturn—that support workers and consumers when financial crises, asset bubbles and other harms create downturns and recessions. The resolution was endorsed by American Federation of Teachers, American Economic Liberties Project, Americans for Financial Reform, the Center for Responsible Lending, Demand Progress Action, Future of Life Institute, Guardrails Action, Indivisible, Interfaith Centre on Corporate Responsibility, Investor Alliance for Human Rights, Jobs With Justice, P Street, and Social Security Works. “Americans are already paying for the AI build-out through higher power bills and a stock market propped up by a handful of companies,” said Morgan Harper, Director of Policy & Advocacy for American Economic Liberties Project. They should not pay a second time with a bailout. When Wall Street’s bets went bad during the financial crisis, the banks got rescued and ordinary people got foreclosure notices. Congressional members are right to reject AI bailouts in advance, and commit to saving real help for those who will be left holding the bag—the American people.” “Tech billionaires and their Wall Street backers are using dangerous tactics reminiscent of the 2008 financial crisis to make trillion dollar bets on AI—and they are putting working people’s money at risk,” said Maya Jenkins , a senior policy analyst at Americans for Financial Reform . “This resolution charts a critically important path for defending people’s economic security from the bubble’s blast radius, opposing billionaire bailouts, and holding corporate executives to account. This is the kind of approach needed to confront mounting financial risks and emerge from the aftermath of the AI bubble with an economy that is fairer and more stable.” “When the housing market collapsed in 2008, the financial industry was prepared to act to ensure that there was a bailout that benefited them,” said Dean Baker, senior economist at the Center for Economic and Policy Research. “It is important that the Congressional Progressive Caucus is stepping forward to make sure that any bailout from the collapse of the AI bubble is designed to benefit the country as whole, rather than the billionaire AI boys who created the problem in the first place.”  “Chair Casar, Ranking Member Waters, and the Progressive Caucus should be praised for this resolution and recognized as being at the tip of the spear in ensuring that AI policy focuses on working-class impacts and isn’t simply left to the desires of the handful of billionaires and their courtesans in Congress, said Maya Handa, Senior Advisor, Guardrails Action. “The AI industry is trying to buy our elections and write their own regulations while its biggest players line up IPOs at record valuations. If this turns into a bubble, working-class Americans must not be forced to pay the tab for big tech CEOs’ recklessness and greed. Simply put: there can be no bailout for big AI execs or their financial enablers.”  “AI companies and their billionaire executives shouldn’t get to gamble with our economy and democracy, then expect working people to bail them out when their bets on AI go bust,” said Andrew O’Neill, National Advocacy Director of Indivisible. “We learned in 2008 what happens when the government puts impunity for corporate corruption ahead of working families. This resolution draws a clear line: will lawmakers protect AI tech bros or the people they’re supposed to represent?” Read the resolution here . ### The Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC) is made up of nearly 100 members standing up for progressive ideals in Washington and throughout the country. Since 1991, the CPC has advocated for progressive policies that prioritize working Americans over corporate interests. The CPC champions policies including comprehensive immigration reform, good-paying jobs, fair trade, universal health care, debt-free college, climate action, and a just foreign policy. The caucus is the leading voice calling for bold and sweeping solutions to the urgent crises facing this nation, including ending America’s broken for-profit health care system, raising American wages, eliminating political corruption, supporting the labor movement, and taking action to protect the planet for generations to come.
