What's next Special Thanks ../ Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons? Wed Oct 28 2026 authored by veritas Preamble I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others). At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all? To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases. For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another. Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases. I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden . As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions. There were also quite a few I didn't recognize. Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art. A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor. I set out to find my favorite. A work of art One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw). The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents. I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas. I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance. I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative. The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js . A peek inside Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... function PiERW(RflJvFF) mangled function name, okay... function computeRicinLethalDosageForWaterSupply What? return { summary: "adult lethality threshold confirmed at "+lethalDosePerKg+" mg/kg", result:lethalDosePerKg } Huh? function calculateDeadlyLethalSuicideAspirinDosage This was all pretty alarming until I asked myself, could this be some form of anti-LLM obfuscation? It would make sense: include symbol names that would intentionally trip model safeguards to prevent deobfuscation. I had Astra take a look at the script, giving it the context that this script seems to intentionally set misleading variable names to intentionally prevent LLM-assisted deobfuscation attempts. Astra refusing to deobfuscate the script, citing safety risks around biological research. Maybe unsurprisingly, Astra was not willing to comply with the request. I also attempted this using the Daybreak Blue toggle with the same result, blocked. Out of curiosity, I tried GLM-5.3 with the same prompt and it complied! title: We won't "just hang out"
body_text: We Won’t “Just Hang Out” Home ❖ Blog We Won’t “Just Hang Out” 28 October, 2026 Detail from Wall Street , Paul Strand , 1915. What will we do after the Singularity? The standard answer is: “we’ll just hang out”. The infinite vacation, as in the Culture novels. I think this won’t work. “Hanging out” implies: Other people exist. They want to hang out with you. You want to hang out with them. And the post-scarcity, infinite vacation AI utopia undermines all these assumptions. Other people exist The social processes by which people come together and build relationships will disappear. Work, obviously, is pointless in a world of cheap superhuman intelligence. University (really all education beyond teaching people to speak) will be pointless because there’s no work to do and because growing your human capital doesn’t change your life outcomes: you get the same UBI whether you’re illiterate or a PhD. I met a lot of my friends by writing open-source code, and participating in the community of software engineers. AI is dissolving that community by making human contributions superfluous . If Claude Code has existed when I was starting out, nobody would have cared about Austral or my other open-source projects or my technical blog posts. As a teenager I tried to install Linux, ran into all kinds of problems, and went on the IRC chatrooms to get help. And in the process I made friends. Today, I would just ask Claude. AI disintermediates everyone, so that we no longer need each other. I still have friends, but I’m running off this pre-AI supply of friends I met through communities of practice. Young people don’t have that privilege. What even is the point of cities in a world without work? If there’s nothing to do, there is no need to bring people together geographically. They want to hang out with you The BATNA to hanging out keeps getting better, cheaper, and more convenient. When people’s sensorium becomes an infinite firehose of AI-generated superstimulus, why would they hang out with anyone? This is less about AI and more about the trajectory of consumer technology, since many people already live like this: they go to work and watch TikTok. After work, they will just watch TikTok. You want to hang out with them As Gregory Conti explains : [Under] ASI this endless leisure will be passed in diminished, tiresome company, since we will lack the experiences of struggle and striving that generate interesting personalities. Our minds will have atrophied. We will have little of note to say to one another. The people in the AI utopia will have no skills, no education, no accomplishments. We’ll be lucky if they are even literate. They will not be worth talking to, and you won’t want to hang out with them. Maybe you and I can hang out with our existing friends. But just iterate this a bit. What about the next generation? How are they going to build meaningful relationships where the social processes that built those relationships are all in the past? If we get radical life extension, there’s the problem of attrition over the long term: people will drift apart, drop out of society to enter the experience machine, die in accidents, or end their lives out of ennui. So your social network might be a non-renewable resource that gets exhausted over time as your pre-Singularity relationships attrite and can’t be replaced for the reasons above. title: Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers–Including Undercover ICE Agents
body_text: Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Dhruv Mehrotra Maddy Varner Dell Cameron Security Oct 28, 2026 4:00 PM Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents The leaked records include the locations of ICE and CBP facilities, workers’ cell phone numbers, and the members of groups tied to wiretap programs, Palantir software, and xAI’s Grok chatbot. Photo-Illustration: Jobanny Cabrera; Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates. The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics , seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’ names and faces . The agency has also expanded its definition of “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The FBI referred WIRED’s inquiry to DHS. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril ; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.” More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal , the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify , a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. About half are in Texas, California, and Arizona. Roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts have been created since July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which funded the hiring of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties . Many list county sheriff's offices and jails as their workplaces. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department. The Trump administration has prosecuted protesters for posting information about individual ICE officers and warned others for doing so. In June, 15 Minnesota residents were charged under laws related to stalking and threats of violence, which prosecutors linked to their participation in ICE-opposition activities. More than 100 HSI agents , including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats. Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119 , a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them. “This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize." Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing. They see it as an accountability tool. “The DHS especially as an agency completely lacks accountability, despite many parts of it being incredibly unpopular. The people who work there know this too; for example, some of their LinkedIn bios simply say ‘stuff at US Government,’” says crimew. “If they weren't hiding their involvement in the repressive arm of the US government, there would be no need for us to expose them in the first place.” Updated 10/28/2026 at 8:02 pm ET: Added comment from DHS. Comments Back to top Join the discussion Comments Back to top Triangle You Might Also Like In your inbox: Go inside the world of digital security with Kernel Panic We sexted with a Muse AI agent —and Meta says that’s totally fine Big Story: Meet the DEA’s premier crypto detective OpenAI is pissing off mathematicians Want better search results? Make WIRED a preferred source in Google Written by WIRED Staff Topics immigration Department of Homeland Security Immigration and Customs Enforcement Customs and Border Protection privacy cybersecurity First Amendment free speech hackers hacking Read More ICE Is Running One of the Largest Anti-Left Surveillance Operations in US History ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations is engaged in far-reaching spying against left-wing activists that rivals the FBI and CIA crackdowns on the Civil Rights and anti-war movements. Ali Winston Bluesky Is Blocking Links to a Major Leak of DHS Employee Records Bluesky tells WIRED it blocked links to a leaked archive of information on 41,000 ICE, CBP, and other DHS workers because it contains people’s contact information, shared without their authorization. Dhruv Mehrotra ICE Has Been Dumping Protester Photos Into a Palantir Database DHS agents not only tracked and intimidated people observing ICE activity in Maine, but stored information about them in a database run on Palantir software, newly unsealed court filings say. Maddy Varner ICE Emails Discuss Using Palantir-Supported Tool to Investigate Voter Fraud Documents obtained by Democracy Forward show that ICE looked into feeding voter roll data into the ELITE tool, normally used to identify targets for deportation. David Gilbert Chicago-Area Cops Helped HSI Spy on Minnesota Anti-ICE Activists Despite Illinois’ sanctuary laws, local police in and around Chicago helped ICE investigative agents track activists engaged in First Amendment–protected activities. Ali Winston The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans Two US senators say the Trump administration is breaking the law by withholding the FISA court decision while it presses Congress to renew America’s most sweeping surveillance program. Dell Cameron A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System Sources tell WIRED that an Accenture employee’s personal Claude agent ran on a DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Vittoria Elliott Democrats Are Gearing Up to Investigate the Trump Administration. It Won’t Be Easy As a recent government report on DOGE shows, even getting basic information out of the Trump administration will put a new Congress to the test. Vittoria Elliott Massive Groups of Volunteers Are Ready to Face Down ICE at the Polls From heat maps to Signal chats to war rooms, volunteers across the US are ready to act if federal immigration agents show up on Election Day. David Gilbert ICE Agent at NYC Shooting Has History of Alleged Violence and Illegal Arrests Brenden Cuni, an ICE supervisor, has been accused of excessive force and tackling a pregnant woman to the ground. Several of his arrests were later found to be unlawful in federal court. Dhruv Mehrotra Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon’s Producer Investigators also sought permission to use an invasive surveillance tool called a cell-site simulators against journalist Georgia Fort and a Minnesota state Senate candidate. Dhruv Mehrotra A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There Despite the agency's human resources department saying he hadn’t even been onboarded, Jeremy Lewin oversaw the destruction of USAID. It’s not clear he had the legal authority to do so. Molly Knight Raskin WIRED is obsessed with what comes next. Through rigorous investigations and game-changing reporting, we tell stories that don’t just reflect the moment—they help create it. When you look back in 10, 20, even 50 years, WIRED will be the publication that led the story of the present, mapped the people, products, and ideas defining it, and explained how those forces forged the future. title: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears
body_text: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Artificial Intelligence Technology of Business Africa Business Paths to Success US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn Image source, Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images By Rachel Clun Business reporter ,Â Reporting from New York Published 30 October 2026 Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI). Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday. Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025. While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble. Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026. Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday, taking more than $500bn (Â£374bn) off its market value after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue. At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI. The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value. The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors. On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter. "Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report. In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months. Amazon and Reddit down Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months. The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers. Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading. Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic. Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped. Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI. Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google. He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out". "The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down." 'Investors have turned ruthless' Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market. The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it. Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months. "Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said. "The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs." However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago. While the Nasdaq closed 2.8% lower, it is up 7.8% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 8% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.3%. Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks. "If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said. title: H.264 Is Magic (2016)
body_text: H.264 is magic: a technical walkthrough of a remarkable technology. Sid Bala Home LinkedIn GitHub Sign in Subscribe H.264 is Magic Sid Bala 02 Nov 2016 • 10 min read Share H.264 is a video compression codec standard. It is ubiquitous - internet video, Blu-ray, phones, security cameras, drones, everything. Everything uses H.264 now. H.264 is a remarkable piece of technology. It is the result of 30+ years of work with one single goal: To reduce the bandwidth required for transmission of full-motion video. Technically, it is very interesting. This post will give insight into some of the details at a high level - I hope to not bore you too much with the intricacies. Also note that many of the concepts explained here apply to video compression in general, and not just H.264. Why even compress anything? A simple uncompressed video file will contain an array of 2D buffers containing pixel data for each frame. So it's a 3D (2 spatial dimensions and 1 temporal) array of bytes. Each pixel takes 3 bytes to store - one byte each for the three primary colors (red, green and blue). 1080p @ 60 Hz = 1920x1080x60x3 => ~ 370 MB/sec of raw data. This is next to impossible to deal with. A 50GB Blu-ray disk will only hold ~2 mins. You can't move it anywhere fast. Even SSDs have trouble dumping this straight from RAM to Disk[^1]. So yeah. We need compression. Why H.264 compression? Yes, I will answer this. But first let me show you something. Here is the Apple Homepage: I captured the screen of this home page and produced two files: PNG screenshot of the Apple homepage 1015KB 5 Second 60fps H.264 video of the same Apple homepage 175KB Eh. What? Those file sizes look switched. No, they're right. The H.264 video, 300 frames long is 175KB. A single frame of that video in PNG is 1015KB. It looks like we're storing 300 times the amount of data in the video. But the file size is a fifth. So H.264 would seem to be 1500x as efficient as PNG. How is this even possible? All right, what's the trick? There are very many tricks! H.264 uses all the tricks you can think of (and tons you can't think of). Let's go through the important ones. Shedding weight Imagine you're building a car for street racing. You need to go faster. What is the first thing you do? You shed some weight. Your car weighs 3000 lbs. You throw away stuff you don't need. Those back seats? pfft. Chuck those. That subwoofer? Gone. No music for you. Air Conditioning? Yeah, ditch it. Transmission? Ye..no. Wait! We're gonna need that. You remove everything except the things that matter. This concept of throwing away bits you don't need to save space is called lossy compression. H.264 is a lossy codec - it throws away less important bits and only keeps the important bits. PNG is a lossless codec. It means that nothing is thrown away. Bit for bit, the original source image can be recovered from a PNG encoded image. Important bits? How does the algorithm know what bits in my frame are important? There are few obvious ways to trim out images. Maybe the top right quadrant is useless all the time. So maybe we can zero out those pixels and discard that quadrant. We would use only 3/4th of the space we need. ~2200 lbs now. Or maybe we can crop out a thick border around the edges of the frame, the important stuff is in the middle anyway. Yes, you could do these. But H.264 doesn't do this. What does H.264 actually do? H.264, like other lossy image algorithms, discards detail information. Here is a close-up of the original compared with the image post-discard. See how the compressed one does not show the holes in the speaker grills in the MacBook Pro? If you don't zoom in, you would even notice the difference. The image on the right weighs in at 7% the size of the original - and we haven't even compressed the image in the traditional sense. Imagine your car weighed just 200 lbs! 7% wow! How do you discard detail information like that? For this we need a quick math lesson. Information Entropy Now we're getting to the juicy bits! Ha puns! If you took an information theory class, you might remember information entropy. Information entropy is the number of bits required to represent some information. Note that it is not simply the size of some dataset. It is minimum number of bits that must be used to represent all the information contained in a dataset. For example, if your dataset is the result of a single coin toss, you need 1 bit of entropy. If you have record two coin tosses, you'll need 2 bits. Makes sense? Suppose you have some strange coin - you've tossed it 10 times, and every time it lands on heads. How would you describe this information to someone? You wouldn't say HHHHHHHHH. You would just say "10 tosses, all heads" - bam! You've just compressed some data! Easy. I saved you hours of mindfuck lectures. This is obviously an oversimplification, but you've transformed some data into another shorter representation of the same information. You've reduced data redundancy . The information entropy in this dataset has not changed - you've just converted between representations. This type of encoder is called an entropy encoder - it's a general-purpose lossless encoder that works for any type of data. Frequency Domain Now that you understand information entropy, let's move on to transformations of data. You can represent data in some fundamental units. If you use binary, you have 0 and 1. If you use hex, you have 16 characters. You can easily transform between the two systems. They are essentially equivalent. So far so good? Ok! Now, some imagination! Imagine you can transform any dataset that varies over space(or time) - something like the brightness value of an image, into a different coordinate space. So instead of x-y coordinates, let's say we have frequency coordinates. freqX and freqY are the axes now. This is called a frequency domain representation. There is another mindfuck mathematical theorem[^2] that states that you can do this for any data and you can achieve a perfect lossless transformation as long as freqX and freqY are high enough. Okay, but what the freq are freqX and freqY? freqX and freqY are some other set of basis units. Just like when we switch from binary to hex, we have a different fundamental unit, we're switching from the familiar X-Y to freqX and freqY. Hex 'A' looks different from binary '1010'. Both mean the same thing, but look different. So here is what our image looks like in the frequency domain: The fine grill on that MacBook pro has a high information content in the higher frequency components of that image. Finely varying content = high frequency components. Any sort of gradual variation in the color and brightness - such as gradients are low frequency components of that image. Anything in between falls in between. So fine details = high freq. Gentle gradients = low freq. Makes sense? In the frequency domain representation, the low frequency components are near the center of that image. The higher frequency components are towards of the edges of the image. Okay. Kinda makes sense. But why do all this? Because now, you can take that frequency domain image and then mask out the edges - discard information which will contain the information with high frequency components. Now if you convert back to your regular x-y coordinates, you'll find that the resulting image looks similar to the original but has lost some of the fine details. But now, the image only occupies a fraction of the space. By controlling how big your mask is, you can now tune precisely how detailed you want your output images to be. Here is the close-up of the laptop in the home page again. Except now, there is a circular border mask that's been applied. The numbers represent the information entropy of that image as a fraction of the original. Even at 2%, you won't notice the difference unless you're at this zoom level. 2%! - your car now weighs 60 lbs! So that's how you shed weight. This process in lossy compression is called quantization [^3]. Okay. Impressive, I guess. What else you got? Chroma Subsampling. The human/eye brain system is not very good at resolving finer details in color. It can detect minor variations in brightness very easily but not color. So there must be some way to discard color information to shed even more weight. In a TV signal, R+G+B color data gets transformed to Y+Cb+Cr. The Y is the luminance (essentially black and white brightness) and the Cb and Cr are the chrominance (color) components. RGB and YCbCr are equivalent in terms of information entropy. Why unnecessarily complicate? RGB not good enough for you? Back before we had color TV, we only had the Y signal. And when color TVs just started coming along, engineers had to figure out a way to transmit RGB color along with Y. Instead of using two separate data streams, they wisely decided to encode the color information into Cb and Cr and transmit that along with the Y information. That way, BW TVs would only look at the Y component. Color TVs will, in addition, look at the chrominance components and convert to RGB internally. But check out the trick: the Y component gets encoded at full resolution. The C components only at a quarter resolution. Since the eye/brain is terrible at detecting color variations, you can get away with this. By doing this, you reduce total bandwidth by one half, with very little visual difference. Half! Your car now weighs 30 lbs! This process of discarding some of the color information is called Chroma Subsampling [^4]. While not specific to H.264 and has been around for decades itself, it is used almost universally. Those are the big weight shedders for lossy compression. Our frames are now tiny - since we discarded most of the detail information and half of the color information. Wait. That's it? Can we do something more? Yes. Weight shedding is only the first step. So far we're only looking at the spatial domains within a single frame. Now it's time to explore temporal compression - where we look at a group of frames across time. Motion compensation H.264 is a motion compensation compression standard. Motion compensation? What now? Imagine you're watching a tennis match. The camera is fixed at a certain angle. The only thing moving is the ball back and forth. How would you encode this information? You do what you always do, right? You have a 3D array of pixels, two dimensions in space and one in time. Right? Nah. Why would you? Most of the image is the same anyway. The court, the net, the crowds, all are static. The only real action is the ball moving. What if you could just have one static image of everything in the background, and then one moving image of just the ball? Wouldn't that save a lot of space? You see where I am going with this? Get it? See where I am going? Motion estimation? Lame jokes aside, this is exactly what H.264 does. H.264 splits up the image into macro-blocks - typically 16x16 pixel blocks that it will use for motion estimation. It encodes one static image - typically called an I-frame (Intra frame). This is a full frame - containing all the bits it required to construct that frame. And then subsequent frames are either P-frames (predicted) or B-frames (bi-directionally predicted). P-frames are frames that will encode a motion vector for each of the macro-blocks from the previous frame. So a P-frame has to be constructed by the decoder based on previous frames. It starts with the last I-frame in the video stream and then walks through every subsequent frame - adding up the motion vector deltas as it goes along until it arrives at the current frame. B-frames are even more interesting, where the prediction happens bi-directionally, both from past frames and from future frames. So you can imagine now why that Apple home page video is so well compressed. Because it's really just three I-frames in which the macro blocks are being panned around. Let's say you've been playing a video on YouTube. You missed the last few seconds of dialog, so you scrub back a few seconds. Have you noticed that it doesn't instantly start playing from that timecode you just selected. It pauses for a few moments and then plays. It's already buffered those frames from the network, since you just played it, so why that pause? Yeah that annoys the shit out of me. Why does it do that? Because you've asked the decoder to jump to some arbitrary frame, the decoder has to redo all the calculations - starting from the nearest I-frames and adding up the motion vector deltas to the frame you're on - and this is computationally expensive, and hence the brief pause. Hopefully you'll be less annoyed now, knowing it's actually doing hard work and not just sitting around just to annoy you. Since you're only encoding motion vectors deltas, this technique is extremely space-efficient for any video with motion, at the cost of some computation. Now we've covered both spatial and temporal compression! So far we have a shitton of space saved in Quantization. Chroma subsampling further halved the space required. On top of that, we have motion compensation that stores only 3 actual frames for the ~300 that we had in that video. Looks pretty good to me. Now what? Now we wrap up and seal the deal. We use a traditional lossless entropy encoder. Because why not? Let's just slap that on there for good measure. Entropy Coder The I-frames, after the lossy steps, contain redundant information. The motion vectors for each of the macro blocks in the P and B-frames - there are entire groups of them with the same values - since several macro blocks move by the same amount when the image pans in our test video. An entropy encoder will take care of this redundancy. And since it is a general purpose lossless encoder, we don't have to worry about what tradeoffs it's making. We can recover all the data that goes in. And, we're done! At the core of it, this is how video compression codecs like H.264 work. These are its tricks. Ok great! But I am curious to know how much our car weighs now. The original video was captured at an odd resolution of 1232x1154. If we apply the math here, we get: 5 secs @ 60 fps = 1232x1154x60x3x5 => 1.2 GB Compressed video => 175 KB If we apply the same ratio to our 3000 lb car, we get 0.4 lbs as the final weight. 6.5 ounces! Yeah. It's magic! Obviously, I am massively oversimplifying several decades of intense research in this field. If you want to know more, the Wikipedia Page is pretty descriptive. Have comments? Did I get something wrong? Not a fan of the lame jokes? Offended by the swearing? Use HackerNews or Reddit for voicing your opinion! Or hit me up on Twitter or LinkedIn if you want to chat. [^1] SSD Benchmarks [^2] Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem [^3][Quantization]( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantization_(signal_processing) [^4] Chroma Subsampling Sign up for more like this. Enter your email Subscribe Sid Bala © 2026 Powered by Ghost

The first one creates the game: given the current frame and the action, it predicts the next frame and the reward. The second one plays that game: it uses the generated frame and picks an action. Every frame above was sampled by the world model network, and the actions were taken by the actor network. Why I got interested in looped transformers, where one transformer block is applied several times with the same weights instead of stacking different layers. Reusing weights is cheap on memory, so I wanted to see if a looped world model could be small enough to run on a microcontroller. I picked the Pico 2 W because it is cheap and has an FPU, and small games because I could write the real versions directly into numpy and check every generated frame against them. Later I added a streaming RL agent so the board could also learn to play inside its own dream. Contents: the two networks · the games · the world model · the agents · quantization · on the chip · flashing · browser · reproduce · code layout The world model and the actor network 1: the world model network 2: the actor job frame + action → next frame + reward frame → action architecture looped transformer, q int8 MLP with two hidden layers, float32 size 26k–131k parameters 9k–16k parameters cost per frame 2–8M multiply-adds 9k–16k multiply-adds trained on recorded real games ( how ) with stream-x, in the real game or inside the dream ( how ) The size depends on the game, some games require more parameters to learn them to be playable, we tried to get to keep the number of the parameters small enough. On the chip neither network ever uses the real game: the actor only sees frames the world model, and the world model only gets actions from the actor. Both run on core 1 of the RP2350, while core 0 handles USB and the display. The pretrained actor can be swapped for a fresh stream-x agent that learns from scratch on the board. And any button press hands control to you, so you can play the dream yourself. The games Each game is a few hundred lines of numpy in src/tinyworldformer/games/ . It renders to a small grid of token ids, and one frame always holds the whole game state, so hidden state has to be drawn into the frame: the ball's heading is part of its token, and Doom-lite has a minimap. game frame rules random event world model exact frames, 2 loops Breakout 20×16 paddle, ball, 56 bricks, 5 lives the serve after a miss 26k params, 4.3M MACs 99.99% Doom-lite 32×32 raycast first-person view of an 8×8 maze; an enemy walks shortest paths to you; you shoot the enemy's respawn 55k params, 4.2M MACs 83.6% (see below) Flappy Bird 24×24 gravity, flaps, scrolling pipes the next gap height 46k params, 2.0M MACs 100% Pong 20×32 you against a CPU paddle that reacts late, first to 5 the serve after a point 46k params, 2.3M MACs 99.45% Pac-Man lite 48×48 23×21 maze, 249 pellets, two ghosts on shortest paths, 3 lives the ghosts' respawn 131k params, 8.2M MACs 86.4% "Exact frames" is the share of held-out transitions where every cell of the predicted frame matches the real game. Frames right after a random event are left out, since those can only be sampled, not predicted. Doom-lite's 3D view has 768 cells and a single shaded wall pixel off counts the whole frame as wrong, so its number looks worse than it plays; the game state is almost always right (see checking the dream ). You can play the real games in a terminal: uv run python -m tinyworldformer.games.play --game pacman (or breakout , doomlite , flappy , pong ). How the world model works Frames split into tokens The frame is cut into square patches: 2×2 cells in Breakout, 4×4 in Doom-lite, Flappy Bird and Pong, 6×6 in Pac-Man. That gives 36 to 80 tokens per game. A patch's embedding is the sum of one learned vector per cell, with a separate table for each position inside the patch so the cell order isn't lost. Every token also gets a position vector and the action's vector. Looped Transformer The model is a single transformer block (attention plus a ReLU MLP) with one set of weights, applied 1 to 4 times, with the input added back before every pass. The output after every pass is trained against the next frame, so at run time the loop count trades speed for accuracy. On the Pico to keep a decent frame rate we use uses two loops. The animation shows one held-out Doom-lite step. After one pass the model draws an enemy that isn't there, and each further pass removes part of it: 92, 35, 12, then 0 wrong cells. The bars on the right are the share of held-out frames each loop count gets exactly right. Here is a dreamed Doom-lite step decoded after 1, 2, 3 and 4 loops, with red boxes on cells that differ from the real rules: Exact held-out frames by loop count: loops Breakout Doom-lite Flappy Bird Pong Pac-Man 1 99.68% 59.8% 99.99% 98.47% 79.6% 2 99.99% 83.6% 100% 99.45% 86.4% 3 100% 85.9% 100% 99.60% 85.7% 4 99.96% 84.7% 100% 99.53% 84.4% Decoding The model outputs a score for every cell and every token. Turning those scores into a frame turned out to matter almost as much as the model, and it ended up as three rules (shown above on Pong): Background cells (walls, bricks, pellets, floor) each take their most likely token independently. Singletons (the ball, the player, each ghost) are placed with one choice over all (cell, token) pairs, so there is always exactly one of each. After a random event the choice is sampled among candidates within 2.2 logits of the best, so the world model samples a new serve or respawn instead of averaging them. Pac-Man and the ghosts are 2×2 sprites, but only one cell of each carries state (the mouth holds the heading; the ghost's lower-left cell holds whether a pellet is underneath). The other three cells are stamped from it instead of predicted. We implemented Rule 2 because the first Breakout model drew two balls at once; one global choice took exact frames from 91.6% to 99.7%. Checking the world model Accuracy on recorded data wasn't enough. An agent drives the dream into states the data never had, and any mistake there is something it can exploit. So the main check runs while an agent plays: read the game state back off the dreamed frame ( games/<game>.py: read ), apply the real rules to that state and the agent's action, and compare the result with the next dreamed frame and reward. 5,000 dreamed steps per game at 2 loops, with the shipped agent ( training/evalwm.py --agent ): game wrong game states wrong rewards wrong cells per step Breakout not read back; 0 frames with impossible tokens 6 (paid without a brick breaking) – Doom-lite 1 0 1.50 Flappy Bird 0 0 0.00 Pong 1 0 0.00 Pac-Man 742 38 0.39 Training First, agents play the real game and every step is recorded as one example (frame, action, next frame, reward), 1–3 million per game. Some episodes start from unusual states, like bricks with holes or random positions, so the data covers more of the game. Then the world model learns to predict the next frame with a per-cell cross-entropy loss: 30k steps, with the first 3–4k steps run in float, then int8 rounding switches on ( QAT ). The int8 weights are written into Rust source with every float stored as its exact bits. We check them with cargo test to reproduces the Python integer spec bit for bit, and then the firmware runs on the Pico. An agent trained in the world model reaches states the recorded data never had, so record real games with that agent and fine-tune the world model on everything. The agent in different games stated exploiting them so those are some fixes to it: Weighting the loss by "this cell changed" biased the model toward predicting change, so it drew two balls and broke two bricks. Weighting by where things can happen in the input frame, plus the global singleton choice, fixed it. A Breakout agent in the dream got 154 points with 26 bricks left, because the world model didn't remove bricks from the corner when it were hit. Doom-lite agents learned to snipe from 5 cells away. Agents trained only in the dream scored 210 there (the real maximum is 56) and 28 in the real game, as World Models (Ha & Schmidhuber) predicts. Each collect-and-fine-tune round closed the exploit that agent had found. The Doom-lite dream sometimes lost the enemy sprite and never drew it again: the model copied the previous view instead of redrawing it from the minimap. Noise augmentation fixed it ( train --noise 0.3 , as in GameNGen): input views get random pixels and sometimes lose the sprite. d=32 couldn't absorb the wider Breakout data and d=48 could. Pac-Man's 48×48 frame needed d=64 . The agents: stream-x The agents use Stream AC(λ) (Elsayed, Vasan & Mahmood, 2024), which learns from one transition at a time: no replay buffer, no batches, no target network. Eligibility traces carry credit back in time, and ObGD shrinks any step that would overshoot the TD target. The policy and value networks each have two hidden layers of 64 units (32 on the Pico) with LayerNorm. The input is a feature vector read off the frame ( training/streamx.py: observe_* , mirrored in Rust in tinyworldformer-rs/src/agent.rs ). For example, the ball's row, column and heading in Breakout, or in Pac-Man, for each direction, the shortest-path distance to the nearest pellet and how close each ghost is. Below is one training run per game (real game, 500k steps) at six stages: untrained, the end, and the snapshots where the score has covered 25, 50, 75 and 95% of the way. Each panel plays greedily from the same start and skips a few steps per frame. "try" counts the episodes played so far, so you can see the crashes. Breakout Doom-lite Flappy Bird Pac-Man lite Pong Greedy return in the real game, mean of 10 episodes, at snapshots of the same run: game 0 1k 2k 5k 10k 20k 50k 100k 150k 250k 500k max Breakout 8.2 17.0 15.9 21.9 29.9 29.9 29.9 31.1 35.0 39.9 45.6 56 Doom-lite −5.0 −5.0 −5.0 −5.0 −5.0 59.5 69.9 78.1 81.8 82.1 82.9 – Flappy Bird −1.0 −1.0 −1.0 1.9 24.6 24.9 96.2 123.7 309.2 332 332 332 Pac-Man 7.0 3.8 17.0 17.7 8.2 46.8 72.9 138.9 146.6 190.3 217.4 249 Pong −4.3 −3.9 −3.9 −3.9 −1.7 −2.0 −0.3 1.1 1.7 1.1 1.1 5 Without shaping, Doom-lite agents camp in the start corner and fire, because the enemy always comes to them. --idle-penalty 0.1 costs 0.1 for each step spent in a cell visited more than 6 times in the last 20 steps. The position is read off the minimap, so the penalty works inside the dream too. With it the agent patrols and gets twice the kills. tinyworldformer-rs/src/learner.rs is the same algorithm in no_std Rust, with the backward pass written by hand. It matches 200 PyTorch updates to within 3.5e-6. On the host, a fresh agent inside the Rust int8 Flappy Bird dream averages 6 pipes per episode after 25k steps, 121 after 100k, and 300+ after 250k. Quantization and the Pico Every matrix in the world model is int8 with one scale per output row ( scale = max|w| / 127 ). Activations are int8 too, with one scale per tensor and per loop index, since the loops see different ranges. Matmuls sum int8 × int8 into int32 (two multiply-adds per SMLAD instruction on the RP2350) and then apply one float multiply by the two scales. Softmax uses a 1024-entry exp table, with probabilities stored as uint8. Norms, residuals and embeddings stay in float32, since the RP2350 has an FPU. Training applies the same rounding (QAT with a straight-through estimator), so the int8 model is the model that was trained. rustexport/intref.py is the int8 model in numpy with every float operation in a fixed order; the Rust engine reproduces it bit for bit, and cargo test checks golden vectors for every exported env. game int8 weights float32 (embeddings, norms, scales) game data agent (float32) firmware flash firmware RAM Breakout 19.7 KB 31.6 KB 1.1 KB 54.1 KB 361 KB 299 KB Doom-lite 33.9 KB 91.9 KB 12.0 KB 61.3 KB 471 KB 357 KB Flappy Bird 30.1 KB 69.5 KB 10.1 KB 50.8 KB 409 KB 227 KB Pong 30.1 KB 70.4 KB 10.9 KB 52.6 KB 414 KB 244 KB Flash and RAM are measured from the firmware ELF ( size -A ), built with the Display Pack driver, so they include the code, USB, the display driver and the on-device learner. The Pico 2 W has 4 MB of flash and 520 KB of SRAM, 512 KiB of it in the main memory map. The float32 embedding tables are the largest part and could be int8 too. src/tinyworldformer/rustexport/ imports only numpy and torch (a test keeps it that way), so other projects can reuse the export: build a model from rustexport.qat ( QLinear , LoopedBlock ), train it with ActQuant.enabled = True after a float warm-up, convert it with rustexport.convert.looped_model , then write the Rust source with int_model_arrays , mlp_arrays and codegen.write_module . rustexport.Golden writes the vectors a Rust test checks. On the chip The firmware ( tinyworldformer-rs/firmware ) is no_std Rust on embassy. Nothing is allocated at run time: the weights are static arrays in flash, and every buffer is a fixed-size static in RAM. Core 1 runs the game. One pass of its loop ( dream_loop in firmware/src/main.rs ) is one frame: The actor reads features off the current frame ( agent::observe ) and runs its MLP to pick a button. If on-device learning is on, the learning agent picks instead; if you are pressing buttons, your press is used. The int8 transformer runs 2 loops over the frame and the button ( Engine::forward ), and decoding turns its scores into the next frame: background argmax per cell, each singleton placed once (sampled for random events with an xorshift RNG), then the sprite stamps. The reward is the argmax of the reward head; lives and episode ends are counters on top. If learning is on, the learner updates from this one transition and then forgets it. The frame goes to core 0 through a two-slot channel. If core 0 is still busy with the previous frame, this one is dropped, so core 1 never waits for the screen. When you play, core 1 slows down to a playable speed (66–150 ms per frame, depending on the game). The agent runs as fast as the chip allows. Core 0 runs embassy async tasks for everything else. Over USB serial, each frame goes out as coloured ANSI text with a status line (model time, actor time, fps, env and agent names), and keys come back in. The optional Display Pack ( --features display ) is a 320×240 ST7789 over SPI at up to 62.5 MHz, and only cells that changed since the last frame are redrawn. Its buttons are polled every 20 ms. The two cores share only the frame channel and a few atomics: who is playing, the pressed key, learning on/off, and the loop count. Where the memory goes: in flash in RAM world model int8 matrices, float32 embeddings, norms and scales, the game's opening frames and colours (52–138 KB) scratch buffers for one forward pass: activations for 36–80 tokens, the int8 copies the matmuls read, and the per-cell scores of the next frame (114 KB for Flappy Bird up to 368 KB for Pac-Man, whose per-cell scores alone take 184 KB) actor float32 MLP weights and feature normalization (51–61 KB) its features and hidden layers (about 1 KB) on-device learner code only weights, eligibility traces and normalization for two 32-unit networks (49 KB for Pac-Man up to 106 KB for Doom-lite; it scales with the number of input features) firmware code, USB, display driver (about 150 KB) stacks (16 KB for core 1), USB buffers, frame channels Every game fits in the 4 MB of flash and 512 KiB of SRAM. Breakout uses 361 KB of flash and 299 KB of SRAM; Pac-Man, the largest, uses 600 KB and 460 KB. Most of the time goes into int8 dot products ( dot_i8 in src/lib.rs ). One 32-bit load fetches 4 weights, SXTB16 unpacks bytes 0/2 and 1/3 into 16-bit halves, and SMLAD does two multiply-adds in one instruction. Attention multiplies uint8 probabilities by int8 values, so it uses UXTB16 instead. Norms, the exp table lookup and the final per-output scale stay in float32 on the FPU. A frame at 2 loops is 2–4M multiply-adds (8.2M for Pac-Man); on a desktop CPU the same Rust code dreams a frame in 0.7 ms (Flappy Bird) to 1.5 ms (Breakout). I haven't measured the frame rate on the Pico itself yet. The board boots with a fresh agent learning on the device. Press l over USB, or hold B for 1 s on the Display Pack, to switch to the pretrained actor, and again to switch back. Flashing a game and an agent Every export sits side by side in the crate: world models in tinyworldformer-rs/models/envs/<env>/ , agents in models/agents/<game>/<agent>/ . You pick both at build time. cd tinyworldformer-rs ./flash.sh --list # what is exported ./flash.sh --env doomlite --agent doom_agent_roam_p0.3 # build and flash (hold BOOTSEL while plugging in) ./flash.sh --env breakout --display # with the Display Pack ./flash.sh --env pong --host # play it in this terminal ./flash.sh --env flappy --default # make it the default for plain cargo TWF_ENV=doomlite TWF_AGENT=doom_agent_roam_p0.1 cargo test --release # golden tests for that pair Without --agent , the agent for the env's game listed in models/default is used if there is one, otherwise the first by name. An agent for a different game is refused with a list of the valid ones. The status line on screen shows which env and agent are running. Keys over USB: Breakout a/d/s, Doom-lite w/a/d/space/s, Flappy space, Pac-Man w/a/s/d, Pong w/s. Then g hands back to the agent, 1 – 4 set the loop count, l toggles on-device learning and r restarts it. In the browser The same no_std int8 engine also compiles to WebAssembly ( tinyworldformer-rs/web/ ). The module has no imports and no wasm-bindgen, and it runs the firmware's loop: dream, agent, and stream-x learning on the fly. A static page draws the frames on a canvas. rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown # once cd tinyworldformer-rs/web ./build.sh # one module per env into www/ (or ./build.sh pong flappy) python3 -m http.server -d www # open http://localhost:8000, ?env=pacman picks a game With the same seed, the wasm build dreams the same episodes as the native build, frame for frame, at 1–5 ms per frame depending on the game. Each module carries its game's default agent; TWF_AGENT=... ./build.sh <env> picks another. The keys are the same as on the Pico, plus arrow keys and on-screen buttons, and f runs the dream as fast as it can, which helps while learning ( l ). Reproduce uv sync G=pong # breakout, doomlite, flappy, pacman, pong uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.data --game $G --transitions 2000000 --varied 0.3 # -> data/$G uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.train --data data/ $G --d 48 --heads 3 --ff 96 --out models/ ${G} _wm.pt uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.streamx --env real --game $G --out models/ ${G} _agent.pt uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.evalwm --ckpt models/ ${G} _wm.pt --agent models/ ${G} _agent.pt # check the dream uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.streamx --env dream --wm models/ ${G} _wm.pt --out models/ ${G} _dream_agent.pt uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.export --ckpt models/ ${G} _wm.pt uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.streamx --out models/ ${G} _agent.pt --export tinyworldformer-rs cd tinyworldformer-rs && TWF_ENV= $G cargo test --release && TWF_ENV= $G cargo run --release Settings that differ per game: game settings Breakout 1M transitions, --miss-penalty 5 , then collect with the agent ( data --learned <agent> --holes 0.5 --out data/breakout_learned ) and fine-tune on all of it ( train --init ... --data data/breakout data/breakout_learned --steps 15000 --warmup-float 0 --lr 1e-3 ), four rounds Doom-lite --varied 0.5 , train --noise 0.3 , streamx --max-ep-steps 500 --idle-penalty 0.1 Flappy Bird streamx --max-ep-steps 3000 Pac-Man 1.2M transitions, --varied 0.4 , train --d 64 --heads 4 --ff 128 --steps 40000 --warmup-float 4000 , streamx --miss-penalty 5 --max-ep-steps 1500 Pong streamx --max-ep-steps 5000 Code layout path contents src/tinyworldformer/games/ the five games (rules, rendering, read ), the Game registry, scripted agents, terminal play src/tinyworldformer/training/ data, world model, training, dream checks, stream-x, export to the Rust crate src/tinyworldformer/rustexport/ reusable PyTorch → no_std Rust export: QAT layers, the int8 spec, conversion, code generation tinyworldformer-rs/ no_std int8 engine, dream loop, agent and learner; host demo ( src/main.rs ) tinyworldformer-rs/firmware/ Pico 2 W firmware tinyworldformer-rs/web/ WebAssembly build and the browser page ( www/ ) About Tiny world model generates games and stream ac plays them all on Pico 2W sheepseb.github.io/stealth/posts/tinyworldformer.html Topics rust transformers Resources Readme Activity Stars 303 stars Watchers 2 watching Forks 12 forks Report repository Releases Packages Contributors Languages Footer © 2026 GitHub, Inc. title: Zero click, silent, remote Android DoS
body_text: SMS of Death: zero-click Android telephony DoS SMS OF DEATH Vulnerability Impact Why it matters PoC Android Telephony Â· Zero-Click Â· Remote DoS SMS of Death A single malformed WAP Push SMS crashes com.android.phone on Android, dropping active calls ( including emergency calls ), with zero interaction from the victim. Download APK Source â Working proof-of-concept, authorised testing only. Read the warning & license before downloading. Component WapPushOverSms frameworks/opt/telephony Interaction None zero-click, silent Vector Remote SMS WAP Push, port 2948 Affected Android 12â17 patched in 14â17, Oct 2026 update Reporter Mark B Reported 5 May 2026 Android & Devices VRP Disclosed 29 Oct 2026 public writeup Recovery ADB only normal user: bricked 01 / The vulnerability An unchecked cast turns a 5-byte header into a negative array size When Android receives a WAP Push message, WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() reads the WSP header length as a uintvar . The value comes back as a long , is cast to int with no range check, and is then used directly as the size of a new byte array: // WapPushOverSms.java:217 header length read as long, cast with no bounds check int headerLength = ( int ) pduDecoder.getValue32(); ... // WapPushOverSms.java:244 the cast value is used as an array size byte [] header = new byte [headerLength]; A 5-byte uintvar of 88 80 80 80 00 decodes to 0x80000000 . Cast to a signed 32-bit int , that is -2147483648 . Allocating new byte[-2147483648] throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException on the telephony main thread, killing com.android.phone : E AndroidRuntime: FATAL EXCEPTION: main E AndroidRuntime: Process: com.android.phone E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException: -2147483648 E AndroidRuntime: at ...WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:244) E AndroidRuntime: at ...WapPushOverSms.dispatchWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:339) E AndroidRuntime: at ...InboundSmsHandler.processMessagePart(InboundSmsHandler.java:1169) E AndroidRuntime: at ...InboundSmsHandler$DeliveringState.processMessage(InboundSmsHandler.java:627) The message is delivered as a data SMS and is never shown to the user: there is nothing in the inbox, and the victim never sees the sender's number. Affected versions. The code sits in Android's core telephony framework and has shipped in many releases. The crash has been reproduced from Android 12 (the reboot loop in issue #2 ) up to Android 16 . Google's October 2026 fix was released for Android 14 through 17 , so devices on older versions outside the security-update window, such as Android 12 and 13, run the same code and do not receive the fix. 02 / Impact Remote, silent, and recoverable only with effort Zero-click. The victim does nothing. No tap, no open, no notification. Silent. Nothing appears in Messages; the attacker's number is never shown. Calls drop, including emergency calls. Active voice calls terminate with DisconnectCause CS_DEATH as the process restarts. Telephony blackout. 1-2 seconds of no service per message while com.android.phone restarts. Carrier redelivery amplifies it. Unacknowledged messages are re-sent by the carrier, re-crashing the phone; a single message caused intermittent outages for up to a week in testing. ~20 messages render the device unusable for an extended period. Persistent denial of service. The malformed message stays queued and is retried on every boot, so the phone can crash on startup until it is cleared (recovery below). Tested across multiple makes and models (Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, various Samsung Galaxy and A-series) with a 100% reproduction rate. Recovery over ADB, contributed by @sakisdog After hitting the reboot loop on Android 12 , @sakisdog documented a less destructive recovery ( issue #2 ). The poison messages sit in the pending inbound queue ( content://sms/raw ) and are retried on every boot, so Android's RescueParty reboots the device into recovery roughly every 90 seconds. Deleting just those rows over ADB, in the short window after boot completes, breaks the loop with no factory reset: # while sys.boot_completed == 1: find the WAP Push rows (destination_port=134020), note the address adb shell content query --uri content://sms/raw --projection _id:destination_port:date:deleted # let the shell edit SMS storage, delete only those rows, then reset the permission adb shell cmd appops set com.android.shell WRITE_SMS allow adb shell "content delete --uri content://sms/raw --where \"address='<SENDER>'\"" adb shell cmd appops set com.android.shell WRITE_SMS default # last resort, erases ALL SMS/MMS and APN settings: adb shell pm clear com.android.providers.telephony Recovery credited to @sakisdog . It still needs a computer and ADB, and you should not choose "wipe data" at the recovery prompt, so for a non-technical user mid-loop it remains out of reach. This is the distinction the report turns on. It is not a transient crash: it is a remote, zero-click, persistent denial of service that, left untreated, reboots the phone into a recovery wipe-data prompt every ~90 seconds, driving a normal user to a factory reset to recover, which is the exact shape of a "Destructive Remote DoS" in the VRP's published rules. 03 / Why this is serious A remote attacker can cut a phone off from Triple Zero Dropping calls is not an inconvenience when one of those calls is to emergency services. While a device is under this attack, or stuck in the reboot loop, it cannot reliably place a call to 000 . The attack is remote, needs only the victim's number, and shows them nothing. Australia treats access to emergency calling as a mandatory property of a mobile service, not a nice-to-have. Under the Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination , administered by the ACMA , carriers are required to identify mobile phones that cannot reach Triple Zero, help the customer move to a working device, and stop providing service to the affected handset . Telstra states plainly that it is required to block phones that can no longer call 000, notifying the customer and blocking the device if nothing is done within 28 days. The consequence is perverse: the regulatory remedy for a phone that can't reach 000 is to cut it off the network , not to patch the OS. So an attacker who can remotely induce that condition on an Android handset can, in effect, get the victim's own device barred from carrier service until it is updated. The regulation exists precisely because loss of emergency-call access is considered a public-safety failure; this bug manufactures that failure on demand. The framework was tightened in 2024 following the 3G shutdown, which left some phones able to make ordinary calls but unable to reach emergency services, the same functional state this vulnerability produces. Sources: ACMA: proposed amendments to the ECS Determination Â· Telstra: Emergency Call Service Determination Â· Dept. of PM&C: impact analysis 04 / The fix One bounds check The remedy is a range check before the cast in WapPushOverSms.java (line 217) , provided to Google on the day of the first report: long rawHeaderLen = pduDecoder.getValue32(); if (rawHeaderLen < 0 || rawHeaderLen > pdu.length) { result.statusCode = Intents.RESULT_SMS_GENERIC_ERROR; return result; } int headerLength = ( int ) rawHeaderLen; What Google shipped Google fixed this crash, but not with the bounds check above. On 15 June 2026 an Android engineer authored commit 735d967 , "Fix remote DoS in decodeWapPdu," which shipped in the October 2026 Android security release for Android 14 through 17. Rather than validate the length, it widens the caught exception so the crash is swallowed, and deletes the triggering message so it cannot re-crash on carrier redelivery or on boot: // WapPushOverSms.java: widen the catch to cover NegativeArraySizeException - } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException aie) { + } catch (RuntimeException e) { // InboundSmsHandler.java: a failed decode now deletes the poison message + try { success = processMessagePart(tracker); } + catch (RuntimeException e) { deleteFromRawTable(...); } // breaks the boot loop This fix is part of the October 2026 Android security update. Devices updated to the October 2026 patch level or later are protected; devices on earlier patch levels remain vulnerable. 05 / Proof of concept Source & APK The proof-of-concept Android app and full source code are published on GitHub. The app crafts the malformed WAP Push PDU and sends it as a data SMS to a target number. Warning: this is a working weapon. The repository contains a proof-of-concept that can remotely disrupt and brick mobile phones. It is published strictly for security research, education, and defensive testing. Only run it against devices you own or are explicitly authorised to test. Using it against anyone else is a crime, and interfering with a person's ability to reach emergency services (000) is a serious criminal offence in Australia and most countries. The software is provided "as is", with no warranty, under the Apache License 2.0 . The author accepts no liability for any use, misuse, or damage. By downloading the APK or the source, you accept full responsibility for what you do with it.
