title: Ghostty 1.4
body_text: 1.4.0 - Release Notes Search docs Ctrl K Esc Docs Discord GitHub Download Download Discord GitHub Ghostty Docs About Ghostty Install Configuration Linux Features Terminal API (VT) Help Financial Support Ghostty Docs About Ghostty Install Binaries and Packages Build from Source Packaging Ghostty Prerelease Builds Release Notes Overview 1.4.0 1.3.1 1.3.0 1.2.3 1.2.2 1.2.1 1.2.0 1.1.3 1.1.2 1.1.1 1.1.0 1.0.1 Configuration Linux Features Terminal API (VT) Help Financial Support Ghostty Docs Install Release Notes 1.4.0 Ghostty 1.4.0 Release notes for Ghostty 1.4.0, released on October 27, 2026. Ghostty 1.4.0 is a major release that includes large performance and memory improvements, a 100% complete Kitty graphics implementation including animation and relative placements (the first non-Kitty terminal to do so), SSH integration improvements, and hundreds more improvements and fixes across all platforms. This release features 7 months of work with changes from 172 contributors over 2,889 commits . Thank you to all the contributors, maintainers, community moderators, translators, packagers, and users who each helped make this release possible. These release notes are painstakingly and lovingly hand-crafted by human Ghostty maintainers, including the full changelog. They take a combined 16+ hours to write, so please enjoy. 🥰 Ghostty is non-profit! Please support development. Almost all donations go directly to paying contributors. Learn more about how you can help. Learn more → Security GHSA-4hwh-wx3w-3fqg . Paste protection didn't treat carriage returns as line endings, so a paste could run a command without confirmation in programs that don't use bracketed paste. This requires user interaction (copy-paste) to trigger. GHSA-mhff-mv4q-fp63 . Malicious Kitty graphics commands could crash or hang Ghostty, force huge allocations, or in limited cases read or delete files outside the allowed temporary directories. This only requires displaying malicious output. GHSA-hcr9-7hcr-mjm8 . Malicious terminal output could crash Ghostty, closing every window, via tmux control mode. tmux doesn't need to be installed. This affects Ghostty 1.3.0 and 1.3.1. GHSA-hp9c-qp4q-cpw3 . The same impact as above, via a tmux control mode layout with a zero-sized or oversized pane. This affects Ghostty 1.3.0 and 1.3.1. GHSA-w9q4-5jvv-mcv4 . Clearing the screen into scrollback could corrupt memory if it deleted the scrollback page holding a styled or hyperlinked cursor. This only requires displaying malicious output, but only with a small scrollback-limit such as 0 . The default isn't known to be affected. GHSA-2r63-vmw6-3m3c . A crafted directory name could make the zsh shell integration send arbitrary escape sequences, such as silently replacing the clipboard via OSC 52. bash was affected in a more limited way. This only requires cd -ing into a directory from untrusted content, such as a cloned repository. macOS: GHSA-cw69-wm67-5pv8 . Cmd-clicking a crafted OSC 8 hyperlink could open unsafe local files or custom URL schemes, leading to arbitrary command execution. Ghostty now blocks unsafe targets and confirms custom URL schemes. This requires user interaction (cmd-click) to trigger. macOS: GHSA-mfw9-xcr3-7gfp . The same issue as above for links detected by the link configuration, including the default URL matcher. This requires user interaction (cmd-click) to trigger. macOS: GHSA-v8cw-fg4j-jcc4 . Drag-and-drop text skipped paste protection, with the same impact as above. This requires user interaction (drag-and-drop) to trigger. macOS: GHSA-mxqx-236q-wrv7 . Opening a file whose name contains control characters could run a different command than the one shown in the confirmation dialog. This requires a crafted file on your system and confirming the dialog. Note: I requested CVEs for the above advisories weeks ago, but GitHub hasn't assigned them yet. If/when they're assigned, I will update the above with proper CVE numbers. Highlights macOS 27 Support PRs: #12999 #13069 #13393 #14413 #14414 Ghostty 1.4 supports macOS 27 (Golden Gate). Most of the work was compatibility fixes: Tabs in the titlebar ( macos-titlebar-style = tabs ) lay out correctly again. The native tab bar no longer draws as a solid gray bar on top of your theme. It now lets the new glass style blend with your terminal background. macos-titlebar-style = hidden no longer covers the top lines of the terminal when Reduce Transparency is on. The app icon no longer has a thin border. The Shortcuts "New Window" action no longer opens two windows when Ghostty is running without any windows. Ghostty 1.4 remains fully compatible with prior macOS versions back to and including macOS 13 (Ventura). See the system requirements for more details. Note Ghostty 1.3.1 works on macOS 27, but it has some of the visual issues listed above, such as the gray tab bar. Kitty Graphics Animation and Relative Placements PRs: #13943 #13939 #13935 #13934 #13893 #13933 #13389 #13270 #13281 Ghostty now supports Kitty graphics animation and relative placements . These were the last major features of the Kitty graphics protocol that Ghostty didn't support. Programs that display animated images with the Kitty protocol, such as an animated GIF shown with kitten icat , now animate in Ghostty instead of showing a single still frame. Frame transmission, composition, and playback control are all supported, and animations pause while the terminal isn't visible. Relative placements let a program position one image relative to another image's placement, so the child image moves along with its parent. We also did a full conformance pass against the specification and Kitty itself, fixing dozens of behavioral differences. For example, images now scroll with text inside scroll regions ( #4323 ), retransmitting an image ID replaces the old image ( #6711 ), and invalid image data now gets an error response instead of silence, which could leave clients hanging. The full list is in the terminal capabilities section. Kitty graphics are faster, too. Image payloads are now parsed in bulk with SIMD instead of one byte at a time, making large image transfers about 16x faster to parse in our benchmarks (64 MiB of image data, x86_64 Linux), and drawing images costs much less per frame. Our Kitty graphics implementation now covers 100% of the published specification, making Ghostty (and libghostty) the first terminal to do this outside of Kitty itself. Scrollback Compression and Lower Memory Usage PRs: #13264 #13473 #13240 #13245 #14130 #14137 #14138 #14017 Ghostty now transparently compresses scrollback that isn't visible, reducing the physical memory those pages use by 70% to 90% for typical text-heavy history. Compression only runs while the terminal is idle and pages are decompressed on demand when you scroll back or search, so it has no measurable impact on I/O throughput. Thanks to compression, the default scrollback limit has been raised from 10 MB to 50 MB per terminal. On platforms that support compression, a full scrollback still generally uses less physical memory than the old 10 MB limit did. Note Compression lowers resident (physical) memory, not virtual memory, so look at resident memory when measuring it. It is currently available on macOS and 64-bit Linux. Beyond scrollback, memory usage is lower in many places: A new, empty terminal now uses about 16 KiB of terminal page memory on macOS, down from 128 KiB in Ghostty 1.3.1. On macOS and Linux, memory freed by clearing or trimming scrollback is now returned to the OS instead of being held until the terminal closes. Hidden tabs release their GPU resources. On macOS, with one visible tab and 20 hidden tabs, GPU memory dropped from about 385 MiB to 18 MiB. Rebuilding them when a tab becomes visible again takes under a millisecond. Performance Improvements PRs: #13209 #13220 #13226 #13227 #13537 #13827 #13587 #14011 #13722 #14035 #12760 There are performance improvements across the board in Ghostty 1.4 that yield significant gains compared to prior Ghostty versions. The biggest win came from a surprising discovery: on macOS, the kernel caps every read from a pty at about 1 KiB no matter how large the read buffer is. Previously, Ghostty processed each read as it arrived, so per-read overhead was paid every kilobyte, and the program writing output sat blocked while we parsed. Ghostty now drains the pty on one thread while parsing on another, raising end-to-end I/O throughput by 25% to 55% on macOS (M4 Max, plain and Unicode text) over Ghostty 1.3.x. VT processing itself is also much faster. In parser benchmarks, plain ASCII text went from 128 MB/s to 725 MB/s (5.7x), CJK text got 3.4x faster, and a 2.6 GB dataset of real-world terminal recordings from asciinema is processed about 25% faster. Together, these changes took cat -ing a 150 MB text file on macOS from 1.5 seconds to 566 milliseconds. Other notable improvements: Resize: resizing a terminal with a large scrollback is about 6x faster (120x80 with 10,000 lines of scrollback), and 3x to 5x faster with history full of CJK text or emoji. Rendering: the renderer holds the terminal lock 2.7x to 11x less per frame, leaving more time for the I/O thread during heavy output. Copy and search: formatting terminal contents as plain text, HTML, or VT, which backs clipboard copy, write_screen_file , and scrollback search, is 1.5x to 8x faster. Launch (macOS): about 15% faster from launch to visible window, and 27% faster to the first rendered frame. Idle energy: on macOS, the renderer's display link now sleeps when there's nothing to draw. On GTK, hidden tabs stop rendering, matching macOS. Large OSC sequences: OSC 52 clipboard payloads parse about 30x faster , and even short sequences like title changes are about 6x faster. New OpenGL Renderer (Linux, FreeBSD) PRs: #14052 #14269 The GTK app has a new rendering pipeline. It no longer uses GtkGLArea . Instead, the renderer draws with EGL on its own thread, exports each frame as a DMABUF, and hands it to GTK to display. Rendering is now triple-buffered, which should greatly reduce tearing, and no OpenGL calls run on the main thread anymore, which let us remove a number of workarounds. The most visible result is crisp text under fractional scaling. Text and box-drawing characters are no longer blurry with fractional display scaling such as 125% or 150% ( #1938 ). We fixed this once before, but it came back after upstream GTK changes. Ghostty now renders at the window's true fractional scale, so every rendered pixel maps to exactly one pixel on screen. The new render surface needs a system EGL library (see Changes for Package Maintainers ). On GPU drivers that can't export DMABUFs, Ghostty falls back to copying frames through the CPU, which is slower but works. Kitty Clipboard Protocol PRs: #13962 #13993 #13995 #13998 #14002 #14061 Ghostty now implements the Kitty clipboard protocol (OSC 5522) on both macOS and GTK. Ghostty 1.3 could parse the protocol but didn't implement it. OSC 52 can only read and write plain text. The Kitty clipboard protocol lets programs running in the terminal read and write any kind of clipboard data, such as images or HTML, and lets them pick among the formats on the clipboard. Programs can also enable paste events (mode 5522), which tell the program what formats a paste contains so it can read the one it wants. This is how a terminal program can accept a pasted image, for example. Clipboard access follows the existing clipboard-read and clipboard-write configurations. By default, reads prompt for permission and writes are allowed. The permission prompt shows a preview of the clipboard contents, including images. Programs that send a password can have your answer remembered for the rest of that terminal session. A new clipboard-write-limit-bytes configuration limits the size of a single write (default 64 MiB). A write over the limit fails and leaves the clipboard untouched. Split Drag and Drop (GTK) PRs: #10423 #13706 You can now rearrange splits on GTK by dragging them, matching the macOS feature introduced in Ghostty 1.3. When a tab has two or more splits, each split shows a drag handle at the top. Grab the handle and drop the split onto any other split, including splits in other tabs and windows. An overlay shows which side of the target split it will land on. The terminal contents, working directory, and running processes all move with it. A new drag-handle configuration controls when drag handles are shown on both macOS and GTK: auto (default), always , or never . With never , splits can't be rearranged with the mouse. Hiding the handles was a common request from users who found them in the way. On GTK, splits can only be dropped onto other splits. Dragging a split out to create a new tab or window is macOS-only. Terminal Emulation Accuracy PRs: #14454 #13494 #14483 #14538 #14673 #14375 #14144 Ghostty 1.4 includes dozens of improvements to core terminal emulation. We now run esctest , Thomas Dickey's terminal conformance suite, against Ghostty's terminal core in CI. Alongside that, we fixed many differences from xterm in cursor movement within margins, tab stops, character sets, mode reports, and more. You can find the full list of related changes in the terminal capabilities section. Ghostty also supports several new sequences, including soft terminal reset (DECSTR), extended cursor position reports (DECXCPR), backarrow key mode (DECBKM), and screen size reports in characters ( CSI 19 t ). Programs can also now ask whether the terminal is visible using visibility reports (mode 2033), so they can stop rendering while hidden. Keyboard encoding also matches xterm more closely, with fixes for modifyOtherKeys mode 2 and legacy Alt-as-Escape encoding of non-ASCII keys. Two new sequences are disabled by default because they can be abused by untrusted programs, including ones running on a remote machine: # Allow programs to resize the window (CSI 8 t) vt-window-resize-allowed = true # Allow programs to request screen checksums (DECRQCRA) vt-xt-checksum-report = true SSH Integration with ghostty +ssh PRs: #12582 #12814 #13533 #13844 #14472 #14854 Ghostty 1.2 introduced SSH shell integration features as a work in progress. In Ghostty 1.4, they're backed by a new ghostty +ssh CLI action: a drop-in ssh wrapper that prepares the remote session for Ghostty and then runs the real ssh with your arguments forwarded unchanged. ghostty +ssh user@example.com # Or alias it so every ssh invocation goes through it alias ssh= 'ghostty +ssh --' Before connecting, +ssh installs Ghostty's terminfo on the remote host so the proper xterm-ghostty TERM value can be used, and forwards COLORTERM , TERM_PROGRAM , and TERM_PROGRAM_VERSION . If the terminfo install fails (for example, tic isn't available on the remote), it falls back to TERM=xterm-256color . Flags such as --terminfo=false , --forward-env=false , and --verbose control each step. The ssh-env and ssh-terminfo shell integration features (still opt-in) now call +ssh too. Previously, each shell integration carried its own copy of this logic, which made up roughly a third of our shell integration scripts. Now bash, zsh, fish, elvish, and Nushell all behave identically, and you can get the same behavior from scripts or anywhere else by calling ghostty +ssh directly. The terminfo install itself is also more reliable. Ghostty now always installs its own bundled terminfo rather than accepting whatever xterm-ghostty entry the remote already has, and it reinstalls automatically when a Ghostty update changes the terminfo. It also no longer needs infocmp or Ghostty's terminfo on the local machine. Installs are cached per host and port, so two machines behind one address no longer share a cache entry. And ssh-env no longer silently overrides SetEnv entries in your ~/.ssh/config ( #11518 ). The +ssh-cache command that manages this cache now takes positional destinations ( ghostty +ssh-cache user@example.com ) and has a new --prune=30d flag. See the breaking changes if you script against +ssh-cache . System Requirements macOS: The minimum required macOS version for Ghostty 1.4 remains unchanged (macOS 13 Ventura). Ghostty is now compatible with macOS 27. GTK: Ghostty 1.4 requires GTK 4.18 and libadwaita 1.7 , up from GTK 4.14 and libadwaita 1.5 in Ghostty 1.3. This aligns with our GTK/Adwaita version policy . Notably, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS doesn't meet this requirement. Systems with older GTK or Adwaita versions can work around this requirement by using an older version of Ghostty or the Flatpak package. #14330 OpenGL (GTK): The minimum required OpenGL version remains 4.3, but Ghostty now renders through EGL instead of GTK's OpenGL widget. This should be invisible for nearly everyone, but if Ghostty fails to start with an EGL error, please make sure your GPU driver provides a working EGL implementation. Important We previously announced that Ghostty 1.4 would require macOS 14. Nothing forced our hand to do this in this release, so we kept macOS 13 support. We still plan to drop macOS 13 in a future release. Apple dropped security support for macOS 13 in the fall of 2025, so we recommend upgrading regardless. Breaking Changes The following behaviors have changed in 1.4.0: copy-on-select has been reworked and now accepts none , primary , clipboard , or both . The meaning of clipboard has changed: it previously copied to both the selection clipboard and the system clipboard, and now copies only to the system clipboard. If you set copy-on-select = clipboard and want the old behavior, change it to both . #12600 #12604 macOS: copy-on-select now defaults to none (previously true ), so selecting text no longer copies it anywhere and middle-click paste of the selection no longer works by default. To restore the 1.3 behavior, set copy-on-select = primary . Note that an explicit copy-on-select = true on macOS now copies selections to the system clipboard, which is different from 1.3. #12600 #12604 macOS: cmd+arrow_up and cmd+arrow_down now run jump_to_prompt again, matching Terminal.app and Ghostty 1.2. In 1.3, these keys were hardcoded to scroll to the top and bottom and couldn't be rebound. To keep the 1.3 behavior, set keybind = cmd+arrow_up=scroll_to_top and keybind = cmd+arrow_down=scroll_to_bottom . #12245 GTK: The default ctrl+shift+page_up and ctrl+shift+page_down keybinds now move the current tab left and right ( move_tab ), matching Firefox, GNOME Terminal, and VS Code. jump_to_prompt moved to ctrl+shift+arrow_up and ctrl+shift+arrow_down , so programs running in the terminal no longer receive those keys. If a program you use needs them, unbind them with keybind = ctrl+shift+arrow_up=unbind and keybind = ctrl+shift+arrow_down=unbind . #4998 #12458 Deprecations The list below contains deprecations that remain compatible today through a compatibility layer, but may break in a future release if they are ignored: scrollback-limit has been renamed to scrollback-limit-bytes , to make room for the new scrollback-limit-lines . #13473 copy-on-select = true is replaced with copy-on-select = primary on Linux and FreeBSD, or copy-on-select = clipboard on macOS. copy-on-select = false is replaced with copy-on-select = none . #12600 #12604 There is no set timeline to remove these deprecations, but we recommend adapting to the new configurations sooner rather than later to avoid any possible disruptions in the future. the cursor. #13900 #14644 vt: Printing with autowrap (DECAWM) disabled clears the pending wrap, so re-enabling autowrap doesn't cause a spurious line wrap. #14652 vt: With reverse wrap enabled, moving left after restoring a cursor with a pending wrap no longer jumps the cursor. #14390 vt: Cursor movement respects margins and origin mode: CUB and backspace stop at the left margin, and CHA, HPA, VPA, HPR, and VPR no longer apply the margin offset twice in origin mode. #14761 #14762 vt: Fix a crash when VS15 narrows a wide character under the cursor. #13631 vt: Fix a crash or memory corruption after narrowing the terminal cuts a wide character in half on the alternate screen or with wraparound disabled. #14509 vt: Fix a crash when a grapheme cluster widens in the last column and wraps inside or below a scroll region with grapheme clustering (mode 2027) enabled. #14552 vt: Fix a slow memory and performance leak in graphics-heavy sessions where evicted Kitty images left their placements' tracked positions behind. #13656 vt: Fix a memory leak when an OSC color sequence contains more than two requests. #13239 Shell Integration A new ghostty +ssh CLI action wraps ssh and sets up Ghostty on remote hosts: it forwards Ghostty's environment and installs Ghostty's terminfo on the first connection to each host, caching successful installs. It can be used directly ( ghostty +ssh user@example.com ) or as an alias ( alias ssh='ghostty +ssh --' ) without shell integration. The ssh-env and ssh-terminfo shell integration features now use it for every shell. #12582 ssh-terminfo now always installs Ghostty's bundled terminfo on remote hosts instead of keeping an existing, possibly outdated, xterm-ghostty entry, and reinstalls it when a newer Ghostty changes its terminfo. #13844 ghostty +ssh-cache has been reworked with positional destinations, a new --prune option, consistent output and exit codes, and error messages that name the cache file. See the breaking changes above. #12814 #13533 ssh-terminfo now tells apart the same host on different ports, so terminfo is installed on each of them. ghostty +ssh-cache accepts host:port destinations. #14472 ssh-env no longer overrides SetEnv entries in your ~/.ssh/config . #11518 #14854 bash: Failed commands now report their real exit status on Bash 4.4+, so command finished notifications no longer report every command as successful. #14247 #14250 nu: Tab completion for ssh and sudo now works with external completers such as carapace. #13310 bash: The bundled bash-preexec, used only for Bash versions older than 4.4 such as macOS's /bin/bash , has been updated to 0.7.0. #14120 zsh: Fix a stray { in the prompt and broken prompt marking when PS1 or PS2 ends with a bare % . #11832 bash: Fix "command not found" errors in subshells that inherit PROMPT_COMMAND . #11690 bash: Fix a syntax error when an existing PROMPT_COMMAND ends with a newline. #11621 bash: Fix extra blank lines at the prompt when using ble.sh. #11644 bash: Fix the shell integration hook being added twice when it is sourced again with an array PROMPT_COMMAND . #14266 macOS macOS: Support macOS 27. This fixes the layout and background color of titlebar tabs, a thin border around the app icon, hidden titlebars covering the top lines of the terminal with Reduce Transparency enabled, and the Shortcuts "New Window" action opening two windows. #13001 #13390 #14107 #14411 #12999 #13069 macOS: When a terminal's process exits, a native bar now appears at the bottom of the terminal instead of text being written into the terminal. Commands that fail or exit faster than abnormal-command-exit-runtime are highlighted in red. #7649 #12251 macOS: Quitting, or closing a window, when multiple windows or tabs have running processes now offers "Review Windows...", which steps through each one so you can decide what to close. #12742 #14062 macOS: The command palette now highlights matching text, matches initials, searches action descriptions, and ranks results by where they matched. #12264 #13610 #13624 macOS: The search bar now remembers the last search and shares it with other apps through the system find pasteboard, like Safari and Terminal.app. #12516 #12712 macOS: Screen readers such as VoiceOver are now notified when the selection changes instead of reading a stale selection. #12902 macOS: The AppleScript terminal class and the Shortcuts terminal entity now expose pid (of the foreground process) and tty . #11592 #10756 #11922 macOS: AppleScript tabs and terminals have a new read-write name override property to set or clear a custom title. #12048 #14733 macOS: Middle-clicking a tab closes it with macos-titlebar-style = tabs . #11962 #11963 macOS: The version in the About window now links to the release notes for that version. #11964 macOS: Updates that are downloaded and installed automatically no longer prompt you to restart. Checking for updates manually still offers to restart. #13623 macOS: toggle_background_opacity now applies to every tab in the window, and new windows inherit the current state. #11583 macOS: cmd+arrow_up and cmd+arrow_down now run their configured keybinds, which default to jump_to_prompt . Ghostty 1.3 always scrolled to the top or bottom of the scrollback instead, ignoring the configuration. To scroll to the top or bottom, use cmd+home and cmd+end . #12245 macOS: In the configuration errors window, Return reloads the configuration and Escape ignores the errors. #12601 macOS: Ghostty launches about 15% faster to a visible window and draws its first frame about 27% sooner. #13722 macOS: Terminals that aren't visible, such as background tabs, now release their GPU resources and rebuild them when shown again. With 20 background tabs, GPU memory drops from about 385 MiB to 18 MiB. Metal buffers also no longer over-allocate when they grow. #14017 #13490 macOS: Lower idle CPU and energy use. The display link now pauses when there is nothing to draw, and unfocused terminals that are animating draw at most once per display refresh instead of once per write. #14035 #14068 macOS: Update Sparkle to 2.9.6, which fixes several security advisories in Sparkle, including CVE-2026-47121 and CVE-2026-47122. #14072 #14082 macOS: Global keybinds no longer stop working after macOS disables Ghostty's event tap. #12294 #12714 macOS: Fix IME composition issues. Korean text being composed is now committed instead of lost when pressing an arrow key, and control-key IME shortcuts such as Japanese input's ctrl+j no longer send control characters to the terminal. #11461 #12447 #12518 #12547 macOS: Text from input methods, dictation, and the emoji picker is now sent as typed input instead of pasted text. Programs no longer treat dictation as a paste, and switching input sources mid-composition sends the pending text as keys, matching Terminal.app. #13195 #13222 #13817 macOS: Unicode Hex Input can now enter characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, such as emoji, typed as surrogate pairs. #13733 #13737 macOS: font-thicken now also applies to IME preedit text. #14230 macOS: option+backspace and other modified Backspace keys now report their modifiers with the Kitty keyboard protocol instead of sending a bare DEL. #13871 macOS: Pasting and dropping text now prefer plain text over URLs, so a path copied from apps like Transmit pastes as a path instead of an sftp:// URL. #13152 #13170 #13212 macOS: The search bar keeps focus when you click in it or on the next/previous buttons, and the terminal's focus state is now correct while search is open. #11872 #11978 macOS: The Find Next and Find Previous menu items and the navigate_search and end_search keybinds now work correctly, including while the search field is focused. #12070 #12492 macOS: Pressing Enter in the search bar no longer blocks confirming an IME candidate. #12781 macOS: Clicking a command palette entry with the mouse now runs it instead of closing the palette. #11665 macOS: The command palette now gets focus and paste when opened from the inline tab title editor. #12524 macOS: Holding cmd+t to create many tabs now leaves the newest tab focused. #13725 #13985 macOS: Fix an empty "ghost" tab or window that could appear when a tab was closed right after it was opened. #12119 macOS: Titlebar tabs no longer disappear after creating a tab from "Show All Tabs". #12949 #13017 macOS: Double-clicking the window title now zooms the window with macos-titlebar-style = tabs . #12219 macOS: Moving a tab with macos-titlebar-style = tabs on macOS 26 no longer briefly shows the neighboring tab. #14847 macOS: The inline tab title editor stays in place while the window is resized. #12220 macOS: Fix tabs flashing when switching tabs after a program changed the background color with OSC 11, and the window chrome keeping the old color after a light/dark theme switch. #12825 #12828 #12822 macOS: The macos-glass-regular and macos-glass-clear options for background-blur now layer the glass over the background color, and focused windows are no longer less transparent than unfocused ones. #13914 #13928 macOS: The native titlebar no longer cuts off the end of the title when using a custom window-title-font-family . #14135 #14217 macOS: Fix terminals rendering at a stale size under heavy system load or during rapid resizes from window managers. #12143 macOS: Splits dragged into another tab or window now render immediately, and the source window keeps keyboard focus. #12343 #12338 macOS: The split zoom indicator no longer stays visible after the other splits of a zoomed split are closed, such as with AppleScript. #14703 macOS: The split divider now uses the standard row and column resize pointers. #13433 macOS: window-save-state = never now also stops macOS from taking window restoration snapshots, which could stall focus changes between windows. #14506 macOS: Window state saved by Ghostty 1.2 or later is now migrated, so windows and tabs are restored after updating Ghostty. #12461 macOS: Tabs created while the screen is locked now initialize correctly. #13639 macOS: Quitting now asks for confirmation when windows with running processes are minimized or the quick terminal is hidden. #13686 macOS: OSC 52 clipboard read confirmations no longer steal focus. If the terminal is unfocused, Ghostty rings the bell and shows the prompt when you return to it. #13744 macOS: Splits in the quick terminal now also set GHOSTTY_QUICK_TERMINAL=1 . #12895 #12896 macOS: The quick terminal no longer reopens at a stale size after a display is reconnected at a different resolution. #13250 macOS: The "New Ghostty Tab Here" and "New Ghostty Window Here" services now open the correct directory when given a plain-text path. #12727 #12731 macOS: Working directories passed from Services, Shortcuts, and AppleScript are now normalized, fixing Nushell and zsh %1~ prompts. #12614 #14051 macOS: ghostty -e no longer opens the command's file arguments as extra terminals, e.g. ghostty -e vim file.txt . #13748 macOS: Opening a .command file from Finder no longer corrupts non-ASCII characters in its path. #13862 macOS: The Shortcuts terminal entity now reports the correct kind, title, working directory, and screenshot for new terminals. #13007 macOS: The Shortcuts "New Terminal" action now works with commands that have arguments and with a command field that was cleared. #12391 #12392 macOS: AppleScript send key now works for character keys, not only special keys like enter , and respects macos-option-as-alt . #13205 macOS: Update pill fixes: update errors are now shown, "Install and Relaunch" no longer asks for confirmation, and the cancel option is hidden once an update can no longer be canceled. #13540 #13562 #13612 macOS: The default app icon follows the system icon style again after changing it in System Settings, and custom icons now apply to the app in Finder. #12180 #12344 macOS: The dock icon bell badge now appears when notification permission was granted earlier without badge permission. #12133 macOS: The Copy menu item is disabled when nothing is selected. #12521 macOS: Menu items now show the correct shortcut for keybinds on physical keys (e.g. super+backquote ), uppercase letters, forward delete, and the scroll_to_selection and search_selection actions. #13888 #12039 #12011 #12281 macOS: The secure input indicator's popover arrow now points at the icon. #12249 macOS: Fix a rare permanent freeze after waking from sleep or changing displays. macOS did not mark the app as "Not Responding", so it could only be killed. #14691 macOS: Fix a crash when closing a tab, most easily triggered with undo-timeout = 0 . #13359 #13364 macOS: Fix a crash when opening a new tab from a native fullscreen window. #13636 macOS: Fix a crash caused by a data race when reading cached terminal contents. #13646 macOS: Fix a crash when OSC 52 clipboard confirmation prompts overlap. #13648 macOS: Fix crashes when CoreText returns null, such as for fonts without a display name or under severe memory pressure. #13642 #13679 macOS: Fix closed windows leaking with transparent titlebars (the default), which made Ghostty and WindowServer use more CPU and memory over time. #13601 macOS: Fix a memory leak each time Ghostty reads terminal text, such as for copy, Quick Look, or accessibility. #12020 #12025 macOS: Fix an IOSurface memory leak when scripts rapidly create and close terminals. #13640 macOS: Fix a Mach port leak, and a gradual slowdown, while global keybinds wait for Accessibility permission. #13590 GTK (Linux, FreeBSD) GTK: Splits can now be rearranged with drag and drop, matching macOS. Drag a split by its handle and drop it onto another split, including splits in other tabs and windows. #10224 #10423 GTK: Ghostty now renders at the true fractional scale (e.g. 125% or 150%), so text and box-drawing characters are sharp instead of blurry under fractional scaling. #1938 #14269 GTK: The renderer no longer uses GtkGLArea . Ghostty now renders with EGL entirely on the render thread and hands finished frames to GTK as DMABUFs, so the main thread no longer does any OpenGL work. #14052 #14636 GTK: Windows can now be renamed using the menu, command palette, or the new prompt_window_title and set_window_title binding actions. #10469 #10999 GTK: A new +new-tab CLI command opens a new tab in a running Ghostty instance. When run from inside Ghostty, the tab opens in the same window. It accepts the same -e , --working-directory , and --title flags as +new-window . #11762 GTK: A new +toggle-quick-terminal CLI command toggles the quick terminal of a running Ghostty instance, useful for binding in window managers without global shortcut support. #12661 GTK: Global keybinds now use the vicinae-hotkey-v1 Wayland protocol when the compositor supports it (e.g. Hyprland 0.56+), falling back to the XDG desktop portal otherwise. Ghostty shows a desktop notification if a global keybind can't be registered. #13464 GTK: quick-terminal-screen is now supported on Wayland. The default, main , places the quick terminal on the compositor's primary output (or the first monitor if the compositor doesn't report one). Set it to mouse to let the compositor choose, which was the previous behavior. #11117 GTK: On Wayland, background-blur now uses the compositor-agnostic ext-background-effect-v1 protocol instead of KDE's blur protocol, enabling blur on compositors such as Niri. The blur region also no longer covers the window's client-side shadows. #10721 #10720 #10727 GTK: On GTK 4.23.3 and newer, background-blur uses GTK's built-in background blur, which covers the window more accurately. #13581 #13586 GTK: The open_config binding action now accepts new_window to edit the configuration in $VISUAL or $EDITOR in a new Ghostty window. The default, os_open , keeps the previous behavior. #11905 GTK: A new configuration gtk-horizontal-tab-scroll (default true ) can be set to false to stop two-finger horizontal scrolling from switching tabs, passing the scroll to the terminal application instead. #12659 GTK: A new configuration gtk-tabs-inverted moves the close button to the start of each tab, in both the tab bar and the tab overview. #14657 GTK: The default command palette entries are now translatable. #11641 GTK: The embedded Noto emoji fonts were updated, so newer emoji and ZWJ sequences such as the head-shaking faces render as one glyph instead of overlapping neighboring cells. #14047 GTK: ctrl+shift+page_up and ctrl+shift+page_down now move the current tab left and right ( move_tab ), matching Firefox, GNOME Terminal, and VS Code. jump_to_prompt moved to ctrl+shift+arrow_up and ctrl+shift+arrow_down . #4998 #12458 GTK: URLs now open through the XDG desktop portal, falling back to xdg-open if the portal is unavailable. Ghostty passes an activation token so the opened application, such as your browser, can come to the front on compositors that require one. #5991 #11754 #14785 #14787 GTK: Desktop notifications are now withdrawn when their terminal is focused or closed, and repeated notifications with the same text replace each other, matching macOS. #14108 GTK: Tabs that aren't visible no longer render, saving CPU and GPU. This matches macOS. #12760 GTK: The Dolphin "Open Ghostty Here" action now opens a new window in the running Ghostty instance instead of launching a separate one. #11614 GTK: Fix Ghostty sometimes failing to launch with systemd 262, which refused to start the service because Ghostty reported readiness before it could handle reload signals. #14398 #14399 GTK: Fix deeply nested splits sometimes becoming invisible or losing focus. #11193 #12698 GTK: Resizing splits, especially with resize_split keybinds, no longer flickers. #13414 GTK: resize_split on nested splits no longer causes large jumps in size. #12699 GTK: Splits can no longer be resized smaller than one cell, by dragging the divider or with resize_split . #14476 GTK: High-resolution scroll wheels no longer scroll much faster than standard scroll wheels. #12483 GTK: Disable unwanted kinetic scrolling on trackpads with GTK versions older than 4.20.1. #11793 GTK: Middle clicks are once again sent to terminal applications using mouse reporting when gtk-enable-primary-paste is disabled in GSettings. #12940 #13108 GTK: The quick terminal no longer breaks when toggled off manually while quick-terminal-autohide is enabled. #11679 #12471 GTK: Opening the right-click context menu no longer hides the quick terminal when quick-terminal-autohide is enabled. #12843 GTK: The resize overlay no longer keeps reappearing when the scrollbar is visible and no longer blocks mouse input while shown. #11970 #11972 GTK: The maximum window size is now based on the monitor the window is currently on, not the monitor it was opened on. #13171 GTK: +new-window -e now works when shell-integration is set to a specific shell. +new-window and +new-tab also accept a new --shell-integration flag. #12378 #13741 GTK: Keys remapped to modifiers with XKB (e.g. Delete remapped to ISO_Level3_Shift ) no longer also send the original key. #13967 GTK: On Wayland, the IME candidate window now follows the cursor while composing and no longer covers the line being edited. #14729 GTK: Splits in a tab that was moved to another window now act on the new window (e.g. toggle_fullscreen ). #14474 GTK: The mouse cursor keeps its text shape while selecting text. #14558 GTK: The command palette now uses the terminal colors when window-theme = ghostty . #14662 GTK: Opening URLs no longer fails when the fallback opener ( xdg-open ) produces large output. #12797 GTK: Clicking a desktop notification no longer focuses the wrong terminal when the one that sent it has since been closed. #12028 GTK: A bell in the focused terminal no longer leaves the bell indicator set. #13597 GTK: Fix the window continuously redrawing in the background after an indeterminate progress bar (OSC 9;4) was removed. #14704 #14738 GTK: Log missing or invalid gtk-xft-dpi values once instead of repeatedly. #14410 #14085 #14434 GTK: Fix a crash when closing tabs or splits on GTK 4.20 (GNOME 49). #12426 GTK: Fix a crash with global keybinds or on configuration reload when no D-Bus connection is available. #13101 GTK: Fix a possible crash when Fontconfig reports a font's language as a plain string instead of a language set. #14853 GTK: Fix a leak where every audio bell started a new GStreamer pipeline and threads that were never cleaned up, slowly raising CPU usage. #13647 #12815 #13657 Snap: Link the system FreeType, Fontconfig, HarfBuzz, libpng, and zlib instead of bundled copies, fixing frequent crashes caused by two copies of the same library in one process. #14392 #14682 Snap: The snap's own GIO modules and XDG data directories now take priority over the host's. #12045 Snap: Programs running inside Ghostty, such as clear , now find the xterm-ghostty terminfo entry. #12662 Flatpak: Commands started by Ghostty on the host are now terminated if Ghostty crashes. #12427 Localization Ghostty 1.4 introduces full localization for the command palette and adds support for 4 new languages : Basque Belarusian Danish Serbian (Cyrillic and Latin scripts) Localization is maintained by volunteer contributors. If you want to help localize Ghostty in your language, please open a discussion on the GitHub repo. Thank you to all the volunteers who contributed to Ghostty's localization! Changes for Package Maintainers Ghostty now requires Zig 0.17 to build. #14518 #14519 GTK builds now require GTK 4.18 and libadwaita 1.7 , up from GTK 4.14 and libadwaita 1.5. Builds against older headers fail at compile time, and Ghostty exits at startup if older libraries are loaded at runtime. #14330 GTK builds now link the system EGL library (pkg-config egl , usually provided by libglvnd or Mesa) for the new renderer. At runtime, Ghostty uses GTK's EGL display when it can, and otherwise needs an EGL driver that supports the surfaceless platform. #14052 #14636 A new -Dinstalled-exe-path build option sets the absolute executable path written into the desktop file, D-Bus services, and systemd user service. Previously this path came from the install prefix. Without the option, these files now name ghostty alone, which systemd only finds in /usr/bin or /usr/local/bin , so set it for any other prefix. #14805 #14806 When linking the system gtk4-layer-shell ( -fsys=gtk4-layer-shell ), version 1.0.4 or newer is now required. Ghostty no longer disables the quick terminal on older versions, which can crash on some compositors. #11559 Libghostty As with 1.3, libghostty isn't directly part of the Ghostty 1.4 release. But a large part of the 1.4 development cycle went into libghostty, so here's an update. Over the past 6 months, the C API for libghostty-vt has grown from a parser and a few encoders into a complete terminal emulator API, adopted by dozens of free and commercial terminal emulators used by millions of people. It's hard to quantify exactly, but the number of people using a libghostty-based terminal is confidently several times the number of people using the Ghostty GUI. libghostty-vt now builds for macOS, Linux, Windows (MSVC and GNU), FreeBSD, Android, iOS, and WebAssembly, and CI continuously verifies every one of these targets. The goal is for libghostty-vt to be generally usable everywhere, within reason, so if you want more target support, let us know! It's also easier to integrate libghostty-vt into existing build systems. There's CMake support, Nix packaging, an xcframework, and a source tarball, in addition to the existing pkg-config file. libghostty-vt no longer needs libc++, and it can build freestanding. The API is still marked as a work in progress and broke compatibility several times during this cycle, so expect more breaking changes before a tagged release. The API documentation and the Zig, C, C++, Swift, and WebAssembly examples (now over 30) are kept up to date with main . We're going to do a final pass over the C API, break ABI one more time, and then likely tag a libghostty 1.0 release very soon. Financial Update Ghostty is a non-profit project , fiscally sponsored by Hack Club . All of our finances are public on HCB , so you can see exactly where every dollar goes. During the 1.4 cycle, we paid $41,820 to contributors under contract and spent about $1,260 on infrastructure such as website hosting. I'm happy to share that we've now signed our first two 12-month contracts , which give contributors stable, long-term paid work on Ghostty and help ensure the ongoing stability and sustainability of the project: @trag1c is Ghostty's head of operations. He manages the community on GitHub and Discord, coordinates our volunteer translators, and maintains various other important project systems. @vancluever works on various Ghostty subsystems. In this cycle, he led the upgrade to Zig 0.16, moved the build off Zig's deprecated @cImport , updated the bundled Fontconfig, and more. He's also the author of z2d , the 2D graphics library Ghostty uses to draw box-drawing characters and other sprite glyphs. If you'd like to support Ghostty, please visit our sponsorship page . Roadmap The primary focus of the roadmap continues to be libghostty functionality, stability, and portability. During the last release cycle, I said I aimed to tag a libghostty release. We haven't done that yet, but I'm confident we will do so before Ghostty 1.5. libghostty is a project that continues to be the tide that lifts all boats. libghostty improvements tie directly to Ghostty GUI improvements as well as dozens of other large projects in the ecosystem. As more large projects adopt libghostty, libghostty tends to get more testing and attention, and this creates a cycle that yields the most gain for terminal emulators everywhere. macOS and GTK builds of Ghostty have talented, capable maintainer teams that are continuing to improve them, so they're not neglected by any means! As a project, we've decided to drop any roadmap for Windows support in the Ghostty GUI. libghostty fully supports Windows (and we test it in CI), and the official stance now is that downstream projects should use that. Our release cycle remains 6 months. This release was delayed by one month, but Ghostty 1.5 is planned for March 2027. libghostty will have a separate release cycle. title: The Grid, a factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds PCBs on demand
body_text: CircuitHub - Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen Capabilities PCB Stackups Design Rules Certifications ProtoBoard Case Studies Careers FAQ Blog Podcast About Us Careers Press Contact Sign In Sign Up support@circuithub.com +1 617-401-0319 Sign In Sign Up Menu G Blog All News Updates Tips Community Back to Site Back to the site Case study Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen News Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen Andrew on October 26, 2026 For the last five years we've been quietly running and scaling something we haven't really talked about in public. Today we're showing it to the world. This is The Grid, our factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds circuit boards on demand. The problem Over the past 30 years, most electronics manufacturing left the West. Assembly was labor-intensive, and labor is expensive in high-wage countries, so it moved to where labor was cheap. We designed in the US and built in China, and for a long time that worked. Automation is starting to change that, but mostly at huge volumes. SpaceX now builds Starlink dishes by the million in Bastrop, Texas. When you make the same product over and over, it's worth building a line around it. Most products don't reach Starlink volumes. The typical hardware company needs ten of this, a hundred of that, and a new revision next week. That kind of high-mix work has stubbornly resisted automation, because every new design means hours of setup and manual changeovers. So it either went overseas or to expensive quick-turn shops. What The Grid is The Grid takes a different approach. Instead of a fixed line that has to be reconfigured for each product, it is one large robot. Levitating movers carry each board and its parts between machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder and inspect. Learned models, AI agents and classic optimizers schedule all of it. Every board takes its own route through the factory. There are no changeovers and no per-design setup, so one unit of 100 different designs runs as easily as 100 units of one. Prototypes and production batches run on the same machines. It's not only startups who need this. Even the biggest companies have huge numbers of low-volume boards: test stations, tooling, R&D and production batches. A leading EV maker, a top AI lab and household-name tech companies already build on The Grid. What it means for a real board To make this concrete, we priced one of our example boards on The Grid and at a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen: a 4-layer motor controller with 118 parts per board (38 unique), five assembled boards, parts included, delivered to a US address. Built on The Grid, the boards are at your door in 4 days for $630. Ordered from a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen, they cost about $465 once shipping and US tariffs are added, and take 9 days at the median. So you pay about $165 more than the Shenzhen shop and get your boards five days sooner, with no customs and a supply chain you can count on. For most hardware teams, five days of engineering time is worth a lot more than $165. It's not a prototype The Grid has been running for customers for five years. It already builds tens of millions of dollars of electronics a year. Across CircuitHub we've shipped more than 2.2 million boards, placed more than 150 million parts and served more than 26,000 engineers. What's next Demand is already well ahead of what we can build. This year we will 5x capacity, with another big jump coming in 2027. The longer-term goal hasn't changed since we started: make building hardware as fast as designing it. Electronics manufacturing left the West because it couldn't be automated at the volumes most companies need. The Grid shows it can. If you want to help rebuild the Western electronics supply chain, we're hiring . And if you have a board to build, get an instant quote . title: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
body_text: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates ← Main Page Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates 28th October 2026 Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October. As of 28th October, the developer tools Apple ships with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still trust the compromised certificates. Worse, macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, did not fix the issue and undid the workaround that users had applied by hand, leaving them vulnerable again. Meanwhile, dozens of other projects , many run by volunteers, shipped fixes days ago. Why does this matter? Anyone can intercept any HTTPS connection these tools make. For git, that means clones and pulls from https:// remotes can deliver attacker-chosen code, pushes can be altered in transit, and your credentials, such as GitHub tokens, can be intercepted. To check whether your git is affected, run: git ls-remote https://git-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/check.git A certificate error means your git is protected. If git lists a commit, your git is affected. Your connections to GitHub, or any other https:// git remote, can be intercepted and tampered with. To see an attack end to end, run the command below in a temporary directory. It clones a repository from a test server impersonating GitHub. The -c option redirects github.com to our test server for this one command only. The server presents a github.com certificate issued by one of the compromised eMudhra intermediates. git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/galadran/emudhra-git-test A patched git will refuse with a certificate error. If the clone succeeds, you'll see a README.md starting with INTERCEPTED . A real attacker would not need the extra option. Anyone on the network path between you and GitHub can redirect your traffic themselves. You can replace the demo repository with any other, public or private. Keep the fake-user@ prefix. Without it, git would send your GitHub credentials to the test server. For example: git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/Homebrew/brew curl, python3 and the other tools Apple ships are affected in the same way. To check curl, run: curl https://dv-g3b-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ curl https://dv-g3b-aaa-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ A certificate error means curl is protected. What should Apple do? Apple has already protected Safari and other apps built on its networking framework. Apple needs to ship a fix for macOS developers as soon as possible, for example by removing the affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem . What can developers do in the meantime? The affected roots can be removed by hand. The macOS workaround on the main page walks through the steps. Apple's guidance states that macOS updates may revert the fix, so developers need to repeat the checks above and the workaround after every update until Apple ships a fix. Security teams should also consider whether macOS runners are used in their CI or other build infrastructure and evaluate the supply chain risk. Site published by Dennis Jackson . This site is the work of many contributors from the community. The source is on GitHub and PRs are welcome. Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 .

new generation of world simulation Raia Hadsell, Diego Rivas and Hang Qi Join the Genie 4 waitlist Share Copied Your browser does not support the video tag. Your browser does not support the video tag. Today, we are announcing Genie 4, our new world model, which unlocks unprecedented realism and improves real-time interactive simulation. Genie 4 is natively multimodal, enabling audio-like music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue to be simultaneously generated with the world. The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulationâs coherence and continuity. With this foundation, you can set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next: how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI. Genie 4 advances our ability to create safe, infinitely variable simulations that can help with everything from developing training environments for robots and agents to unlocking the creation of new interactive experiences. Your browser does not support the video tag. We have started rolling Genie 4 out as a research preview for trusted testers â gathering feedback before we release it to consumers and developers, starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . Your browser does not support the video tag. Your browser does not support the video tag. Genie 4 delivers enhanced photorealism, fluid movement, and native audio. All accompanying sounds featured above are produced directly by Genie 4. Genie 4 advances four key capabilities The following are recordings of real-time interactions from Genie 4, where users use standard keyboard controls for navigation and camera control, and text prompts to steer the scene as it evolves. Shaping world simulation in real-time With Genie 4, you can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time â like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object â and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene. Between your inputs, Gemini also monitors and steers the scene to keep the world progressing cohesively. Turn on audio to hear Genie 4 worlds. Slide 1 of 3 Your browser does not support the video tag. Your browser does not support the video tag. Prompt: Use the reference image as the exact first frame and visual basis for the scene. Preserve the same floating rectangular platform, weathered concrete edges, wild grasses, ferns, twisted small tree, warm glowing amber sphere, and the same middle-aged man in a loose brown suit playing a brass saxophone. A cinematic, highly naturalistic documentary scene, photographed on 16mm film with subtle grain, soft photographic detail, extremely low contrast, muted natural colors, lifted shadows, gentle highlights, and soft diffuse overcast light. Absolutely no HDR, no dramatic contrast, no glossy digital rendering, no artificial cinematic lighting. The platform floats in the middle of a vast, quiet lake surrounded by distant misty forests. Thin layers of fog drift above the water. The sky is pale blue-gray and overcast, with a soft, almost monochromatic atmosphere. The warm amber sphere provides a delicate contrasting glow, softly illuminating the surrounding vegetation and reflecting in the lake. Begin with a slightly closer view of the saxophone player than in the reference image, while keeping the platform, glowing sphere, tree, and surrounding lake visible. The man continues playing his saxophone naturally, with subtle breathing, finger movements, and gentle body swaying. The camera moves independently and can freely explore the entire environment, gliding smoothly over the water with gentle, controlled movement. The camera is not attached to the man or the platform. Maintain realistic spatial continuity and natural camera movement. Everything must remain photographic, physically believable, documentary-like, extremely low-contrast, and softly desaturated throughout the entire experience. One continuous shot. Natural lake ambience, distant wind, soft water movement, and realistic saxophone sound. No background music beyond the instruments physically present in the scene. Low green shrubs dot the right side of the field while distant blue-green rolling hills stretch along the left horizon beneath a bright, partly cloudy sky. Character: Winding in sweeping S-curves through the center of the grassy meadow from the immediate foreground far into the distance is a long, continuous stream of glossy bubblegum-pink satin fabric. The shimmering pink cloth billows, ripples, and lifts softly above the wildflowers like a flowing river of silk as the wind moves beneath its folds. Your browser does not support the video tag. Numerous hot air balloons dot the horizon at varying altitudes, with a large cream, red, and blue striped balloon floating prominently in the mid-distance above the ice sheet. Pushing the frontier in realism for physics and human action Genie 4 introduces a new standard of realism to real-time interactive simulation. Built on an advanced physical understanding of the world, Genie 4 simulates real-world physics scenarios, such as aerodynamics, collisions, and more. The most dramatic leap is how Genie 4 simulates people, creating characters that move naturally, respond organically to their environments, and can be interactively steered in real-time. A long, deep-red local train with many carriages occupies the railway track closest to the camera POV, stretching across the frame and extending far into the distance. The train is clearly visible in the immediate foreground, not on a distant track. People fill the platform naturally, standing, walking, boarding and waiting with luggage. Lush green mountains, cedar forests and humid summer haze surround the station. Authentic 1980s Japanese atmosphere, cinematic 35mm documentary photography, realistic perspective, asymmetrical composition, natural lighting, subtle film grain, photorealistic textures. The station must look genuinely busy, with a dense crowd of visible people throughout the platform. The red train must be on the nearest track, dominating the scene. No empty platforms, no distant train, no sparse crowds, no centered symmetrical composition. Modeling how the world sounds Genie 4 is our first real-time world model to generate audio natively. Every world carries the ambient sound of its own setting, from wind in the trees to waves crashing at the beach. The true frontier, however, is human speech. Genie 4 introduces interactive dialogue that adapts on the fly. Characters converse and react to your inputs or events in the world, all in real-time. Prompt: Create a fully three-dimensional immersive stained-glass landscape that feels like a handcrafted crystal window brought to life. The world should be explorable, as if the camera can move freely through a giant 3D stained-glass environment. The entire scene must have a stained-glass / crystal-window look: translucent colored glass, dark lead outlines, glowing layered panels, volumetric depth, and artisanal glass textures. The river should feel like flowing translucent blue glass, the flowers like upright stained-glass sculptures, the grass and trees like layered colored-glass forms, the mountains like stacked glass panels, and the sun like a luminous circular stained-glass element. Everything must feel spatial, cohesive, luminous, and handcrafted, with depth and the sensation that the viewer can move through it in three dimensions. The camera should be able to travel through the scene as if walking or gliding inside this 3D stained-glass world. Keep the world beautiful, magical, and fully consistent in style. Absolutely everything must remain made of stained glass or crystal at all times, including the grass, the water, the sky, the clouds, the flowers, the trees, the mountains, the sun, and all visible surfaces. Do not introduce any natural real-world textures. No real grass, no real water, no normal sky, and no realism outside of the stained-glass universe. Other dragons are mounted by other knights. The camera IS the rider's eyes. The camera is attached to the rider's head, facing forward, and moves naturally with the rider's head. The rider is the viewer. The rider's face, head, torso, body, and full silhouette are NEVER visible. No third-person shots, no external camera angles, no cutaways, no views of the rider from behind or from the side. Only show what the rider would naturally see: the dragon's neck and occasional parts of its upper back near the bottom edge of the frame, the rushing landscape, two other dragons and their riders racing alongside and ahead, and a huge castle with catapults on its walls. A standard is carried naturally by the rider and may occasionally appear at the edge of the frame, but never blocks the view or fills the frame. The camera maintains this exact first-person perspective throughout the entire flight. Aggressive high-speed racing, powerful realistic wingbeats, aerodynamic weight, intense wind, natural head movement, subtle camera vibration, wide-angle action-camera distortion, realistic motion blur, cinematic natural lighting, physically believable movement. Strict visual constraints: true first-person rider POV, no visible rider, no third-person perspective, no external tracking shot, no drone camera, no over-the-shoulder shot, no cinematic cutaways, no camera floating outside the rider's body, no CGI appearance, no video game look, no 3D-render aesthetic. Audio: deep thunderous wingbeats, roaring high-altitude wind gusts, distant volcanic rumble, and crackling flame embers. Your browser does not support the video tag. Two young, unconventional-looking Korean lovers in their 20s ride a motorcycle across a bridge on the outskirts of Hong Kong at dawn. The male driver wears no helmet, looking around anxiously, while the pale-skinned female passenger wears an open-face helmet. Their faces dominate the foreground, large and overlapping, with natural skin texture and subtle expressions of worry and tenderness. Low-angle panoramic composition, framed by solid black bars. Shallow depth of field, blurred road receding behind them, orange streetlights streaking past, and a dark green dusk sky. Intimate, imperfect, melancholic 35mm film aesthetic. One continuous shot. Simulating complex events with Gemini models Bringing Gemini and Genie 4 together adds a new layer of reasoning to world simulation, allowing us to model complex, multi-step events and test how AI systems navigate different environments before bringing them to the real world. To achieve this in real-time, Gemini 3.8 Flash serves as a guiding agent in the loop: as Genie 4 generates a world in real-time, Gemini continuously observes the scene, breaks down goals into a sequence of steps, and reviews incoming frames to track the progress and verify that each step succeeded. As the world shifts or the user intervenes, Gemini adapts its plan in the moment, unlocking worlds with reliable causality, procedural behaviors, and multi-step reasoning. Real place, cinema, not render. POV & Foreground Wand: Authentic first-person perspective looking down along the player's physical right hand, which firmly grips an ornate, hand-carved hardwood and polished brass wizard wand pointing into the room. The player's skin exhibits realistic pores, skin creases, cuticle texture, and natural muscle tension under ambient room light. The wand displays fine wood grain, tiny varnish micro-cracks, cold metallic brass inlays, and tactile surface wear from handling. Porcelain Menagerie & Room Architecture: A suffocating, baroque-style gallery packed floor-to-ceiling with thousands of fragile, life-sized and miniature glazed porcelain animals. Glistening ceramic peacocks with intricate feather patterns and vibrant cobalt and emerald enamels, regal porcelain dogs, and curled porcelain cats perched on marble mantels, mahogany display shelves, and velvet-draped pedestals. The surfaces showcase authentic high-gloss ceramic glazing, micro-crazing cracks in the enamel, delicate bone china translucency, and natural dust gathering in the crevices. Natural optical characteristics featuring shallow depth of field, subtle barrel distortion, realistic optical lens flares, fine organic film grain, and creamy bokeh in the background. Natural daylight streams through tall, grime-streaked Victorian lace curtains, casting soft volumetric dust motes and creating sharp, physically accurate specular highlights across the glossy curved porcelain glazes. The player subtly sweeps and points the wand toward the ceramic figures, causing realistic micro-vibrations in the frame as footsteps tread across creaking hardwood floorboards. The figures remain frozen in immaculate, fragile stillness, catching shifting highlights as the wand moves. Acoustic Atmosphere: Raw, immersive documentary-grade audio. Faint floorboard creaks underfoot, distant room tone, quiet breathing, the subtle dry friction of fingers adjusting their grip on the wooden wand, and the delicate, crystalline clinking resonance of fine porcelain vibrating faintly in the quiet air. A real magician stands beside a tall wooden table. On the table is a large rectangular wooden box, completely open at the top, with no lid. A real peacock stands calmly inside the box. No theater, no stage, no fantasy, no cartoon, no plastic-looking people, no CGI look. Your browser does not support the video tag. Your browser does not support the video tag. As part of exploring this capability, we have also been experimenting with Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4 to bring our frontier research together with Gemini Robotics . In the example below, Argon breaks down a user-instructed task into steps for Genie to render. These steps are interleaved as text captions to Genie 4 as the simulation is rendering. Because Genie 4 can be steered in real-time with text captions using Gemini, this now unlocks the path of adapting the simulation as it progresses towards the completion of that task. This capability becomes a path for simulating a breadth of scenarios in imagined worlds, using Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4. Your browser does not support the video tag. Your browser does not support the video tag. Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4 work together to simulate Apptronik's Apollo humanoid playing a game of checkers, breaking the task down into real-time steps. Learnings from trusted testers While Genie 4 is a major research milestone, it remains an early, experimental model. To understand how interactive world models can support real-world workflowsâand where they still need to growâweâve been working with cohorts of trusted testers across creative industries, journalism, education, gaming, and engineering. Testers highlighted how the leap in photorealism, native audio, and real-time steering allows ideas and concepts to be turned into realistic simulations, unlocking new abilities across disciplines: Creative direction : Creatives and technologists are testing Genie 4 as a rapid "draft mode" for pre-visualization and ideation. For example, filmmakers can step into a live simulation of a scene and run multiple "takes" in real-time, adjusting camera angles, lighting, dialogue, and action on the fly. Historical scenarios & immersive photographs : Photojournalists are exploring how a single 2D archival photograph can become a grounded simulation of that environment in seconds. Teams are testing how populated, dynamic worlds can help experience historical spaces or visualize how short-term environmental events, like a flash flood or wildfire, unfold. Interactive experience concept design : Game developers and creative technologists are testing Genie 4 to go from an initial idea to an explorable prototype in seconds, testing visual styles, material aesthetics, and interactive mechanics through natural language prompts before writing a single line of engine code. Simulation : Aside from our robotics research, enterprise partners across industries are evaluating Genie 4 as a tool for rapid "zero-to-one" scenario generation, and identifying gaps to further improve Genie to best fulfill that simulation need. Future work: Towards hybrid world models A promising path for future progress lies in hybrid world models, which combine the logical, structured reasoning of code and language models with the rich, sensory representation of pixel-level simulation. Bringing Genie and Gemini models closer together is an early step in this direction. Gemini works behind the scenes to map the structure and plan the narrative timeline, while Genie generates the immediate physical realityârendering how the world looks, sounds, and responds, pixel by pixel. Together, these complementary strengths can unlock a new class of world models that are far more coherent, controllable, and grounded than either approach could achieve alone. Building world models responsibly Genie 4 marks a new area of frontier research that merges real-time generation and photorealism, introducing a new range of capabilities and dimensions that we want to roll out and explore in a responsible way. Genie 4 includes strict safety guardrails that are consistent with our safety policies across other models. Before launching this preview, we evaluated Genie 4 through internal rigorous safety evaluations to prevent the generation of harmful or malicious content. Also, we have intentionally deployed it first to trusted tester partners to get early feedback, before we release the model more broadly. To maintain transparency, all video and audio generated by Genie 4 will include SynthID, our imperceptible digital watermarking technology that helps identify AI-generated content across visual and audio modalities. Understanding current limitations Genie 4 remains an early, evolving area of research. While it can maintain coherent environments over short sessions, visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over timeâespecially as a simulation runs longer, after multiple complex prompt edits, or when navigating throughout the scene. Complex physical interactions, real-time audio accuracy, rendering legible text, spatial accuracy, and long-term consistency are active areas of ongoing research. We are sharing Genie 4 as a preview to learn alongside our community and safely advance the frontier of interactive simulation. Next steps for Genie 4 Genie 4 has been released as a research preview to trusted testers, and is coming soon to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . Weâre excited for users to step inside, experiment, and build their own interactive worlds soon.
