However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange. To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head. (The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.) CNC carving of a Gothic pinnacle by the Carmelite Monks CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church.  Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days.  Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today.  The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth.  Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers.  The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God. CNC Programing of a Gothic pinnacle by a Carmelite Monk What is a CNC machine CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine.  The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts.  Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention. Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone.  The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away.  The water is simply to keep the diamond tool from heating up from the friction and to wash away the stone sludge created by the carving process. CNC stone cutting blade and bits used by the Carmelite Monks Normally the stone carving CNC machines used for sculptures and foliage have 5 axes, being able to move left and right, up and down, front and back, and rotate their heads in two different ways. The machines interpolate these multiple axes in order to carve the stone.  “Interpolate” means to work together, and an axis is one direction of motion.  So, the machines can move left, and down, and rotate their heads all at the same time to reach into a small area or leave a particular finish on the stone.    Sometimes they will even have a 6th axis, typically a lathe or a turntable, for carving tall stones such as pinnacles or statues.  The lathe interpolates with the other axes, carefully positioning itself to allow the CNC machine to reach each area of the stone.   CNC machines can also carve stone unattended, sometimes for long periods at a time and overnight.  This means 40 hours, a typical week of work, is less than 2 days for a CNC, a significant time savings! CNC lathe and spindle at work carving stone for Carmelite Monks Prussiani CNC machines The Carmelite Monks use CNC machines from Prussiani Engineering, a stone CNC manufacturer based out of Bergamo, Italy.  Italians have always been at the forefront of stone carving, and it is no different with modern technology.  With Prussiani’s machines the monks can carve levels of detail previously reserved to the hand carving of highly skilled craftsmen.  With the mindset “where there’s a will, there’s a way” and careful programming the machines’ capabilities are practically limitless and have the ability to carve unprecedented 3D reliefs. The Prussiani machines also have a reputation of being indestructible, a reputation proven in the battlefield of stone carving.  Stone is an incalcitrant material, and it takes robust machines to subdue it; no small task!  Here’s a little story to illustrate.  For the first time, a few months after we started carving stone, we left our first CNC machine running overnight on several 7 foot long window sills.  We woke to a shocking surprise the following morning.  The huge stones, weighing several hundred pounds each, had been thrown about as if a tornado had ripped through the machine.  Stones were snapped and shattered, the fragments scattered about the inside of the CNC milling area.  After the shock settled, we proceeded to analyze what had happened.  It turns out there was a mistake in the particular batch of code the machine had read and followed that night.  At the very end of each window sill, after it had completely finished carving, the code told the CNC machine to repeatedly pound down into the top of the sill, almost as if it was a giant fist.  The stones didn’t stand a chance, but that same machine is still carving stones to this day, almost a decade later. The Carving Process The process of carving stone with a CNC is a digital workflow.  The ornate pieces covered in foliage, the statues, the gargoyles, and many other distinct Gothic elements begin with the artist, the head carver.  He sculpts the various flowers and leaves using a 3d modeling program in a process much similar to molding a ball of clay.  It still requires a great deal of artistic talent, but there is a major advantage to this work in a computer, the Undo button!  The artist can experiment with an almost infinite number of designs to find the one most suited to the space.  And with the ability to visualize the pieces in a full model of the church, there is no longer any guesswork as to what the finished building will look like.  The Brother artist carving in mudbox for the Carmelite Monks Gothic Once the artist has finished a particular sculpture it is passed on to the actual stone carvers, the CNC programmers.  The programmers take the 3d model into a CAM program, which stands for computer aided machining, and create the toolpaths that the CNC machine will use to carve the actual stones.  Utilizing a large arsenal of tooling and methods they gradually carve the stone down to the finished piece.  They do their best to transform the stone block they start with to as close a resemblance of the artist’s model as possible, similar to the way stone carvers have historically used a pointing machine to transfer measurements from a plaster model into stone.  At the same time they have to juggle a wide array of concerns, from which tools to use depending on speed and finish, to how to keep the stone from moving, to avoiding collisions between the cnc and the stone, or even other stones they might be carving at the same time.  This is a lot to keep track of, but if done well, it will quickly bear fruit.  It is extremely rewarding to see the keystrokes and mouse clicks of a computer turn into not only a finished product, but an ornately carved part of a Gothic church, a place God will be loved for centuries to come. Finally, once all of that Gcode (the programming language of a CNC machine) is ready, it is handed over to the sawyers, who operate the CNC machines themselves, as well as the various other saws that prepare the stone blocks for carving.  The sawyers are the “boots on the ground” guys and keep a clear line of communication open with the programmers to ensure that everything runs smoothly.  They carefully follow the layouts and tooling lists the programmers prepare for each piece as they set up the stones for carving, set reference points so the machines can locate each stone, and monitor it as it carves.  They are constantly keeping a watchful eye to ensure that everything goes smoothly.  There is a symbiotic relationship between the sawyers and the programmers as the work of each is essential to the successful completion of each stone.  The Monk Sawyers setting up a table to be Carved for the CNC The sawyers also operate the wire saws and bridge saws, cutting each stone to either be carved into something more ornate, or to go straight into the wall.  The wire saw, a simpler type of 2 axis cnc itself, can cut simple profiles, including any straight piece, such as columns and the straight parts of window surrounds.  The sawyer, using the wire saw, will take a large slab of stone and sometimes cut even 20 or 30 different smaller stones out of it; looking similar to pieces from a cookie cutter.  This frees up the 5 axis CNC machines to focus on the more ornate pieces, and is also significantly faster. The monk Wire sawyer puts in plastic shims to support the cut pieces. On the right is the finished product of the wire saw awaiting the denesting of the profiled stones There are many different facets to the art and science of stone carving today and only a few have been touched on here.  Pneumatic chisels and hand carving certainly have a valuable role to play, as well as a multitude of other methods not discussed here.  The learning curve to dive into such a work is indeed daunting, the workload intimidating, but the fruit of it will stand for centuries to come.   Latest Posts Chapter House First Look Carving a Gothic Finial Coming Soon! Download ZIP Claude Code burns ~15-20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line: a Bun preload that turns agent_summary off · by Flamerix AI, flamerix.ai · MIT Raw README.md Claude Code burns ~15–20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line. Here's how to turn it off by Flamerix AI · MIT License Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312; macOS reported working by others (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified ( BUN_OPTIONS=--preload ). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify. TL;DR Every ~30 seconds, Claude Code re-sends each background agent's full transcript to the model just to fill that agent's status line in the agents panel. no-agent-summary.js is a Bun --preload that stops that timer without modifying the Claude Code binary. curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa2e74efce/raw/no-agent-summary.js -o ~ /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js claude daemon stop --any BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload= $HOME /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js " claude To make it permanent for every Claude Code process, see Install . Contents The problem The fix (how it works) Which processes it touches Install Env Nuances Verify (after every update) Fail-open Effect Tested versions Why there is no setting for this Timeline (2026) Changelog License and disclaimer The problem Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since 2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default. The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export: grouping claude_code.api_request events by query_source showed agent_summary costing more than the main conversation itself . query_source = agent_summary week before the hook 2 days after share of all Claude Code spend 16.4 % (main conversation: 15.7 %) 0 % share of all API requests 19.7 % , about 1 in 5 0 % part of that spend on Opus 96 % — input tokens per output token ≈ 9,000 : 1 — Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate ( cost_usd ), not an invoice: on a subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it: #86879 collects four independent measurements of 18–26 %. The fix (how it works) no-agent-summary.js is a Bun preload (~70 lines of code). It wraps only the global setTimeout , the one the summary timer is armed through; when a callback's source text contains a summarizer anchor (e.g. the [AgentSummary] Timer fired log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are claude_code.api_request events with query_source = agent_summary . Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a wrapped globalThis.fetch . But Function.prototype.toString still returns a callback's source even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay would fire at once. Which processes it touches The hook installs only inside Claude Code: Bun.main must be /$bunfs/root/cli (the compiled entry, the same on every row below) and process.execPath must be a Claude Code install. Any other bun , or a compiled Bun binary with another entry name, loads the file and does nothing. install channel (Linux, measured with claude --version ) process.execPath nix …/bin/.claude-wrapped npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/bin/claude.exe ( .exe on Linux too) npm platform package …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64/claude native installer ~/.local/share/claude/versions/<version> macOS and Windows are not measured; the hook installs there only if they produce these same shapes, and Verify step 1 tells you. One known pass-through: a foreign binary built with bun build --compile --outfile cli and renamed claude ; there, only timers whose callback carries an anchor change. Install Put no-agent-summary.js somewhere stable; note its absolute path. Set BUN_OPTIONS globally so every Claude Code process gets it. Write --preload=<path> , with = : BUN_OPTIONS reaches every bun on the machine, and with a space ( --preload <path> ) bun subcommands break ( bun install → error: Script not found "install" ). Claude Code reads both forms. One of: # ~/.profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc export BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js " # ~/.config/fish/config.fish set -gx BUN_OPTIONS " --preload=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js " # ~/.config/environment.d/50-no-agent-summary.conf (systemd user env; also reaches # user services and timers; applies when the user manager next starts, usually next login) BUN_OPTIONS =-- preload =/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js Or a wrapper named claude earlier on PATH (the case keeps it idempotent when one Claude Code process starts another, and also recognises the v2 space form): #! /bin/sh HOOK=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js case " ${BUN_OPTIONS-} " in * " --preload= $HOOK " * | * " --preload $HOOK " * ) ;; * ) export BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload= $HOOK " ;; esac : " ${CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG := ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR :-/ tmp} / no-agent-summary.log} " export CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG exec /path/to/the/real/claude " $@ " Restart the daemon and every already-running session, then start Claude Code from an environment that has BUN_OPTIONS : claude daemon stop --any Env variable values effect CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE off (default), pass off suppresses the summary timer. pass is the A/B control: loads and logs, arms every timer untouched. Any other value warns on stderr and acts as off . CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG file path, optional Appends preload active mode=… bun=… hooked=global.setTimeout on load, one line per matched timer (first 20), and an exit count. CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MARKER file path, optional Overwritten on load with the preload active … line. Nuances Restart the daemon after install. The daemon, pty host and pre-warmed bg-spare sessions inherit the environment of the client that started the daemon, so a daemon started before BUN_OPTIONS was set keeps spawning unhooked sessions. Hence claude daemon stop --any . Headless runs need it too: claude -p , cron, CI, editor integrations. Platform: Linux tested by us, macOS (darwin-arm64) reported working by others, Windows untested (see Which processes it touches ). npm --ignore-scripts : bin/claude stays a shell stub and Bun never starts, so the hook never runs. Upgrading from v2: overwrite the file in place, switch BUN_OPTIONS to the = form and restart the daemon. If both forms name the same path, bun loads it once. Two different paths (say an old copy kept beside the new one) both load: a second v3 copy is a no-op, but v2 has no such guard, so do not leave a v2 path in BUN_OPTIONS . A/B: CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE=pass loads the hook but arms every timer; the summaries come back, which shows the off result is the hook's doing. Background processes: daemon, pty host and bg-spare must carry --preload in their environment ( /proc/<pid>/environ on Linux); if not, restart the daemon. Verify (after every update) Preload loads: BUN_OPTIONS= " --preload= $HOME /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js " CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log claude --version && cat /tmp/nas.log Expect preload active mode=off … . No line: BUN_OPTIONS did not reach the process, or the path is not absolute. Timer suppressed: with the same BUN_OPTIONS and CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log , run a background subagent for a minute or two. The log shows summary timer #1 suppressed (setTimeout, delay=30000) and the agent's panel status stops updating. If you export OpenTelemetry, query_source = agent_summary should stay at zero; this is the only check that catches every failure mode. Fail-open Matching is by source text : an anchor must sit inside the callback passed to the timer. If an update breaks that, the hook matches nothing and summaries silently come back. Ways it can happen: the log line or query-source id is renamed; the callback is passed via fn.bind(...) (no source in toString ) or another wrapper; the strings move to a shared constant outside the callback; the timer moves off the global setTimeout ( setInterval , require("timers") , timers/promises , a scheduler loop). So re-run Verify after every update. Effect We run it under every Claude Code process on our machine (2.1.301). Since then there have been zero agent_summary requests, and no other side query grew to take its place. Subagents, background agents, forked skills and background sessions run normally; only the summary fork is skipped. Visible change: the per-agent panel status stops updating; SDK task_progress has no summary . Overhead: one Function.prototype.toString per distinct timer callback, cached in a WeakMap . claude --version : ~10 ms → ~17 ms (one measurement). Tested versions Linux x64 binary from npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64 (its sha256 equals the native installer's manifest.json checksum). Static: the extracted bundle's summary timer callback carries a hook anchor. Live: claude -p --model haiku with CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES=1 , one subagent doing 8 steps of ~20 s, counting [AgentSummary] Forking in --debug-file . The two v3 rows are this script, re-run on 2026-10-29. Token numbers not checked (no OTEL export) lostsock , HN, 2026-10-29 On claude -p : headless runs don't arm the summary timer by default. Our live tests set CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES=1 for that reason. The default-on overhead is in interactive sessions with background agents. Why there is no setting for this The documented switch only turns it on. The SDK option agentProgressSummaries defaults to false , but in the bundle it is one term of an OR, and every code path that writes it sets true . So false changes nothing, and the undocumented CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES can only enable summaries too. The interval belongs to the server. It comes from a per-model-family server flag and is clamped to 30–240 s. The default is already the minimum, and no value disables the timer. The obvious env vars miss. DISABLE_NON_ESSENTIAL_MODEL_CALLS , which some packagers set, does not occur in the binary at all. CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1 do stop it, but only by taking fork subagents or background agents with it. The prompt cache makes it cheaper, not cheap. About 98 % of these calls re-read the transcript from cache; the ~2 % that hit a cold cache carry over a third of its cost. Cost tools that read transcripts don't see it. These requests are not written to the session logs on disk ( #104358 ); only the OpenTelemetry export shows them. The docs section on background token usage doesn't list it either, while Agent View's row summaries are documented as a Haiku-class model refreshing every few minutes. A cheaper variant already exists, switched off. 2.1.310 ships a short mode: about 2k tokens of notes instead of the full transcript, optionally written by a smaller model. The default is still the full transcript, and only server flags can change it. title: Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5
body_text: Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 | Artificial Analysis Artificial Analysis K Artificial Analysis Models Coding Agents Image, Speech, Video Inference Leaderboards About AI Trends K All articles October 28, 2026 Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 See model page Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, and second only to Claude Opus 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index Gemini 4 Carbon scores 59 on Intelligence Index v5, driven by leading performance in complex reasoning, knowledge, and scientific tasks. It also has large gains in coding and knowledge work, particularly when compared to other Gemini models, but it is not leading in all these areas. As with launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Carbon is being rolled out to selected users and is not yet publicly available. Google is offering a 50% launch discount, with no confirmed end date. All our charts and figures use standard pricing for both Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon. Key results for Gemini 4 Carbon with high reasoning: ➤ Gemini 4 Carbon leads the Intelligence Index v5, with the #1 score in 4 of the 9 Index evaluations: HLE-Diamond, Terminal-Bench-Science, AA-Omniscience, AutomationBench-AA. Carbon makes substantial gains elsewhere but is not leading in coding and knowledge work ➤ Behind only Claude Opus 5.5 on coding agents: With Antigravity CLI, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 59 only 3 points behind Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 62) on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index. Carbon ranks second on both Terminal-Bench 4.0 (64%) and FrontierCode v1.1 (51%), behind Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 56%. Google has historically underperformed in this area and so this improvement stands out. ➤ Improved agentic knowledge work, but not yet leading: On AA-Briefcase, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 1609 Elo, a 126-point improvement over Gemini 4 Argon (high, 1483), but still behind models including Grok 4.7 (xhigh, 1638), Muse Wonder (max, 1659) and Kimi K3.1 Pro (1678). The largest gain comes from Presentation, up 293 Elo to 1598, alongside a 120-point improvement in Analytical Quality to 1671 ➤ Lower Cost per Task than Claude Opus 5.5 for comparable overall intelligence: With standard pricing, Gemini 4 Carbon costs $7.76 per Intelligence Index task, ~23% less than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, $10.04) but ~1.2x GPT-6 Astra (max, $6.25). It uses 123k output tokens per task, 29% fewer than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 173k). At the same $4/$20 standard pricing, its Cost per Task is in line with Gemini 4 Argon ($7.68), while scoring 9 points higher on the Intelligence Index ➤ Leading AA-Omniscience v1.1 score, with low hallucination: Gemini 4 Carbon scores 54 on our recently updated AA-Omniscience v1.1, 6 points ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 48) and 8 points ahead of Gemini 4 Argon (46). Accuracy (% correct) rises 10 points over Argon to 58%, while its hallucination rate rises from 4% to 11%. This is still the second lowest of any model, behind only Argon, compared with 50% for both Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max) Key model details: ➤ Context Window: 1M tokens ➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output ➤ Pricing: $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens, the same as Gemini 4 Argon’s standard pricing, with a 50% discount. title: A Health Update
body_text: A Health Update • furbo.org Skip to content furbo.org furbo.org furbo.org info About Me I'm Craig Hockenberry and this is where I write for the web. I make apps and run websites . You can learn more about me , view my rÃ©sumÃ© , check out my source code , or follow me . Search for: Recent Writing A Health Update TipKit for the Real World Spotlight: Not Right Pico Names Your Mac and a Canon Printer The Year That Kicked My Ass Tahoe Electron Detector One Size Does Not Fit All FB19914338 UITabAccessory Backward Compatibility Archives 2026 2025 2024 2023 2022 2021 2020 2019 2018 2017 2016 2015 2014 2013 2012 2011 2010 2009 2008 2007 RSS in XML or JSON © 2026 Craig Hockenberry All rights reserved A Health Update I’m writing this post from a hospital bed. And I couldn’t be happier. You hear folks say chemotherapy sucks, but until you go through it yourself, you don’t really know how bad it can be. It remains a popular activity only because it’s better than the alternative. My first exposure to chemotherapy was with this contraption: a fluoroscope. Lovely to look at, less lovely to lie on. Every week, they used this machine to tap into my spine, extract 5 mg of fluid for analysis, and replace it with 5 mg of methotrexate . There was only a local anesthetic during the procedure and the hardest part was knowing that there was a needle, turned up to eleven, going into my back. It was afterwards that things got dicey: the nerves in your spine float in a thecal sac filled with spinal fluid that acts as a kind of insulator. Since we were exchanging the fluids, it was easy for the levels to get out of balance and for the nerves to react. The result were the worst headaches I’ve ever experienced. The good news is that the remedy was simple: to lie flat on my back to ease the pressure gravity was putting on my spine. That was also the bad news: many days were spent lying prone and trying to avoid boredom. Watching shows and scrolling timelines just doesn’t cut it when that’s all you can do. Thankfully, the spinal headaches subsided quickly when the six-week course of lumbar punctures finished at the end of January. But my body began to face a new challenge: chemotherapy infusions of Bendamustine and Rituximab . Everyone experiences chemotherapy differently. Just as every body is different, so is the reaction to the chemicals that are killing the cancer. The first effect I noticed was in my tastebuds: everything I put in my mouth had a slightly metalic taste, so my eating habits changed. My beloved morning coffee was replaced by tea, food needed a lot less salt, and I started eating a blander diet (cottage cheese with berries remains a favorite). Some people experience nausea and other gastric issues: luckily, I avoided that. I also didn’t have any hair loss, but my normally thick and curly hair lost its body and became lifeless: an external expression of what was happening to me internally. As someone who’s always been active and strong, the biggest overall effect of chemo was losing muscle mass and suffering from overall fatigue. It felt very strange to be weak. I was on a 28 day cycle for my infusions: during the first week I got pumped full of chemicals and then spent three weeks letting my body process them. One of the things they gave me with the infusion on a Tuesday was a dose of steroids that gives the body a boost during the initial onslaught. But by the weekend, that wore off and I felt like shit. It usually took until the middle of the second week before I started feeling human again. I didn’t lose my appetite, but I wasn’t eating more than normal. The problem was my metabolism was working overtime and my calorie intake didn’t adjust. I lost 50 pounds over the course of a couple of months and eventually got to the point where I was having five meals a day. Too bad it all tasted bad. This could also be a graph of my happiness. One thing that I did to fight my diminished capacity was a daily walk. Anyone who exercises regularly knows that there are always plenty of reasons to avoid it: you didn’t sleep well, you have an important project to finish, or you’re sore from a previous workout. When you’re doing chemo, add feeling like absolute shit to that list. I still had nerve damage in my spine, so my “walk” was more like a shuffle. Thankfully my wife found some awesome walking sticks to aid with my balance. They are clearly labelled “Not A Medical Device” but they are my most important medical device. Winter sunsets, exercise, and walking sticks are good medicine. My daily exercise was just like any gym workout: dread at the start, joy at the end. Sometimes there wasn’t much behind that joy: at my lowest point, a walk around the block on flat ground got my heart rate up to 160 bpm. Breathtaking, literally. That low point was in March. In the week following my infusion, where I was already feeling like crap, I came down with a type of pneumonia that affects people with weakened immune systems. I had no strength and my blood oxygen level plummeted below 90%. Getting from the living room to the kitchen for a drink of water felt like running a marathon, and then my Apple Watch pinged to inform me that I was having an episode of atrial fibrillation. It was a lot and I honestly had thoughts of “is this how it ends?” Thankfully, antibiotics battled the pneumonia quickly and the chemo effects subsided. My doctor offered to skip the next cycle of chemotherapy, but I decided to push on. There is only one way to be done with a thing. Throughout all of the infusions, the nerve damage that occurred before the lymphoma discovery didn’t improve. As I said above, my gait and balance were severely compromised: going up and down stairs was particularly challenging. The tingling sensations on my backside and numbness near my abdomen became a bigger concern with each passing month. It wasn’t getting better and I feared it was a permanent condition. I finished the last of my infusions in May and my body slowly started to recover. Food started tasting better, and my strength and stamina started to return. My daily walks got longer: first a quarter of a mile, then half a mile, then a mile, and then something fantastic happened. At the end of a walk around our local state park , I went to grab something in the car glovebox. As I did this, I tilted my head forward and the back of my legs lit up with a feeling I had never felt. Something was changing in my spine: and after a couple of weeks it was clear that this was a sign that the nerves were fixing themselves. Our guess is that the chemotherapy infusions, which attack white blood cells and other parts of the blood that aid in recovery, had retarded the healing in my nervous system. Now that my body had a chance to repair itself, it was. I can now go up and down stairs without hanging on for dear life. I’m able to walk without aid, but I still like my walking sticks for longer outings since they let me push myself harder. I’ve also started working out in a gym with a trainer: I told him about my stair issues, and now he has me doing them backwards and by hopping on all fours. I am so happy to look like a doofus, and for the continued improvement I’m seeing with exercise. My regained ability to walk and a stronger immune system allowed me to leave the house. My first night away from home was a short trip to Topanga Canyon to celebrate an August birthday: All hail the sunflower goddess! After that successful trip, we took a short boat ride to have a nice lunch and look at some kelp . It felt so good to be able to do normal things again. A trip to visit The Blue Forest One lingering part of my life that hasn’t been reestablished is swimming. All the chemotherapy that has been put into my body has been through a port catheter : a small device under my skin that hooks directly into my carotid artery. Getting an infection there would be a very bad thing, and water increases that risk: be it from ocean water full of living organisms or a swimming pool that kids pee in. With the current El NiÃ±o conditions, that’s been a hard thing: the water is warm and “interesting”. My new gym also has a beautiful Olympic-sized pool for lap swimming. I’m happy to be in this hospital bed doing a final stint of chemotherapy because when I’m done, the port is removed. This last procedure is to make sure there is no lymphoma in my brain fluids: not a difficult or dangerous treatment and the side effects are minimal. But it does require close monitoring because of the high dosages involved. In six weeks, I’ll be done and spend the winter in that heated pool so that I can finally swim in my beloved Pacific next summer. The buoys are still there, even though the high surf this summer knocked one out! Last year was hard, and it got worse over time. This year has also been hard, but it’s gotten better with each passing month. For that I’m grateful. I’m also grateful for my wife Lauren: it’s impossible to imagine making it through all of this without her help, support, and encouragement. The silver lining in all this strife is that it’s made our relationship much stronger. Thanks sweetie! As with my previous account , there’s an unwanted coda. No matter how hard I try, there’s a complication at the happy ending! I had typed up everything above as the doctors and nurses prepared me for the first dose of methotrexate. It takes a while for your blood’s pH level to reach a point where the treatment is safe, so I spent much of the day lying in bed, peeing into urine cups, reminiscing about my year, and typing. Around 10:30 PM, the medication was in my brain and I was trying to wind down for the night (easier said than done when part of the regimen includes steroids). While scrolling through Tapestry , I noticed quite a few posts about a newly announced PHP vulnerability. This caught my attention because we use it for our blogs, an ad server, delivering Kickstarter rewards, and a bunch of other small things. (This is the point where family that doesn’t understand what I do for a living continues to not understand what I do for a living.) It quickly became apparent that this was a big deal and something that could allow an attacker access to our server. I had to shut things down before my brain shut down. Thank goodness the steroids held out. After a couple of hours, I had blocked access to PHP processes in every nook & cranny of our server. After sending a quick message to our Slack explaining how everything was broken, I collapsed. The next day started with a head and server that were barely working. Our server was out of LTS, so the first order of business was to get it back onto the latest version of Ubuntu using hospital WiFi. It was a good thing my heart rate and blood pressure were being closely monitored. (Thank goodness for Lish , which proved to be immune to hospital IT shutting down my ssh connection to accept terms & conditions every few hours. There’s also a “I should have my head examined” joke in here somewhere.) If you noticed that the Iconfactory sites were kinda broken last week, now you know why. It’s because I was kinda broken last week. Now I’m finishing this post from a comfy chair on our deck. Typing into the latest version of WordPress and PHP. And I couldn’t be happier. Written on October 28th, 2026 for Miscellaneous Latest

title: Hackers expose the identities of more than 40k DHS employees
body_text: Hackers expose the identities of more than 40,000 DHS employees Text-Only Version Go To Full Site NPR > Immigration Hackers expose the identities of more than 40,000 DHS employees By Vanessa Romo Wednesday, October 28, 2026 • 11:28 PM EDT Heard on Morning Edition A hacking group cracked the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's personnel files, exposing the names, phone numbers and addresses of more than 40,000 DHS agents, operatives, and associates, on Wednesday, including those involved in undercover operations. "On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat.' This is what happens to ICE when you do that," a spokesperson for the hacktivist group behind the breach, the Department of Peace, said in an online statement. The hackers said they stole the data by subverting DHS's single sign on system, according to an online post. It said it distributed that material to the group Distributed Denial of Secrets, which posted it online in a database called Icepick. The Department of Peace also shared the trove of data with Ryan Ottignon, a U.S.-based journalist, and a Swiss activist known as maia arson crimew. Together, the two created a searchable online database, with crimew doing all of the technical work, Ottignon told NPR. DDoSecrets cofounder Emma Best called the leak "extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity," because it makes explicit connections between "officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations …along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs." Other activists say the information will be a boon to those investigating DHS and filing freedom of information requests, which, due to a lack of specific information, like names, email addresses, can often yield useless results. In a statement, DHS said it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The department added that it is taking necessary steps to "ensure all are properly protected." More than 21,000 records identify employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Another 10,000 relate to Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees and its Homeland Security Investigations unit. It is an unprecedented breach of intelligence, coming on the heels of similar hacking attacks at the FBI. However, the database is far from comprehensive and represents about a fifth of Homeland Security's workforce, which staffs a little more than 220,000 people. Ottignon, who has worked on similar data leak projects in the past, rejected suggestions that he and others connected to the Department of Peace or Distribution Denials of Secrets were doxing government employees. "We are in a situation in which a group of public officials go around into cities and states and all around the country, and they seek to hide who they are. Very frequently using masks, wearing plain clothes. And they do universally unspeakable things to these communities," Ottignon said. He added that he believed that kind of behavior is unacceptable in a free society. "We need oversight for useful government, if it exists at all. So this is just one step in that oversight process," he added. In a note attached to the files, the Department of Peace wrote, "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs." Transcript LEILA FADEL, HOST: Hackers have exposed the identities of tens of thousands of Department of Homeland Security employees. That includes their names, email addresses and phone numbers. NPR immigration correspondent Vanessa Romo is covering this and joins me now. Good morning, Vanessa. VANESSA ROMO, BYLINE: Good morning, Leila. FADEL: So tell us about the scope of this breach. ROMO: Well, this is a massive breach of intelligence for the government. So there is a lot of information out there. The stolen data set includes contact information for more than 41,000 DHS agents, operatives and associates, including those involved in undercover operations. And of those, more than 21,000 records identify employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Another 10,000 unmask the identities of Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees and people in Homeland Security Investigations units. And about 1,000 show people who work for the cybersecurity defense agency. That and all - a ton more are available in a searchable database. But the really interesting thing about the way the online tool works is that every personnel file includes the names of supervisors and direct reports. So you can actually follow the chain of command, which we haven't been able to see before in such an explicit way. FADEL: A lot of information there. How did the hackers get ahold of it? ROMO: A group of hacktivists calling themselves the Department of Peace said that they obtained the data by subverting DHS' single sign-on system. They then handed all of that raw data over to a group called Distributed Denial of Secrets - or DDoS - which partnered with a Swiss activist who goes by maia arson crimew. And that's who actually created the searchable website that's now available to the public. FADEL: And did they say - these hackers say why they did this? ROMO: In a note that was attached to the data, the Department of Peace basically said that it was to level the playing field. They said, quote, "they have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs." Meanwhile, DDoS and other activists involved said that they did it as a public service so that anyone who was investigating the department can file more complete freedom of information requests. FADEL: What about the argument that this can put ICE officers and others in danger? ROMO: I spoke to Ryan Ottignon, a journalist who worked with the Swiss activist, crimew, to build that searchable database. And he pushed back on that idea that this was doxing. RYAN OTTIGNON: We are in a situation in which a group of public officials go around the country, and they seek to hide who they are, very frequently using masks, and they do universally unspeakable things to these communities. ROMO: He's referring to ICE shooting and killing Americans and noncitizens. FADEL: Now, DHS has been aggressive about protecting ICE agents' identities. What has it said about the hack? ROMO: So in a statement, DHS officials said the department was, quote, "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." They also said that they're taking necessary steps to ensure that everyone is properly protected. And as you mentioned, the Trump administration has pushed back against people publicly naming ICE agents and has regularly said that those who dox ICE officers will be prosecuted to the full extent of the law. FADEL: That's NPR's Vanessa Romo. Thank you, Vanessa. ROMO: Thank you, Leila. Correction Oct. 29th, 2026 A previous version of this story misattributed the quote, "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs," to the DDoS. It was written by the Department of Peace. Topics News Culture Music Contact Us Terms of Use Permissions Privacy Policy &copy NPR

title: Three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics
body_text: Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding | OpenAI Skip to main content Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Log in Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Login OpenAI October 26, 2026 Research Publication Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding Loading… Share Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false Existence of quantum chromodynamics and completions of the Standard Model Supporting scientists Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false Existence of quantum chromodynamics and completions of the Standard Model Supporting scientists We are announcing three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics about harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory. Our release process continues to evolve in response to feedback from the associated academic communities. In our view, these manuscripts are best understood as a form of raw research data. To convert this raw research data into scientific understanding, in this release we are experimenting with a new approach. We reached out to external experts and asked them to act as shepherds, organizing groups to understand the new results. They advised three different release strategies: For the math result, release the AI output, leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result. For the computer science result, form an external group of collaborators to explain the result, while making the AI output publicly available for anyone to examine and build on. For the physics result, form an external group of collaborators and defer to them on the release of materials. We do not yet know which of these three approaches will be most useful, and we welcome feedback on what works and what we can improve. The external collaborations will follow four principles: Transparency. We are transparent about the existence of our collaborations. Participants will not be asked to sign nondisclosure agreements and will be free to discuss the work, share intermediate products, and publish their conclusions. No Academic Credit. We do not seek academic credit for the discoveries produced by our internal models. Inviting a researcher to help steward a collaboration also does not imply that they or their working group made the original discovery. Recognition. This group should receive recognition for the understanding they develop, the writeups they author, and the other materials they create. The group will also help ensure that the work appropriately credits researchers, techniques, and ideas that it draws on. Independence. Participation is voluntary and unpaid. Working-group members participate independently, and their conclusions are their own. They do not speak on behalf of OpenAI, and OpenAI does not speak on their behalf. We will turn over materials and artifacts related to these results to the collaborations. For the computer science collaboration, the group has decided to make the natural language proof and Lean formalization public immediately, and we are publishing them directly to our GitHub repository. For the physics collaboration, the group has decided to hold off on releasing the AI-produced artifacts and instead work on writing it up themselves. All of these approaches involve tradeoffs. On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community. On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful. Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture The result in mathematics concerns harmonic analysis. In 1991, Sogge proposed the local smoothing conjecture, which concerns the behavior of waves as they become focused. In particular, the conjecture states that the most extreme focusing must be short-lived. The amount of focusing at a typical random time is always much smaller than what can happen at the worst-case time. This is a familiar pattern throughout mathematics: what can happen in the worst case is more extreme than what is observed after averaging. Because of how fundamental this conjectured phenomenon is, it also has wide ranging implications throughout mathematical analysis. For instance, it implies the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture. In 2019, Guth, Wang, and Zhang ⁠ (opens in a new window) proved the local smoothing conjecture in two spatial dimensions. In 2025, Wang and Zahl ⁠ (opens in a new window) proved the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions. Our models produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions. The new proof is based on a novel auxiliary partial differential equation. We obtained our AI output on October 18th, 2026, which was formalized in Lean the following day, and then we reached out to an expert to discuss forming a collaboration around this result. Following their recommendation, we decided to release the AI output publicly, following the same strategy for this result as our October 6th, 2026 release ⁠ . We have released both an AI natural language output writeup ⁠ (opens in a new window) produced by our models and a Lean proof ⁠ (opens in a new window) in our public GitHub repository. The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture about the computational complexity of Boolean formula satisfiability, a problem deeply related to the P vs. NP problem. The ETH has been widely believed to be true, and has been used in hundreds of papers to derive conditional computational hardness results across a wide variety of fields including graph theory, computational biology, databases, computational geometry, and more. Surprisingly, our system has recently proved that the ETH is false, a result that was subsequently verified in Lean. The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become, and may help guide the search for better algorithms. Finding such algorithms, and turning theoretical advances into practical improvements, will require significant further research. This work will be verified and shepherded by a group led by Russell Impagliazzo (UC San Diego), Ramamohan Paturi (UC San Diego), and Ryan Williams (MIT). All three are experts in algorithm design and complexity theory. Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with Francis Zane, are the original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and have authored a number ⁠ (opens in a new window) of influential ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) papers ⁠ (opens in a new window) on the topic ⁠ (opens in a new window) over the last 30 years. Williams has refuted strong ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) versions ⁠ (opens in a new window) of the ETH, used ETH for hardness ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) results ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and connected algorithms ⁠ (opens in a new window) and lower bounds ⁠ (opens in a new window) . We have agreed to the group’s requests that all raw data of the results be made public to facilitate independent verification by the community, and that OpenAI commit to funding a conference to understand the implications of this work on the field as a whole. The group invites the community to help organize an open examination of the ETH claim and to discuss the broader questions that AI-generated breakthroughs raise about verification, access, credit, and the future of research. Our AI found its natural language disproof for the ETH on October 16th, 2026 and then subsequently we formalized the result in Lean on October 17th, 2026, which led us to develop the collaboration described here. To that end, we have released both an AI natural language output writeup ⁠ (opens in a new window) produced by our models and a Lean proof ⁠ (opens in a new window) in our public GitHub repository. Computational complexity has many open questions and conjectures, whose proofs or refutations have so far eluded the best efforts of scientists. We hope that humans with AI can provide new understanding in this field, and shed light on the inherent capabilities and limits of efficient computation. Existence of quantum chromodynamics and completions of the Standard Model The physics collaboration will understand and explain a result that gives a mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics. Our work builds on Balaban’s approach ⁠ (opens in a new window) in constructive quantum field theory. As a subproblem, this work also includes a proof of the existence of pure Yang–Mills theory, which is part of the Quantum Yang–Mills Theory Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize problem ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The Standard Model describes the interaction of fundamental subatomic particles for three of the four fundamental forces, excepting gravity. The existence proof pertains to the simplest grand unified theory that includes the gauge fields and fermions of the Standard Model (as the Standard Model itself cannot be extrapolated to arbitrarily short distances). QCD describes the interaction of particles such as quarks and gluons via the strong force. Pure Yang–Mills theory only describes the self-interactions of the gluons, the force carriers, rather than matter such as quarks. David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov that will shepherd this work. Gross’s 1973 work on asymptotic freedom in Yang-Mills theories helped establish QCD as the theory of the strong interactions and earned him a share of the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physics ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Asymptotic freedom is also the key mechanism underlying the existence of these theories as mathematically rigorous objects. Jaffe formulated the Quantum Yang-Mills Theory Millenium Prize problem ⁠ (opens in a new window) with Witten and also envisioned the idea of Millennium Prize problems and co-founded the Clay Mathematics Institute. Douglas has already been a steward of this problem over the last 20 years, reporting on its status in 2004 ⁠ (opens in a new window) and then providing a comprehensive update on the progress ⁠ (opens in a new window) at the beginning of this year. Klebanov helped pioneer the application of gauge–string duality to confinement, an important property of QCD, and now directs the Simons Collaboration on Confinement and QCD Strings ⁠ (opens in a new window) , Nekrasov has done groundbreaking work on exact methods for generalizations of Yang–Mills theory and won the Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics in 2023. The group requests that all communications with any and all members of the group regarding this effort be directed to the following email account: YANGMILLS4D@gmail.com. Our models produced a natural language proof for Yang–Mills existence on September 9th, 2026, and then subsequently produced a proof for QCD on September 18th, 2026. Given the length and complexity of the work, we postponed release until the Lean formalization completed. We finished our formalization of Yang–Mills’ existence on October 16th, 2026, which led us to develop the collaboration described here. We hope that these results mark the beginning of a transition in which quantum field theory, the most important framework in modern theoretical physics, becomes a mathematically rigorous field. We are excited to provide resources for academic-led progress towards that goal. Supporting scientists We are committed to supporting the broader work of understanding and building on these results. These collaborations complement our recently announced $5 million contribution ⁠ (opens in a new window) to a new Simons Foundation initiative. Managed and awarded by the Simons Foundation, that funding will support workshops, conferences, and special programs to help researchers understand and build on results produced by AI. We are committed to ensuring funding for researchers to independently examine, explain, and build on the results above. We continue to invite feedback on the best way to disclose results and engage with scientists to accelerate discovery. 2026 Author OpenAI Keep reading View all Sharing AI progress in mathematics Research Oct 6, 2026 Advisory group on mathematics and artificial intelligence Company Sep 21, 2026 Using thousands of AI agents to uncover new leads in biological data Publication Oct 21, 2026 Research Research Index Research Overview Economic Research Latest Advancements GPT-6.1 Sol GPT-6 Astra GPT-5.6 GPT-5.5 Safety Safety Approach Deployment Safety (opens in a new window) Security & Privacy Trust & Transparency Products ChatGPT (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Business (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Enterprise (opens in a new window) ChatGPT for Education (opens in a new window) Codex Dots (opens in a new window) Release Notes API Platform Overview API Log In (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Business Overview Solutions Resources Plugins Customer Stories Partner Network Contact Sales Developers Plugins (opens in a new window) Models (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Resources (opens in a new window) Developer Forum (opens in a new window) Company About Us Our Charter Careers News Support Help Center (opens in a new window) OpenAI Status (opens in a new window) More Stories Academy Supply Co. title: Survival LLM: AI assistant and emergency library that runs on your own computer
body_text: Survival LLM An AI that still works when the internet doesn't. Survival LLM is a free AI assistant and emergency library that runs entirely on your own computer. Ask it how to keep food safe in a blackout, treat a burn, or purify water, and it answers from trusted sources and shows you exactly where each answer came from. Download for Mac 212 MB Download for Windows 25 MB Source code Free and open source. Set it up while you have internet; after that it needs none. What it does Works with no internet The AI model and the library live on your computer. Nothing you ask leaves it. Shows its sources Every answer lists the articles it read. Click one to read it yourself, with the exact passage highlighted. Made for emergencies Medical references, FEMA and CDC guidance, survival manuals, how-to guides, repair guides and about 930,000 Wikipedia articles. Pick your version The app is the same everywhere. When it opens, it checks your computer's memory and downloads the AI model that fits. More memory means a smarter model. Your computer AI model it uses Our emergency test Model download Mac with 128 GB or more memory NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super 21 of 22 right 80 GB Mac with 32–96 GB Qwen3.8 27B 21 of 22 right 18 GB Windows PC with 32 GB or more NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 19 of 22 right 25 GB Mac or PC with 16–31 GB IBM Granite 4.2 8B 14 of 22 right 6 GB "Right" means it got the main point of official guidance right on 22 blackout and first-aid questions, graded blind, in our tests on an earlier build of the library ( how we tested ). Smaller models make more mistakes, so the app always shows the source to check. Plus the library: a 9 GB download for everything (19 GB once installed), or 1.3 GB (3 GB installed) without Wikipedia and iFixit. Free disk space needed: the model's size plus 5 GB, plus about 27 GB while the full library installs (10 GB for the smaller one). Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or newer) with macOS 14 Sonoma or newer, and 64-bit Windows 10 or 11. Set it up in three steps Setup takes 20 minutes to about 2½ hours, depending on your computer and your internet speed. You only click for about 5 minutes; the rest is downloading. Download Survival LLM for Mac or Windows and unzip it. On Windows, right-click the zip and choose Extract All . Open it. On a Mac, double-click Survival LLM . On Windows, open the extracted folder and double-click Survival LLM.bat . Follow the setup. Pick a library and an AI model on one screen (the best model for your computer is already picked) and click Download . The app downloads the model, the library and, on Windows, the AI engine (it's built into the Mac app). If your internet drops or you quit, it picks up where it left off. Let it finish while you're online. The first time you open it, your computer warns you, because the app isn't sold through an app store. Mac: click Done , open System Settings > Privacy & Security , scroll down to "Survival LLM was blocked", click Open Anyway and confirm with your password. You only do this once. Windows: click More info , then Run anyway . What's in the library Plain-text copies of openly licensed (some for non-commercial use only) and public-domain references, searchable in a fraction of a second: About 930,000 of Wikipedia's most-read articles WikiMed medical encyclopedia MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) UK Medicines A to Z (public sector information) WikEM emergency medicine Ready.gov (FEMA) emergency guides CDC travelers' health U.S. military medicine and survival manuals Risk references for estimating micromorts: life tables and U.S. death rates wikiHow how-to guides iFixit repair guides Appropedia (appropriate technology) Q&A on home repair, cooking, gardening, the outdoors and ham radio (Stack Exchange) Each source keeps its own license, shown with every article; see the full list with licenses . Good to know It can be wrong AI models make mistakes, the small ones more often. Every answer shows the articles it used, so you can check. Private No account, no tracking. Your questions never leave your computer, and once set up it works with the internet off. Your own files Add PDFs, Word documents, ebooks and notes, like your generator's manual or your family's emergency plan, and the AI searches them too. They stay on your computer. Updates Check for updates, at the bottom of the app, installs a new version in one click and keeps your models, library and files. Battery On a MacBook Pro we measured about 100 W while it answers, for 5 to 40 seconds per question: a full battery answers roughly 100 to 300. A small generator or power station runs it easily. Update notes Already have it? Click Check for updates at the bottom of the app. 0.4.1 October 29, 2026 Windows: on a PC without Microsoft's free WebView2, which the app window needs, the app now installs it with Microsoft's own installer (a minute or so, the first time) instead of opening as a broken page. Thanks to Dueynkol for the report and the screenshot. 0.4.0 October 29, 2026 Simpler first-time setup: one screen to pick the library and the AI model, with the best model for your computer already picked. While it downloads, you see the speed and the time left for each part. It keeps the computer awake, retries by itself when the internet drops, and picks up where it left off if you quit. Switch libraries: click the article count at the top (or Search library , then Switch or move the library ) to change between Essentials and Everything. Your library keeps working while the other one downloads. Thanks to jubishop for the idea. Choose where things live: move the library to another folder or an external drive, and pick which folder Your files searches. New installs keep the library out of sight in the app's own folder; existing ones stay where they are. Thanks to Kronopath and remjax. A cleaner library: both libraries were rebuilt without about 2,700 repeated pages, so searches show more different articles. If you already have one, the app offers the new version (1.3 GB for Essentials, 8.7 GB for Everything), and yours keeps working until it's in. Thanks to ahalekelly. If a model download fails because an older Ollama app is running on your computer, the app now says so and what to do, and the message fits on screen. Thanks to zackbloom. Smaller fixes: a reply to "remember this" or "forget that" no longer gets a Sources line, a made-up article title next to a real collection's name is caught, and an answer that never finished no longer says "reasoning before it answered". 0.3.4 October 27, 2026 Reasoning setting: next to Send, choose how much the AI may think before it answers: Off, 1,000, 4,000 or 16,000 tokens, or no limit. At the limit its thinking stops and it answers from what it has, so a model stuck reasoning in circles still answers. It replaces "Think harder". When the AI looked things up but never wrote an answer, it now gets the best articles it found and tries once more, instead of showing nothing. Thanks to betsyisaac for finding this. Ask it to look something up and it searches the library, even if it first answered from memory. Answers say whether they came from memory, from articles it read, or from search results it didn't open. A warning when Reasoning or Length limit is set to no limit. 0.3.3 October 27, 2026 Mac: quitting with Cmd+Q now also stops the AI engine and frees the memory its model used. Before, it kept running in the background. Thanks to wigginthethird for the report and the fix. Library search no longer shows several copies of the same page, so the AI sees more different articles. Thanks to ahalekelly. 0.3.2 October 27, 2026 The AI no longer saves your question as a memory note. Some answers no longer open with a made-up "Sources:" line that listed the AI's search commands instead of articles. Show reasoning reads more clearly: it says when you stopped it, the time shown is how long it thought, and long reasoning scrolls with the page. Windows: cleans up an empty folder that earlier updates could leave behind. 0.3.1 October 27, 2026 Show reasoning: under each answer, open what the AI thought before it answered, with the searches and articles it read in between. It stays hidden until you click it. Most models reason first only when Think harder is ticked. 0.3.0 October 26, 2026 Memory: tell it about yourself, like a family member's allergy or the generator you own, and it keeps a short note for later chats. See and edit every note under Memory , or turn its saving off. Downloads now work on computers whose network or antivirus uses its own certificates. All releases on GitHub Survival LLM is open source (MIT license). Code, library tools and source attributions: GitHub .

Emacs Turns 50
body_text: EMACS turns 50 | MIT Technology Review You need to enable JavaScript to view this site. Skip to Content Menu MIT Technology Review MIT Technology Review The Big Story Artificial intelligence Biotech & health Climate & energy 10 Breakthrough Technologies AI Hype Index The Impossible issue Menu MIT Technology Review MIT Technology Review The Big Story Artificial intelligence Biotech & health Climate & energy 10 Breakthrough Technologies AI Hype Index The Impossible issue MIT Alumni News: 1865 EMACS turns 50 How the MIT AI Lab’s text editor gave birth to the free software movement. By Simson Garfinkel ’87, PhD ’05 archive page October 20, 2026 Artwork from Richard Stallman’s 1981 EMACS manual. Later iterations of the manual featured cover art of a medieval knight riding a yak. The complex yet playful illustrations captured the hacker culture of the era. Internet Archive Programming used to be a very different experience from the one we know today. In fact, the first programmers didn’t write code at all; the six women who worked on the ENIAC, one of the world’s first computers, at the University of Pennsylvania in 1946 did it by physically configuring switches, cables, and plugboards. A few years later, MIT engineers programmed the Whirlwind by punching code onto paper tape that was then loaded into the computer’s memory—making it among the first “stored-program” machines. Later, they and others moved on to punch cards, one for each line of code. By the early 1960s, programmers with interactive computers could use a “line editor” to type their code on teletypes—large, noisy keyboard-and-printer machines. They’d type one line of code at a time, and their work would be saved on a spinning hard disk the size of a modern washing machine. But there was still no such thing as the now-familiar full-screen text editors that allow programmers to see and modify many lines at a time on a display. One of the first such tools, EMACS, turns 50 this year, and it is still widely used. EMACS first ran on the early video terminals at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1976, but its core concepts were so powerful that it was rewritten for many operating systems in the decades that followed. Apple even distributed it with Mac OS X. Beyond that, the software-­sharing community that started around EMACS helped give rise to the modern-day free software movement and the GNU/Linux operating system. EMACS’s roots begin with the TECO text editor (originally the “Tape Editor and Corrector”) that Dan Murphy ’65 created in 1962 for the pioneering PDP-1 computer at MIT. The program’s commands were uppercase letters: A user would type “I” to insert text, “D” to delete a character, and so on. When tape gave way as a storage medium to files on a huge shared disk, the “T” in “TECO” came to stand for “Text.” And as years passed, TECO became a full language that programmers could use to create new commands, called macros, for editing their code. In the fall of 1971, Carl Mikkelsen ’76 created Control-R, an add-on program for TECO that took advantage of “glass teletype” terminals with video displays. Control-R immediately displayed changes to the file being edited on screen; the programmer no longer needed to reprint each line to see the changes. The drawback: The display could show only a few lines of code at a time. “Experienced and sophisticated users found EMACS to be eminently more usable than any of the previous forms of editing.” Bernard S. Greenberg, SM ’74 Then, in 1976, Richard M. Stallman, a researcher at the MIT AI Lab, saw a full-screen editor—called E—on a visit to Stanford’s AI Lab. Inspired, he returned to MIT and set out to improve Control-R. The most important change to the program’s underlying structure: Every key ran its own macro when pressed, making Control-R far easier to customize. The lab’s hackers took to Stallman’s code with gusto and started changing and adding commands. That created an issue for Guy Steele Jr., SM ’77, PhD ’80. A graduate student in the lab, Steele frequently needed to help other lab members debug their programs. “I noticed that it was much harder for me to help someone who was using one of these packages rather than straight TECO,” he recalls. “Eventually, it occurred to me to try [to] broker consensus on a standard set of Control-R commands that everyone could agree to use.” David Moon ’75, another member of the lab, helped out. Stallman jumped in as well, and eventually he took over. Together, the group assigned a standard set of commands that made use of the Meta key found on many of the lab’s early keyboards: Meta-F would move the cursor forward a word, Meta-B would move it back a word, and so on. They called the result EMACS, short for “Editor Macros” or “Editing Macros.” “My goal was not to construct a great new text editor,” says Steele. “I was trying to address a social problem.” Nevertheless, EMACS was a great new text editor. Whereas Control-R could be tricky, EMACS users with “no technical experience at all” could learn to edit letters, emails, and even programs “within minutes or an hour,” according to a history by Bernard S. Greenberg, SM ’74. Meanwhile, “experienced and sophisticated users found EMACS to be eminently more usable than any of the previous forms of editing.” Stallman started distributing EMACS to anyone who sent him a magnetic tape and a postage-paid return envelope. “EMACS does not cost anything; instead, you are joining the EMACS software-sharing commune,” he wrote in the 1981 manual. “The conditions of membership are that you must send back any improvements you make to EMACS.” Programming manuals for the Multics operating system. While working at Honeywell, Bernard S. Greenberg wrote his own version of EMACS for the system. It was so good, Honeywell commercialized it. MIT MUSEUM Greenberg, meanwhile, decided to write his own version for Multics, an early operating system by that time owned by his employer, Honeywell. Greenberg’s EMACS won first prize at the International Honeywell Software Conference in 1980, and Honeywell started selling it. Honeywell wasn’t alone in marketing a version of EMACS: James Arthur Gosling, a Carnegie Mellon graduate who went on to lead the development of the Java programming language, made a version that he eventually sold as a commercial product. This transition from free to paid software ultimately spurred Stallman to launch a project to create an operating system that could be freely shared and improved by its users. He modeled this effort, called the GNU Project, after the increasingly popular Unix operating system from Bell Labs. “GNU” was short for “GNU’s Not Unix,” alluding to the fact that, unlike Unix, it would be free. The project’s first major application was GNU Emacs (now restyled in lowercase). The GNU/Linux operating system was still years away, so, despite the project’s aim to create an entirely free operating system, GNU Emacs initally ran on Unix. It would eventually run on a range of operating systems, including Linux but also other Unix-based systems. When Apple launched Mac OS X, the first release of its Unix-based operating system, in 2001, GNU Emacs was included. Apple stopped shipping GNU Emacs in 2019, but the company still has a program called mg (“Micro GNU Emacs”). Though it supports most EMACS commands, it lacks an integrated programming language, making it what some call an “ersatz EMACS.” Meanwhile, much of Apple’s OS still has hidden support for EMACS commands. The keyboard has no Meta key, but Control-Option-B will move back one word, and Control-Option-F will move one forward. by Simson Garfinkel ’87, PhD ’05 Share Share story on linkedin Share story on facebook Share story on email MIT Alumni News Made by MIT This story was part of our November/December 2026 issue.
